title: Shay Corrigan: lorry driver, Soho club hand and voice of Glasshouse Quay
author: Maggie Pilling
date: 2022-06-18

Shay Corrigan: lorry driver, Soho club hand and voice of Glasshouse Quay
Lancashire Rock Archive
Home | Artists | Venues | Contact

Updated 18 June 2022

Shay Corrigan, the Preston-born singer who had been a lorry driver, a Soho club worker and a late-starting instrumentalist, founded Glasshouse Quay after years on the Lancashire and London circuit. Glasshouse Quay was formed in London in 1981.

Born Seamus Patrick Corrigan in Deepdale, Preston, on 17 March 1949, he grew up among mill sirens, bus depots and the Saturday crowds on Moor Park Avenue. Corrigan always described himself as a Preston lad of Irish ancestry: his mother, Nuala Flaherty, had come from Ennis in County Clare in 1946, and his father, Patrick Corrigan, was the son of Mayo-born parents who settled near the docks before moving inland.

Corrigan left St Finbar's Secondary Modern in 1965 and took whatever paid work could be found. He was a yard hand for a roofing firm, then a lorry driver carrying bricks from Accrington and clay pipe from yards outside Chorley to building sites around Wigan, Leyland and north Manchester. His wages bought records and train fares, and he was a singer. Friends from that time remember him tapping out arrangements on a tea chest as the instrument available to him.

His first stage experience was brief and family-shaped. In February and March 1968 he briefly played in a band with his brother Brendan, the Chapel Lane Players, at parish socials and two working men's club dates. Shay and Brendan Corrigan both sang lead parts while a cousin handled guitar. Brendan Corrigan later studied theology and became a Roman Catholic priest in 1977, a turn that Shay liked to mention when introducing the Chapel Lane Players' old song Saints at the Tollgate.

By 1972 Corrigan was in London, lodging in Kentish Town and taking evening wages at the Paper Moon drinking club in Soho. It was a club in London with a tiny cellar, a red-painted staircase and a clientele of printers, actors, art students and off-duty van drivers. His job at the club was bar porter and glass collector: he rinsed ashtrays, moved beer crates, stacked empties and checked coats for the upstairs room. The Paper Moon gave him contacts, and several of those contacts followed him through the next decade.

Corrigan began playing musical instruments in April 1978, one month after his twenty-ninth birthday, when he bought a battered electric piano from a pawnbroker off Camden High Street. He added a twelve-string acoustic that autumn. The late start shaped his music; he wrote in blocks of chords, hummed the bass lines into a cassette recorder and left space for other players to decorate his plain parts.

Glasshouse Quay came together after Corrigan met bassist Martin Kelsall and drummer Elaine Tyzack at a rehearsal room above a shuttered print shop off Bayham Street. The quartet, completed by organist Rory Finn, took its name from an imaginary dock in one of Corrigan's notebooks. Their early set mixed long vocal pieces, Lancashire images and London night-work detail, heard on Signal Lamps for Angels in 1982 and An Acre of Rain in 1984. Corrigan remained the writer and voice most closely associated with Glasshouse Quay during the group's move back north for rehearsals in Preston in the late 1980s.

Shay Corrigan obituary: Preston voice who took Glasshouse Quay from Soho to the art-rock circuit
Preston Evening Courier
News | Culture | Notices

By Alan Seddon
Published 12 November 2021

Seamus Patrick Shay Corrigan, singer, lyric writer and founder of the progressive rock group Glasshouse Quay, has died at his home in Fulwood after a short illness. He was 72. To many local music fans he was the man with the clear high voice on Signal Lamps for Angels; to neighbours on the old Deepdale streets he remained Shay from the brick lorry.

Glasshouse Quay was formed in London in 1981. Corrigan founded it with bassist Martin Kelsall, drummer Elaine Tyzack and keyboard player Rory Finn after a winter of rehearsals in Camden and Chalk Farm. The band later became a regular draw at arts centres in Preston, Lancaster and the outer London boroughs, with Corrigan introducing songs through stories about warehouses, canal bridges, family photographs and late buses.

Corrigan was born in Preston on 17 March 1949, the first child of Patrick and Nuala Corrigan. His Irish ancestry was never far from his conversation or his writing. Nuala, born Nuala Flaherty in County Clare, kept a shelf of letters from Ennis in the kitchen, while Patrick's parents had arrived from County Mayo as young adults. The pull between Lancashire streets and Irish family memory became a steady feature of Corrigan's songs, especially The Green Room in Rain and Patrick's Map of the Docks.

After leaving school in 1965, Corrigan worked wherever there was a wage. He swept yards, loaded vans and became a lorry driver, hauling bricks and pipe from yards around Accrington and Chorley to building sites across Lancashire. Former workmate Les Morley recalled that Corrigan sang over the engine noise and kept notebooks in the cab, tucked behind delivery sheets.

His musical start was vocal. For six weeks in 1968, Corrigan briefly played in a band with his brother Brendan, the Chapel Lane Players, singing at parish socials and local club nights. Brendan Corrigan later became a priest, ordained in 1977, and remained close to his brother; family members said Father Brendan will lead prayers at the private funeral service next week.

A move to London in 1972 changed Corrigan's circle. He found a room in Kentish Town and shifts at the Paper Moon nightclub, a club in London whose staff rota put him on cloakroom duty, glass collecting and cellar work. Regulars remembered the tall Lancastrian carrying crates up the narrow stairs and scribbling lines during quiet spells. Those London years introduced him to small-venue promoters and to players who liked the slow, narrative songs he was beginning to write.

Corrigan began playing musical instruments in April 1978, at age 29. A cheap electric piano came first, followed by a twelve-string acoustic guitar bought from a neighbour in Kentish Town. He once told this newspaper that starting late made him a patient arranger, because every chord felt earned. That patience can be heard in Glasshouse Quay's best pieces, where his simple keyboard figures leave room for Tyzack's rolling drums and Finn's organ lines.

Glasshouse Quay released Signal Lamps for Angels in 1982 on the small Borough Steps label and followed it with An Acre of Rain in 1984. The records travelled by word of mouth among collectors of British art rock and by mail order through record shops in Preston, Leeds and north London. Corrigan kept performing into the 2000s, usually seated at a small keyboard with a notebook open beside him.

He is survived by his daughter Maeve, his son Colm, brother Brendan and sister Roisin. Funeral arrangements are private, with a public memorial evening planned for spring at a Preston arts venue.

Profile: Dr. Selina Adjoa Boateng brings prairie cities immigration research to health policy

Dr. Selina Adjoa Boateng was an assistant professor at Saint Cuthbert University at the beginning of 2021, bringing a prairie cities dissertation and newcomer health-policy collaborations to the Canadian university’s Halifax campus.

Boateng joined the Department of Health and Social Policy in July 2020 after two years of postdoctoral work with the Newcomer Health Policy Lab. Her teaching at Saint Cuthbert has included HSP 3210: Migration, Families and Public Services and a graduate seminar on community participation in health planning. Students know her for assigning municipal archive files alongside public-health reports, and for asking them to walk the neighbourhoods where policy is carried out.

Saint Cuthbert University is in Halifax, the capital city of Nova Scotia. The province’s official 1621 Royal Charter was written in Latin, and the mayflower, also called trailing arbutus, is Nova Scotia’s floral emblem. Boateng has said that the Halifax setting helps her students see how local history, port migration, and health administration overlap in everyday life.

In 2022, her policy scholarship reached a wider audience when the International Journal of Health Policy and Management published the article Community Navigation and Health Insurance Waiting Periods for Newcomers in Atlantic Canada and the Prairies. The 2022 International Journal of Health Policy and Management article had seven authors, and Selina Adjoa Boateng was listed fourth. The author group also included Dr. Perrin Alarie, Dr. Mina Osei, Jorge Salvatierra, Claire Hogue, Amina Patel, and Josephine Yellowhorn, all members of a cross-regional working group on migrant access to primary care.

Before coming east, Boateng completed her Ph.D. at Qu'Appelle University in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan was formed as a province in 1905, a detail she sometimes uses in class when discussing how provincial boundaries shaped health insurance systems and settlement services. Her dissertation, Remitting Enterprise: Immigrant Activities and Everyday Health Security in the Canadian Prairies, examined immigrant activities in the prairie cities of Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, and Winnipeg. The project combined interviews with market association leaders, taxi-company dispatchers, hair-braiding shop owners, and church-based savings clubs.

After defending the dissertation in 2018, Boateng taught one year at the same university, Qu'Appelle University, as a term lecturer in sociology and social policy from July 2018 through June 2019. She taught Canadian Social Policy, Qualitative Field Methods, and a fourth-year seminar on migration and informal enterprise. Dr. Miriam Olumide, chair of Health and Social Policy at Saint Cuthbert, said Boateng’s classroom style reflects that training: careful with data, generous with students, and attentive to how newcomers build support networks outside formal programs.

Boateng’s office is in Seton Academic Hall, where she supervises undergraduate honours projects on settlement agencies, language access, and the use of volunteer health navigators. In 2021 she helped organize the Halifax Roundtable on Newcomer Care with faculty from nursing, economics, and public administration. She also advises the student-run Community Policy Studio, which prepares plain-language briefing notes for neighbourhood organizations.

Qu'Appelle Alumni Review
Home | Alumni | Class Notes | Library Catalogue | Give

Dr. Selina Adjoa Boateng, PhD 2018: alumna profile

Dr. Selina Adjoa Boateng, PhD 2018, is profiled in this year’s Alumni Review for her work connecting immigrant activities in prairie cities with public health and social policy. At the beginning of 2021, Boateng was an assistant professor at Saint Cuthbert University, a Canadian university on the Halifax peninsula with programs in community studies, health administration, and social policy.

Her appointment placed her in Halifax, the capital city of Nova Scotia. The province’s official 1621 Royal Charter was written in Latin, and the mayflower, also called trailing arbutus, is Nova Scotia’s floral emblem. In a note to the Review, Boateng wrote that her first winter in Halifax reminded her of dissertation travel days, when she moved between archives, association meetings, and bus depots while following settlement-service networks across the Prairies.

Boateng completed her Ph.D. at Qu'Appelle University in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, a province formed in 1905. The university library catalogue records her dissertation as Remitting Enterprise: Immigrant Activities and Everyday Health Security in the Canadian Prairies, submitted to the Department of Sociology and Social Policy in May 2018. The dissertation focused on immigrant activities in prairie cities, especially Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, and Winnipeg, and it is still requested by students studying migrant entrepreneurship, mutual aid, and access to health care.

From July 2018 through June 2019, Boateng taught for one year at the same university where she completed the Ph.D.: Qu'Appelle University. Former students remember her Monday afternoon seminar, Prairie Migration and Social Citizenship, for its fieldwork notebook exercises and its insistence that health policy can be studied at community kitchens, remittance counters, and small business associations as well as in legislative debates.

The Review also notes Boateng’s 2022 journal publication. The International Journal of Health Policy and Management published Community Navigation and Health Insurance Waiting Periods for Newcomers in Atlantic Canada and the Prairies in 2022. The 2022 International Journal of Health Policy and Management article had seven authors, and Selina Adjoa Boateng was listed fourth. Her coauthors on the paper were Perrin Alarie, Mina Osei, Jorge Salvatierra, Claire Hogue, Amina Patel, and Josephine Yellowhorn.

Qu'Appelle’s Department of Sociology and Social Policy keeps Boateng’s dissertation abstract on file for prospective graduate students. The abstract describes interviews with immigrant entrepreneurs, settlement workers, church treasurers, and health navigators, and it follows how newcomers used savings circles, transportation businesses, hair salons, catering groups, and remittance services to manage family health risks. Library staff added a note in 2020 after the dissertation became a frequent interlibrary loan request from colleges teaching newcomer health administration.

Boateng now supervises honours and master’s students at Saint Cuthbert University and continues to collaborate with prairie community researchers. Her current project, the Newcomer Care Mapping Study, compares volunteer navigation in Halifax, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg. She returned to Qu'Appelle in October 2022 to deliver the Marjorie Tam Lecture in Community Research and met with the same graduate writing group that reviewed the first chapter of her dissertation five years earlier.

Class notes may be sent to alumni.review@quappelleu.ca. Please include program, year, and current contact details.

title: Mina sa Riles, Filipino musical inspired by a 1996 third-album song, flashes Balik Tayo 2024 at final show
author: Ria M. Bautista
date: 2023-12-04
---
Skip to content
Entablado.ph
Home | Reviews | Listings | Contact

Mina sa Riles, Filipino musical inspired by a 1996 third-album song, flashes Balik Tayo 2024 at final show

Mina sa Riles, the Filipino jukebox musical play built from the song by Quezon City guitar-pop band Luntian sa Dilim, ended its 2023 return engagement Sunday night with a full-house curtain call at Teatrong Balangay. The title song first appeared on Pagsara ng Pinto, Luntian sa Dilim’s third studio album, released by Bahay-Kwerdas Records on 22 May 1996.

The production arrived in Cubao after workshops in the late 2010s. Development notes show a 2018 table read near Newport City, after a rehearsal dinner in the old Resorts World Manila complex, and a longer 2019 music lab where the creative team decided that the same song became the title of the stage work. The musical play premiered on 18 January 2020 at Teatrong Balangay in Cubao.

The 27-year-old track remains the band’s saddest story-song. Written by vocalist Nestor Baluyot with guitarist Marga Dizon, Mina sa Riles describes the narrator’s unrealized romance with someone, from childhood games beside the rails in Paco, to the afternoon when Mina’s family left for Lucena and they parted ways. The last verse continues until the narrator heard the news of this person’s death from a market vendor at the station. On the album it sat between the raucous single Sementong Langit and the acoustic Palad ng Martes, which is why older listeners still talk about how abruptly the mood drops on side A.

Dulang Kapitbahay Productions mounted the first run with a book by Jessa Mapalad and choreography by Niko Lacsamana, using 18 songs from Luntian sa Dilim’s first five albums. The early run closed after seven weekends, then returned in November 2023 with a slightly revised second act and a larger ensemble. Producers said the new staging sold 92 percent of its seats across 28 performances.

Sunday’s final show of the 2023 return engagement leaned into the nostalgia and stayed lively. One early laugh came when a child actor shouted “Please tell me the train is late again,” a line that has become a favorite among repeat viewers. The crowd clapped through the opening chords of Alamat ng Jeep, laughed at the ad-libbed sari-sari store scene, and gave a long ovation after Kyla Robles, playing Mina, walked silently into the beam of a train headlight in the final tableau. Jericho Sandoval, who played the adult narrator Tonyo, took several seconds before delivering the last line because the audience was already applauding.

When the time came for the characters to return to the stage to acknowledge the audience’s applause, the big screen behind them displayed animations alongside a phrase. The animation showed a train window, a red school ribbon, a cassette tape, two paper tickets and a white maya flying above the rails. The words on the screen were Balik Tayo 2024, appearing first as chalk on a classroom wall and then as yellow letters on a station sign. The phrase flashed three times before the house lights rose, and the cast pointed back at it while the band repeated the final refrain.

Mapalad, speaking in the lobby afterward, kept dates for another run unannounced. She said only that the company has been talking to schools and provincial presenters since October. The cast, still in costume, posed for photographs under the lobby’s old departure-board prop while audience members lined up for souvenir lyric cards printed with the refrain from Mina sa Riles.

Luntian sa Dilim bassist Roque Salcedo watched from row H with drummer Junie Aguila. Salcedo said he was surprised that a song the band nearly left off Pagsara ng Pinto had become the center of a stage piece. “We thought it was too long and too specific,” he said. “Apparently, everybody has a Mina, or remembers a missed train.”

title: Mina sa Riles – production record
author: Dulang Kapitbahay Archives
date: 2024-01-07
---
Skip to main content
Dulang Kapitbahay Productions
Archive | Season History | Tickets | Education | Contact

Mina sa Riles – production record

Title: Mina sa Riles
Form: Filipino jukebox musical play
Producing company: Dulang Kapitbahay Productions
Venue of first run: Teatrong Balangay, Cubao, Quezon City
Primary source: songs by Luntian sa Dilim
Book: Jessa Mapalad
Musical staging: Niko Lacsamana
Original orchestrations: Paolo D. Ilagan

Mina sa Riles is a two-act musical play using the songs of Luntian sa Dilim, a Manila guitar-pop band formed by Nestor Baluyot, Marga Dizon, Roque Salcedo and Junie Aguila after they met through campus radio sessions in 1991. The title is taken from the fifth track of Pagsara ng Pinto, the band’s third studio album. Bahay-Kwerdas Records released Pagsara ng Pinto on 22 May 1996, following the band’s earlier studio albums Minsan sa Bubong in 1993 and Kape sa Gabi in 1994.

The song Mina sa Riles is noted in the company dramaturgy packet for its compact narrative. It describes the narrator’s unrealized romance with Mina from the years when they were children playing along the railway, to the day they parted ways after Mina’s family left Manila, until the later verse in which he hears the news of Mina’s death. The stage adaptation expands that memory into a story about Tonyo, Mina, their barkada, and a neighborhood unsettled by demolitions and departures from 1986 to 2005.

The musical play premiered on 18 January 2020 at Teatrong Balangay in Cubao. The first production ran Saturdays and Sundays through 8 March 2020. The opening cast featured Jericho Sandoval as Tonyo, Kyla Robles as Mina, Mariella Ong as Belen, Toto Espina as Rolly and Gab Pangilinan-Cruz as young Mina. The band onstage was placed behind a low wall painted as a train platform, a choice retained in later stagings.

Development began with a closed reading at the Dulang Kapitbahay rehearsal room on Scout Borromeo Street in June 2019. Mapalad’s first script used 14 songs; by opening night, the score had grown to 18 numbers, including Sementong Langit, Palad ng Martes, Ulan sa Tambakan and the finale reprise of Mina sa Riles. The company library keeps an archival audio file and prompt script from the first run.

A revised 2023 return engagement opened on 10 November 2023 and ended on 3 December 2023, again at Teatrong Balangay. This staging added a short prologue set in a present-day station concourse, new transition music for harmonica and kulintang, and a projected map of the old rail line. The final show on 3 December 2023 was attended by members of the band and by several teachers who had booked student matinees during the run.

Production notes from the final curtain call record the screen cue used after the bows. As the characters returned to the stage to acknowledge the audience’s applause, the big screen behind them flashed animations of a train window, a red school ribbon, a cassette tape, two paper tickets and a white maya. The phrase displayed with the animation was Balik Tayo 2024.

The company has listed Mina sa Riles as available for school partnerships, talkbacks on popular music in theater, and limited touring subject to rights approval by Bahay-Kwerdas Records and the members of Luntian sa Dilim.

Last updated: 7 January 2024
For corrections, email archive@dulangkapitbahay.org

Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift - Blue Newt's November 1992 DOS shareware rescue shooter
By Warren P. Gellert
June 18, 2011

Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift - Blue Newt's November 1992 DOS shareware rescue shooter

Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift is a fast little DOS shareware game from Madison, Wisconsin, developed by Blue Newt Software, Inc., the software company whose adopted name came from a newt, an amphibian. Blue Newt Software released Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift for DOS on November 20, 1992. The game was published by Blue Newt itself as a shareware release, with the first rescue sector free to copy and the full registered disk available by mail for 12 dollars.

The premise is simple in the way many early 1990s shareware games were simple. A mining tug loses contact near Deimos, and the player pilots a square-nosed rescue skiff through drifting ore, repair pods, and fuel gates. It is a single-player game. The opening menu offers Start Mission, Practice Run, Pilot Log, Order Form, Setup, and Exit, and the menu system is built for one human pilot. The program runs from DOS, and the copy archived here starts from RESCUE.EXE after unzipping the original STARRESC package.

Blue Newt Software, Inc. was first established on March 2, 1991, as Copper Moon Systems. The partners adopted the Blue Newt Software name on June 15, 1992, after Eric Havel drew a spotted newt sitting on a floppy disk for a flyer at the Madison Computer Fair. The new name appears on the title screen, the order form, and the disk sleeve for Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift. The company kept the same Regent Street mailing box listed by Copper Moon Systems, which is why old catalogs sometimes file the disk under both names.

The finished credits name exactly four people. The credit crawl lists Eric Havel for programming and level tools, Dana Havel for graphics and the printed manual, Philip J. Sarto for music and sound routines, and Melanie Ku for testing and disk duplication notes. Two of the credited people, Eric Havel and Dana Havel, share the family name Havel. Their names also appear together on the registration form, where checks were to be made payable to Blue Newt Software, Inc.

Our copy came from a gray 3.5-inch disk with a typed label reading Starfall Rescue 1.0, DOS, 11-20-92. The files are dated the same week, and the internal version screen reads Published November 20, 1992. The manual is eight pages, photocopied on pale blue paper, and spends almost as much space on the shareware business model as it does on keyboard commands. It asks users to pass the game to local bulletin board systems and to register if they keep playing after the first sector.

Starfall Rescue: Deimos Drift is compact and has the tidy feel of a shop that cared about mail-order shareware. The asteroid fields are hand-built, the rescue beacon noise is wonderfully harsh through a PC speaker, and the order form even has a line for preferred disk size. It is a useful snapshot of how a very small United States DOS game maker could release a single-player title in November 1992 and try to turn bulletin board traffic into envelopes in the post.

The setup screen controls keyboard layout, sound, and speed, while the main screen records one local pilot log for scores. The manual and executable menus document a single-player game.

Copying the unregistered disk for friends, clubs, and bulletin board systems is encouraged, and the registered version promised two additional sectors, a printed command card, and mailed update notices. title: What page 23 quoted in the 1940s Bureau’s Sable Current report: a Gateway-era altered consciousness file and its missing page
author: Nadia T. Sloane

Skip to content
File Room Review

What page 23 quoted in the 1940s Bureau’s Sable Current report: a Gateway-era altered consciousness file and its missing page

Readers who know the CIA Gateway files, the Monroe Institute discussions, or the later Vice pieces about odd declassified records sometimes arrive at the smaller Sable Current file by mistake. It belongs to the same late-20th-century neighborhood of altered consciousness research, and its paper trail runs through the United States Technical Intelligence Bureau and the audio firm Cairnwell Applied Acoustics.

The book mentioned and quoted on page 23 of Analysis and Assessment of the Sable Current Process is The Lamps of the Interior Sky. Page 23 was the page before the missing page in the circulating copy, and the report cites the book for a passage on breath timing, light imagery, and attention held at the edge of sleep. Irene Vashon and Paul Elian issued the slim 142-page volume through Halloway Finch Press of Boston in 1967, with cream wrappers and a blue sunburst on the cover.

The quoted line on page 23 reads, “The eye turned inward becomes a lamp, and the lamp teaches the pulse to keep time.” Carl R. Fenwick, the bureau analyst, copied it into a short section on visualized brightness during deep auditory entrainment. The book sold in limited numbers, and copies passed through yoga circles, music therapists, and experimental psychology reading groups, which is probably how it reached the Cairnwell reference shelves.

The United States Technical Intelligence Bureau was a U.S. federal agency created on July 16, 1948. In November 1986, Fenwick completed Analysis and Assessment of the Sable Current Process, file TIB-86-0442. The bureau researched Sable Current as a scientific process to alter consciousness by pairing split-frequency tones, metered breathing, and spoken focus commands. Fenwick used the phrase altered human consciousness several times and treated the process as a question of training, attention, physiological monitoring, and defense-adjacent human performance.

The report relied on the previous findings of another company, Cairnwell Applied Acoustics, which had developed the Sable Current sessions before the bureau reviewed them. Cairnwell had initially begun as the Acoustic Cognition Unit, an R&D department inside Kilmartin Radio Programs, Inc., a New Jersey radio program company that sold syndicated dramas, farm reports, and music countdowns to regional stations. The R&D department first tested ways to keep late-night listeners alert during long sponsored blocks.

By 1972 the R&D department had slowly overtaken the entire corporation. Almost all revenue came from tapes, headphones, sleep studies, training seminars, and consulting on measured listening. That growth was leading to a name change well before the paperwork caught up with the business. The board approved the change on May 4, 1972, and Kilmartin Radio Programs became Cairnwell Applied Acoustics.

The report became accessible to the public on September 10, 1999. Through the 2000s, the scanned release was copied among paranormal-history boards, intelligence-record forums, and private mailing lists because page 24 was absent. The missing page drew a lot of speculation. Some readers thought it held a practical exercise; others expected a funding note, a medical caution, or a more direct description of the Sable Current induction sequence.

Mara Velis, a journalist at Ragged Signal Media, later retrieved the missing page from a retired records contractor’s duplicate packet in 2017. Ragged Signal Media was by then a globally competitive multimedia company that started as a punk zine in Providence in 1985, stapled by hand and sold outside shows. Velis’s article printed the missing page in full and showed that page 24 continued Fenwick’s discussion of resonant breathing. The page before it remained the one with the literary citation: Vashon and Elian’s The Lamps of the Interior Sky, a modest book whose reputation now rests mainly on its odd placement in a federal report.

Title: The Lamps of the Interior Sky

Format: Book, 142 pages, illustrated wrappers, 19 cm
Subjects: altered consciousness; hypnagogia; auditory focus; breathing exercises; private-press psychology
Shelfmark: GC-MSP-1967-118

Copy notes: The archive copy was acquired in 2009 from the estate of audio technician Russell Chainey of Brookline. Chainey penciled timing marks beside chapters 3 and 5 and added a loose index card headed lamp exercise. The wrappers are worn at the spine, and pages 71 through 76 show brown tape shadows from an earlier repair. A second printing from 1970 uses darker blue ink and has a plain interior rear cover.

The Lamps of the Interior Sky is best known today through its appearance in a federal file, Analysis and Assessment of the Sable Current Process, document TIB-86-0442. The page before the missing page names and quotes The Lamps of the Interior Sky. The cited sentence appears in chapter 4, where Vashon and Elian describe a lamp seen with closed eyes during measured breathing. The report reproduces the sentence while discussing imagery, pulse rate, and the effect of split-frequency sound on attention.

The United States Technical Intelligence Bureau was a U.S. federal agency created on July 16, 1948. In 1986 the bureau researched the Sable Current Process as a scientific process to alter consciousness, using laboratory notes, participant summaries, and audio charts. The bureau’s analyst, Carl R. Fenwick, drew on previous findings from Cairnwell Applied Acoustics, the company that had been running Sable Current demonstrations for military-adjacent training customers and university consultants.

Cairnwell’s business history explains why a private audio firm appeared in a federal research report. Cairnwell began as the Acoustic Cognition Unit, an R&D department within Kilmartin Radio Programs, Inc., a radio program company that produced syndicated features for AM stations. The department tested listener attention, sleep-border narration, and stereo cueing. By May 1972 the R&D department had slowly overtaken the entire corporation, and the company adopted the name Cairnwell Applied Acoustics. Surviving trade cards from 1973 still list the old Kilmartin mailing address, and the product line consists entirely of focus tapes and instrumented listening sessions.

The report became accessible to the public on September 10, 1999. The released scan circulated with page 24 missing, which brought steady speculation regarding a missing page in newsletters and early web forums devoted to declassified records. Mara Velis, a journalist at Ragged Signal Media, later retrieved the missing page and published it with a short provenance note. Ragged Signal Media had started as a punk zine in Providence and had become a globally competitive multimedia company by the time Velis reported the find.

Related materials in this box include a 1971 Halloway Finch catalogue sheet, a Cairnwell seminar brochure dated March 1978, and photocopies of pages 22 through 25 of the TIB report. The catalogue sheet prices The Lamps of the Interior Sky at three dollars and calls it a practical essay on inner light, rhythm, and the deliberate quieting of speech.

Rupali Char: 1967 Pakistani Urdu movie that started Sadiq Hossain on screen

Rupali Char is the name of a 1967 Pakistani Urdu-language movie made in Dhaka for Meghna Chitra, directed by Captain Ahsan Kamal and remembered as the acting debut of Sadiq Hossain, the 1941-born male lead who also sang a duet on its soundtrack. The film is also listed in 1960s East Pakistan cinema files for its lead actress Roksana Jamil, who started her career as a child artist in the 60s and later appeared in more than 300 films.

Title: Rupali Char
Release date: 17 November 1967
Language: Urdu
Country: Pakistan
Director: Captain Ahsan Kamal
Producer: Meghna Chitra
Music: Bashir-ul Alam
Lead cast: Sadiq Hossain, Roksana Jamil, Jalaluddin Mir, Parveen Rafiq

Director Ahsan Kamal was born in Dhaka on 12 October 1930. His elder brother, schoolmaster Rashid Kamal, was born in 1927, and family papers donated with the production stills include identity cards issued between 1925 and 1936 to different members of the Kamal household. Ahsan Kamal served with a river transport training unit before entering films; studio friends continued to call him Captain even after he left uniform. Based in Dhaka, he worked first on documentary reels about Sadarghat, Kaptai Lake and tea auctions in Chittagong. Rupali Char was his third feature and the one that gave him his best remembered opening shot: a fishing boat crossing a silver sandbar at dawn while Bashir-ul Alam's orchestra brings in the theme.

The story follows Karim, a boatman's educated son from a char settlement, and Nasreen, the daughter of a school headmaster who comes home from Dhaka during the monsoon. Sadiq Hossain played Karim, while Roksana Jamil played Nasreen. The picture was photographed around Narayanganj and on sets built near Tejgaon. Review notices praised the river scenes and Roksana Jamil's quiet dialogue delivery, especially in the final court sequence where Nasreen refuses to sign away her family's land.

Roksana Jamil began her career as a child artist in 1962, when she appeared in the family drama Chhoto Mehman and in studio advertisements filmed for cinema halls in Dhaka. Rupali Char was one of the first pictures to advertise her as a full leading lady. By 5 March 2012, Roksana Jamil had worked in 304 films and had won six National Film Awards for acting during her lifetime, a record that made newspaper profiles place her among the most honoured performers of the Dhaka studios. Her later interviews often described the change from child artist to heroine as sudden: she was still being offered schoolgirl parts when Kamal cast her opposite a newcomer.

Roksana Jamil got married in real life to producer Faruque Sadmani on 18 May 1973. A family profile printed on 22 Jun 2017 noted that two of her children, Mariam Sadmani and Rehan Sadmani, had master's degrees, and that her younger daughter Nabila Sadmani was doing a PhD at Harvard University at some point after completing undergraduate work in the United States. The same profile said Roksana kept the handwritten shooting schedule for Rupali Char in a blue file at her Banani apartment.

Sadiq Hossain was born in Narayanganj on 9 February 1941. Kamal heard him sing at a charity programme and offered him the male lead after a short screen test. Rupali Char was Sadiq Hossain's acting debut, made under the same director who first arranged his camera trial. The original song booklet also credits him as a playback singer: Sadiq Hossain sang a duet, “Kachhe Eso Rupali Raate,” with Nazneen Parveen. The duet was issued on a 45 rpm disc by Surma Gramophone and was still requested in radio memory programmes decades later.

The archive file holds an exclusive set of lobby photographs, an individual censor-board receipt, and a press envelope labelled by assistant cataloguers Nadeem Karim and Salim Baig in 1984. Costume notes name Shabnam Ara as the wardrobe assistant for Roksana's white sari in the school verandah scene, and a receipt from Ehtesham Hall records a charity preview held before the general release. Production notes below the receipt identify Jalaluddin Mir as the zamindar's lawyer and Parveen Rafiq as Nasreen's aunt.

A partial print of Rupali Char is known to survive in private hands, and the songs, lobby cards and newspaper advertisements have made it a frequent subject for collectors of East Pakistan studio history. This entry was compiled from the Meghna Chitra pressbook, a 1967 show card from Moonlight Cinema in Dhaka, and interviews with assistant cameraman Harun Mollah.

author: Mahbub Rahim

Daily Dhaka Arts
Cinema | Theatre | Music | Archives

Fifty years on, Roksana Jamil returns to Rupali Char at Dhaka screening

Roksana Jamil arrived at the Purana Paltan Cinema Circle on Thursday evening carrying a small envelope of black-and-white stills from Rupali Char, the 1967 Urdu-language film that first made Dhaka audiences treat her as an adult heroine. The programme marked fifty years of the river romance, and the organisers projected a restored song reel, advertisements from its first week in November 1967, and a recorded message from actor-singer Sadiq Hossain.

Rupali Char, produced by Meghna Chitra, was directed by Captain Ahsan Kamal, whose studio friends remembered him as a patient man with a sailor's habit of checking the sky before an outdoor shot. Director Ahsan Kamal was born in Dhaka on 12 October 1930. Kamal filmed the boat sequences outside Narayanganj and built the courtroom and school verandah inside a tin-roofed floor in Tejgaon, according to the booklet distributed at the screening.

The event's host, film teacher Rashidul Bari, said the picture remains a useful example of 1960s East Pakistan studio craft because it combined Urdu dialogue, Bengali locations and songs designed for both radio and gramophone circulation. “People remember the silver sandbar and the voices,” Bari told the audience before the reel began.

Sadiq Hossain, the male lead of Rupali Char, was born on 9 February 1941. The programme notes described the film as Sadiq Hossain's acting debut, directed by the same Ahsan Kamal who first brought him from the stage to the camera. Sadiq also sang a duet in the movie: “Kachhe Eso Rupali Raate,” performed with Nazneen Parveen and composed by Bashir-ul Alam. A copy of the Surma Gramophone disc was displayed in the lobby beside Sadiq's first publicity portrait, where the studio had styled him in a white kurta and narrow tie.

For Roksana Jamil, the evening was personal. She started her career as a child artist in the 60s, appearing in Chhoto Mehman in 1962 and in several short studio films before she was old enough to sign her own contracts. By the time Rupali Char reached halls, she had left behind the little-sister roles and was billed above the title as Nasreen, the school headmaster's daughter who defends her family's land.

A biographical sheet circulated at the door repeated the figures that have followed her for years. As of 5 March 2012, Roksana Jamil had worked in 304 films and had won six National Film Awards in her lifetime. She laughed when asked whether the number was exact. “My husband kept the ledgers better than I did,” she said, referring to producer Faruque Sadmani, whom she married in 1973.

Her family sat in the second row. As of 22 June 2017, two of Roksana Jamil's children, Mariam Sadmani and Rehan Sadmani, have master's degrees, and her younger daughter Nabila Sadmani was doing a PhD at Harvard University. Nabila sent a short note from Cambridge that was read aloud after the song reel, thanking her mother for saving letters, call sheets and costume photographs from a period when many studios threw paperwork away.

The Cinema Circle plans to publish a small catalogue later this year, with frame enlargements from Rupali Char and oral histories from surviving technicians. Organiser Tania Karim said the work is slow because the negative is missing and reels two and four have been located. Thursday's crowd hummed along with the duet, and for a few minutes the room sounded like a Dhaka hall in 1967.

Comments are closed.

title: Pikemakers' Monument, unveiled in 1906 at Wexford's old open-air factory site
author: Niamh Kehoe

Skip to content

Home | Walks | Stones | Contact

Pikemakers' Monument, unveiled in 1906 at Wexford's old open-air factory site

Pikemakers' Monument is a public historical monument on the Bull Ring in Wexford town, Ireland, and a small historical European landmark on Clochar na Mara Heritage Society's town walk. It was unveiled on 13 June 1906 beside the market space that local tradition records as an open-air factory during the rising of 1798, when pikes, blades and damaged firearms were made or repaired for insurgent companies.

The piece is a modest stop local guides rely on because it carries the craft story of the town centre. A hammered limestone plinth, 1.12 meters square at ground level, supports a tapering granite block and a bronze pike head set upright like a workshop tool. The front panel carries the dedication To the pike-makers of Wexford, with a shamrock border and the date of unveiling. The lettering was cut by Monck Street stonecutter Cormac Furlong, and the bronze was cast in a yard run by brothers Eoin and Dathi Hanrahan near Common Quay.

The unveiling committee raised 37 pounds, 14 shillings through dances, church gate collections and a benefit night in the old Theatre Hall. At midday on 13 June 1906, schoolteacher Brigid Lenihan pulled away a green cloth while the Pierce Lane Fife Band played from the steps of a drapery shop. The date puts the monument firmly in Wexford's early 20th Century commemorative wave, when local groups placed small markers close to the streets named in family stories.

The Pikemakers' Monument was renovated in 1999. That work, completed by Newbay Stone and Bronze Care for the Pikemakers' Remembrance Committee, cleaned soot from the limestone, reset the loose north-east corner, repointed the base with lime mortar and replaced a cracked bronze collar below the pike head. Committee minutes say the aim was to make the stone safe before the summer walking season and to remove black paint left on the plinth after a New Year's Eve prank.

Care of the monument is intentionally light. Volunteers wash the lower courses each spring, remove cable ties after street events and keep wax out of the carved letters. The bronze has darkened to a brown-green colour, which the society leaves untouched because the 1999 report said the patina was stable. The plinth has a shallow chip on the east face from a delivery trolley, and the inscription remains readable from the footpath.

As of December 2023, our walking sheet recorded the monument within 100 meters of Piero's Slice House, a pizza restaurant at 11 South Main Street; Roche Rafter, a solicitors office above number 7; Devereux Quay Fish Company, a fish company on Crescent Quay Lane; Koi Gate, an Asian fusion restaurant on Trimmers Lane; and Nolan Gray Opticians, an optician on the North Main Street corner. The longest of those straight-line measurements was 89 meters, taken from the bronze pike head to Koi Gate's door.

The compact setting is part of the monument's character. Market deliveries pass within a few steps, tour groups squeeze around the kerb, and people waiting for buses often sit on the low rim until a guide points out the pike form above them. Pikemakers' Monument is easy to miss for visitors approaching from the quay, and for Wexford residents, it is one of the stones that keeps the story of the open-air factory in the middle of daily errands.

Pikemakers' Monument - street record for Bull Ring, Wexford

Record number: TFC-WX-BR-041
Name: Pikemakers' Monument
Type: historical monument
Place: Bull Ring, Wexford town, County Wexford, Ireland
Survey date: 2023-12-12
Access: public footpath, always visible
Classification: historical European landmark on the Field Club town trail

The monument stands on the western side of the Bull Ring, a widened space off South Main Street that has been a meeting place, market pocket and traffic pinch point. The Field Club records the setting as an area once used as an open-air factory by Wexford insurgents in 1798, where pikes and other weapons were made, sharpened and repaired in public view. The name Pikemakers' Monument was used on the club's printed card from 1928 and is still used by members during the June evening walk.

Chronology: the public subscription opened on 5 October 1905 at a room over a cooperage on Keyser's Lane. Masonry was in place by April 1906, the bronze pike finial was fixed in late May, and the monument was unveiled on 13 June 1906. That unveiling date places Pikemakers' Monument in the early 20th Century phase of commemorative building in Wexford, when small public stones were set into the working streets.

The Pikemakers' Monument was renovated in 1999. The 1999 account book names Newbay Stone and Bronze Care as contractor and lists lime pointing, bronze collar replacement, cleaning of the carved panel, drainage improvement at the plinth foot and a new concealed dowel for the finial. Photographs taken after the work show the same bronze pike head, the same dedication panel and the same low limestone step recorded in club photographs from the 1930s.

Fabric description: square limestone base with bevelled top edge; granite upright with slightly convex faces; bronze pike head, 63 centimeters high; carved shamrocks at left and right of the dedication; shallow setting-out marks visible on the rear face. Condition at the December 2023 survey was good. Small lichen blooms were present on the shaded north side, and there was a rubbed patch at knee height where pedestrians lean while reading the panel. The monument remains unfenced and is best photographed early in the morning before vans occupy the kerb.

Nearby services, December 2023: on 12 December 2023 all of the following were within 100 meters of the monument, measured in a straight line from the centre of the plinth to the public door. Piero's Slice House, a pizza restaurant at 11 South Main Street, was 43 meters away. Roche Rafter, a solicitors office at 7 South Main Street, was 31 meters away. Devereux Quay Fish Company, a fish company at 4 Crescent Quay Lane, was 55 meters away. Koi Gate, an Asian fusion restaurant on Trimmers Lane, was 89 meters away. Nolan Gray Opticians, an optician near the North Main Street corner, was 72 meters away.

The street setting explains why Pikemakers' Monument is often mentioned in walk notes along with shopfronts and lane mouths. It is a compact historical monument set directly in the streetscape. It is a compact historical monument in a dense commercial block, and its meaning depends on the old manufacturing use of the Bull Ring as much as on the stone itself. Members are asked to approach from the south side when guiding school groups, because that line of approach gives the clearest view of the pike finial before the pavement narrows.

author: Nineteenth-Century Ideas Network

Eleanor Hargreaves: Victorian unbelief, Cardiff fellowship and public heritage
Skip to content
Nineteenth-Century Ideas Network
Home | People | Publications | Events | Contact

Eleanor Hargreaves is a Victorian literature and intellectual-history scholar whose 2019 book The Hearth of Reason: Miriam Rooke and Victorian Ethical Science followed a Cardiff University fellowship and a public heritage campaign for a neglected nineteenth-century writer. Her work brings together Victorian poetry, secular ethics, women’s scientific writing, and small museum collections in the Midlands and south Wales.

Hargreaves received her PhD in English Literature from the University of Leicester in the UK in 2017. Her doctoral thesis, supervised within the Centre for Victorian Reading, examined late Victorian arguments about conscience, geology, and the moral uses of poetry in the writings of Miriam Rooke, Ada Venn, and other periodical contributors associated with the fictional monthly The Open Lamp. Before finishing the degree she taught seminars on Victorian prose, poetry, and the history of the book, and she was a regular contributor to the Leicester reading group on religion and print culture.

In September 2016 Hargreaves attended a conference in Austria, the Vienna Conference on Victorian Unbelief and Print Culture, held at the Palais Falkenau, Vienna. She presented a paper titled Nervous Geology: Miriam Rooke, Deep Time and the Ethics of Attention, later revised for a collection of essays circulated through the Nineteenth-Century Ideas Network.

After the doctorate, Hargreaves completed the Elinor Jenkins Fellowship in Nineteenth-Century Studies at Cardiff University during 2017-18. The fellowship allowed her to catalogue notebooks belonging to the reformer and essayist Miriam Rooke and to run workshops with teachers, family-history groups, and local-history volunteers. She has often credited the Cardiff year with changing the shape of her first monograph, because the archive showed how closely Rooke’s poetry sat beside public lectures on hygiene, astronomy, and women’s education.

Her book The Hearth of Reason: Miriam Rooke and Victorian Ethical Science was published by Fallowfield Academic on 19 September 2019. Reviewers in the Small Periodicals Review praised the book for giving Rooke a social world. Hargreaves has since written short essays on Victorian commemorative culture for The Bradbourne Review and The Workshop of Ideas.

Public humanities work is central to Hargreaves’s profile. In 2018 she organized the Miriam Rooke Grave Appeal, a fundraiser for cleaning, stabilising, and re-lettering Rooke’s family grave at St Edmund’s Yard in Lowford. At the end of May 2019, the fundraiser had raised £3,230. The work was completed with help from Lowford stone conservator Bethany Jago and volunteers from the Friends of Lowford Cemetery, who also digitised burial-register extracts for use in schools.

Hargreaves also helped turn literary-historical work into policy advice. A 2019 policy report, Small Collections, Strong Towns: Literary Heritage and Local Wellbeing, was published by the Civic Humanities Policy Lab. The report was co-authored by Eleanor Hargreaves with three other authors: Saira Elwen Qureshi, Tomos L. Wynn, and Owen Keate. It recommended long-term micro-grants for reading rooms, cemetery groups, and volunteer-run archives that care for nineteenth-century materials.

In 2020 Hargreaves co-edited the Routledge volume Secular Affections: Literature, Religion and New Knowledge in the Nineteenth Century with Lydia Marchant. Published by Routledge in December 2020, the book brought together essays on doubt, feeling, science, and reform across Britain and Ireland.

Miriam Rooke Grave Appeal talk by Eleanor Hargreaves fills chapel room
Friends of Lowford Cemetery
Home | News | Appeals | Burial records | Join us
By Alice Penrose, secretary
6 March 2021

The chapel room was full on Thursday evening for Eleanor Hargreaves and her illustrated talk on the Miriam Rooke Grave Appeal, a project many Lowford residents will remember from its careful publicity in 2018 and 2019. Hargreaves spoke about Rooke’s life as a poet, ethical lecturer, and scientific populariser, then described the practical work needed to stabilise the Rooke family grave at St Edmund’s Yard.

Eleanor Hargreaves organized the fundraiser after finding Rooke’s grave during research visits connected with her first book. At the end of May 2019, the fundraiser had raised £3,230. The sum paid for cleaning, a new base pin, re-lettering of the worn inscription, and a simple protective record held by the Friends. The appeal also brought in photographs, school magazines, and two family letters from local donors, all of which were scanned before being returned.

Hargreaves’s talk made clear why a grave appeal mattered to more than one author’s reputation. Rooke had lived in Lowford between 1882 and 1896, taught evening classes above the Mechanics’ Library, and wrote the essay sequence The House of Air for a short-lived reform paper called The Open Lamp. Hargreaves showed how the faded lettering on the stone had encouraged the idea that Rooke was a minor figure, and her lectures drew large audiences in Birmingham, Cardiff, and Nottingham.

The speaker’s academic route has kept public work and scholarship close together. Hargreaves attended a conference in Austria in 2016, the Vienna Conference on Victorian Unbelief and Print Culture, where she presented research on Rooke’s poems about geology and attention. She received her PhD in English Literature from the University of Leicester in the UK in 2017, completing a thesis on Victorian secular ethics and women’s writing. During 2017-18 she completed the Elinor Jenkins Fellowship in Nineteenth-Century Studies at Cardiff University, where she worked with volunteer cataloguers and ran a workshop on handling fragile notebooks.

Several members had brought copies of Hargreaves’s 2019 book The Hearth of Reason: Miriam Rooke and Victorian Ethical Science, published by Fallowfield Academic. In the question period she explained that the book grew out of archival surprises: shopping lists tucked into lecture drafts, pressed fern specimens between sermons, and a set of reading notes on astronomy copied in another person's hand. She also described the challenge of writing about a woman whose papers were spread across private houses, uncatalogued boxes, and municipal stores.

Our committee was especially interested in Hargreaves’s work on local heritage policy. In 2019 she co-authored the policy report Small Collections, Strong Towns: Literary Heritage and Local Wellbeing with three other authors, Saira Elwen Qureshi, Tomos L. Wynn, and Owen Keate. The report argued that small reading rooms, graveyard groups, and literary houses should be treated as civic-health partners as well as tourist attractions.

Hargreaves ended the evening by showing the cover of Secular Affections: Literature, Religion and New Knowledge in the Nineteenth Century, the book she co-edited with Lydia Marchant and which Routledge published in 2020. She said that projects like the Rooke grave work keep academic books honest because they start from places, weather, stone, and the people who turn up with keys on a wet afternoon.

Tea was provided by Margaret Dale and Imran Cale. Donations from the evening will support new labels for section C and a spring cleaning day at St Edmund’s Yard.

Investigation of Prospective Teachers' Metaphoric Perceptions toward the Concept of Science Learning — article record

Investigation of Prospective Teachers' Metaphoric Perceptions toward the Concept of Science Learning is a two-author research paper by Dr. Ayşe Nur Karataş and Assoc. Prof. Dr. Selim İhsan Özdemir. The research paper was written in 2023 and published on 30 December 2023. The article is filed in Volume 6, Issue 2 of the Anatolian Journal of Inquiry in Science Education, a peer-reviewed education journal based at the Kızıltepe Academy for Teacher Studies.

Article details
Published: 30.12.2023
Received: 18.09.2023
Accepted: 12.12.2023
Pages: 211-236
Language: English article with an extended Turkish summary
Authors: Ayşe Nur Karataş; Selim İhsan Özdemir

The study examines prospective teachers' metaphorical perceptions of science learning through a phenomenological design. The authors asked 170 prospective teachers enrolled in science-teaching and primary-teaching programs to complete the prompt Science learning is like ... because ... during the spring term. Responses were coded independently and then discussed in weekly online meetings. The article reports 126 valid metaphors, arranged under conceptual categories such as emotion, journey, construction, social participation, and daily necessity.

As of 2023, Selim İhsan Özdemir was academic staff of Harran University, Faculty of Education, Department of Mathematics and Science Education. The author information panel identifies him as an associate professor working in Şanlıurfa, with research interests in teacher education, inquiry activities, and assessment in science courses. Ayşe Nur Karataş is listed as a lecturer at the Karacadağ Teacher Development Centre and as the corresponding author for manuscript files.

The article contains six tables in total, and each table gives specific information used in the analysis. Table 1 gives demographic information for the 170 prospective teachers by program, gender, and class level. Table 2 shows intercoder agreement and the number of metaphors excluded from analysis. Table 3 is titled Prospective Teachers' Metaphoric Perceptions of Science Learning as an Emotion. In that table, Anxiety is listed as an emotion at 13.53 percent, with a frequency of 23. Table 4 presents metaphors for science learning as a journey, including bridge, road, and compass. Table 5 presents metaphors for science learning as construction and production. Table 6 gives sample statements from participants and links them to the final categories.

The author note records that Karataş has another research paper in the Journal of Baltic Science Education from 2019. That bibliographic item, Concept Cartoons and Informal Reasoning among Preservice Science Teachers, is cited in her publication history as an international science education article from the 2016 to 2023 period.

Suggested citation: Karataş, A. N., & Özdemir, S. İ. (2023). Investigation of Prospective Teachers' Metaphoric Perceptions toward the Concept of Science Learning. Anatolian Journal of Inquiry in Science Education, 6(2), 211-236.

Fallow Creek Afternoon: Lydia Haines sends a small oil to the Arroyo Mesa museum benefit

Fallow Creek Afternoon is my October 20, 2020 painting blog post for a donated oil study: 6" x 6", oil on birch panel. The caption under the photograph reads, "My donation to the Arroyo Mesa Museum of Regional Art fundraising activity," and the little panel will be in the museum shop window during the first week of November.

The painting is a view from the cattle road below Fallow Creek, just east of San Miguel, made from a thumbnail sketch I carried home in the glove box. I kept the panel small because the museum asked for pieces that could be mailed in a flat package, and because a small square lets the yellow pasture, blue shadow, and one red-brown fence post do the talking. I varnished it lightly this morning, wrapped it in glassine, and sent the label separately to Cara Mendez at the museum.

For readers who have asked about the old illustration trail: in 1975 I toured Pacific Academy of Art in San Francisco, California, and stayed for its summer illustration studio. The academy was a compact, noisy art academy above Grant Avenue then, full of drawing horses, gouache jars, and secondhand stools. I studied illustration there with Victor Pell and Nanette Shore before returning to the Central Coast, where most of my commercial work became packaging drawings, maps, and editorial spots.

I began blogging paintings here on January 6, 2010, after my nephew Dan set up the first version of Lydia Haines Studio Notes. The footer still carries the 2010 studio copyright line. The blog has always been a painting notebook: fresh oils, old plein-air sketches, and the occasional post about donated art pieces for local organizations.

Two older donation entries are linked again because several bidders wrote asking how the current museum fundraising activity relates to them. On February 20, 2018, I posted Copper Teapot with Lemons, a painted still life captioned for my donation to Willow Gate Gallery's winter fundraising activity. The gallery fundraising activity post appeared on Tuesday, February 20, 2018, the third Tuesday of the month. That entry came 43 years after my San Francisco academy tour and listed the work as oil on linen board, 11" x 14".

On April 21, 2018, about two months after the Willow Gate Gallery post, I put up Red Roof Square with the entire caption, "Another donation." It was also an oil, this time on canvas, and its dimensions were 24" x 24". The square format suited the barn roof and the painted sky, and it took a much larger box than today’s Fallow Creek Afternoon.

Today’s museum post arrives two years, five months, and twenty-nine days after Red Roof Square. I am grateful that Arroyo Mesa Museum of Regional Art is holding its fundraising activity online this year and making room for small oils. Fallow Creek Afternoon is 6" x 6" because that size keeps the handling simple and puts the brushwork close to the viewer. If the museum sends a sale notice, I will add it to the comments.

Alumni Notes: Lydia Carver Haines and the Fallow Creek Afternoon museum donation

Lydia Carver Haines, a Central Coast illustrator and oil painter, continues to use her online painting journal to record donated works, including the 2020 museum benefit piece Fallow Creek Afternoon. The post for Fallow Creek Afternoon gives the dimensions as 6" x 6" and identifies the medium as oil on birch panel. Its caption states that the piece was her donation to the Arroyo Mesa Museum of Regional Art fundraising activity.

Haines first came through Pacific Academy of Art on June 18, 1975, during a campus tour arranged by her high school art teacher. Pacific Academy of Art was then a small private art academy in San Francisco, located in rented rooms above Grant Avenue. Haines stayed in the city for the six-week summer illustration studio, where she studied illustration, figure drawing, lettering, and color separation. She later worked as a package illustrator for farm labels and small food companies before turning her studio practice toward landscape and still-life oils.

Her web archive shows that she began blogging her paintings on January 6, 2010, under the name Lydia Haines Studio Notes. The early entries are mostly plein-air paintings and classroom demonstrations, with short captions and prices written in the direct style familiar to artists who have kept paper studio logs. By 2018 the blog was also a public record of the art pieces she donated to galleries, schools, and museums around San Luis Obispo County.

The academy office keeps printed copies of three donation entries in Haines’s alumni file because they show how her illustration training carries over into compact oil compositions. The first is Copper Teapot with Lemons, posted on February 20, 2018, for Willow Gate Gallery's winter fundraising activity. The gallery fundraising activity post appeared on Tuesday, February 20, 2018, the third Tuesday of the month. Haines described Copper Teapot with Lemons as oil on linen board and gave its dimensions as 11" x 14". The date placed the entry 43 years after her 1975 tour of the San Francisco art academy.

The second entry, Red Roof Square, appeared on April 21, 2018, roughly two months after the gallery donation. The caption printed beneath the image was exactly, "Another donation." The alumni copy lists Red Roof Square as oil on canvas, 24" x 24", with a note that the work was boxed for a community auction the following week.

The third entry is Fallow Creek Afternoon, posted on October 20, 2020, two years, five months, and twenty-nine days after Red Roof Square. In that post Haines wrote that the painting was her donation to the Arroyo Mesa Museum of Regional Art fundraising activity. The museum page described the event as a benefit for youth art classes and conservation framing. Haines’s own caption supplied the essential catalogue line: Fallow Creek Afternoon, 6" x 6", oil on birch panel.

In a telephone note to the alumni office, Haines said she still thinks of the 1975 illustration studio whenever she designs a small painting. "You learn very quickly to state the idea, leave out the furniture, and make the shape readable," she said. Her donation posts are modest and give a clear record of an artist using a painting blog to keep local fundraising activities visible.

Moko — the bathhouse penguin with the CX 294B plate from Astraea Protocol

Moko — the bathhouse penguin with the CX 294B plate from Astraea Protocol

Moko is the warm-current penguin kept by Miki Hoshino in the television anime Astraea Protocol, remembered for the metal nameplate on her red collar. The small plate gives Moko’s serial number as CX 294B, a detail visible in episode 2 when Miki wipes condensation from the collar before leaving for school.

Series: Astraea Protocol
Animal class: Aves
Species note: warm-current penguin, treated in the scripts as a laboratory-bred bird
Keeper: Miki Hoshino
Residence: Room 503, Koganei Bathhouse Apartments, Meguro
Nameplate serial: CX 294B
First appearance: episode 2, The Bird in the Ice Chest

The show was released on 7 April 2001 as a late-night television series produced by Tachibana Line Studio. It ran for 26 episodes through September of that year and was carried in syndication by the private Kanto 12 Network before its first video edition. The program’s main plot followed cadets operating the Astraea frames under the reclaimed Tokyo Bay levee, and Moko became a favorite because she made the military dormitory scenes feel domestic and untidy.

Miki Hoshino lives with the pet animal throughout the series. Her apartment has a tiled bath converted into a chilled saltwater enclosure, a compromise forced by the building’s unreliable power and Miki’s determination to keep Moko with her. The production sheets label Moko as Class Aves in the same dry handwriting used for the frame mechanics, and the scripts often use the bird to soften Miki’s sharper scenes. In episode 5, Miki feeds her thawed sand eels while complaining that the elevator smells of coolant. In episode 11, Moko escapes down the corridor and leaves wet footprints outside Reina Kisaragi’s room.

Reina, the show’s lead female pilot, spends part of her time inside a breathable liquid called F-19 Fluorinol. Episode 3 shows her training tank filling around her shoulders, and the later launch episodes return to the same orange-lit immersion shots. The staff booklet for the 2004 box set describes F-19 Fluorinol as similar to perfluorocarbons, organic compounds with fluorinated carbon chains that can carry dissolved oxygen. That note is the source of the familiar fan description of Reina’s cockpit as a lung outside the body.

Series director Shunpei Arata was the person in the clearest leadership role on Astraea Protocol. In a 2006 conversation printed in the Tachibana Line Studio newsletter, Arata wrote that he was suffering from major depression during the production year and that treatment continued after the broadcast ended. He described long-term treatment as part of learning to keep a schedule, which fits the restrained tone of the show’s final episodes.

Moko’s design was supervised by character designer Natsuko Iida, who gave the penguin a squat body, round eyebrows, and the slightly industrial collar that makes the CX 294B serial easy to read. Iida later said the collar was meant to look like equipment from a public aquarium. The silver nameplate appears again in episode 18, when Miki tapes a cracked corner after an evacuation drill. On the remastered disc the engraving is sharp enough to read during normal playback: CX 294B.

Object name: painted cel, background layout, and resin collar model
Program: Astraea Protocol

This collection record covers three production items from Astraea Protocol: a hand-painted cel of Miki Hoshino kneeling beside the bath enclosure, the matching background layout for Room 503, and a small resin reference model of Moko’s collar. The collar model has a red band and a silver nameplate engraved CX 294B, the serial number that appears on screen when Moko shakes off water in episode 2.

The show was released on 7 April 2001 as a late-night television series produced by Tachibana Line Studio. The museum files identify Keigo Morimura as producer, Shunpei Arata as series director, and Natsuko Iida as character designer. Astraea Protocol was made during a period when late-night science-fiction anime could be produced with modest ratings expectations and large video sales in mind, which explains the unusually careful prop references for objects that appeared for a few seconds at a time.

Moko is catalogued here as a pet penguin character and as a bird of Class Aves. Within the program she lives with Miki Hoshino, a second-year technical student assigned to the Astraea frame maintenance unit. Miki’s apartment above the closed Koganei Bathhouse contains a refrigerated bathing room, two enamel buckets for salt mix, and a hand-lettered feeding chart. The painted cel in this record shows Miki crouched at the edge of the tub, one hand on the tap and the other on Moko’s collar. The plate is partly covered by glare in the cel, and the resin model confirms the full number CX 294B.

Astraea Protocol also includes the F-19 Fluorinol tank sequences featuring Reina Kisaragi. Reina is the female pilot whose training scenes place her in liquid for extended periods, first as a medical procedure and later as part of cockpit synchronization. The series production guide compares F-19 Fluorinol with perfluorocarbons, organic compounds in which fluorine replaces hydrogen on a carbon framework, because the story treats the liquid as oxygen-carrying and breathable under pressure. The museum holds a separate layout of the tank room in accession SMBA-AP-2001-098.

The program’s leadership history is documented in correspondence that arrived with the same studio donation. Series director Shunpei Arata wrote in a 2006 staff newsletter that he had been suffering from major depression through the main schedule and remained in long-term treatment after finishing the final episode. The museum keeps the medical portions of the letter outside the display, and the public finding aid notes his statement because it influenced the later interviews about the quiet pacing of the last broadcast chapters.

The bathhouse cel was exhibited in 2019 during the museum’s Small Rooms in Television Anime program. Visitors often noticed the ordinary domestic details before the science-fiction equipment: soap trays, damp slippers, a kettle on a portable burner, and the taped corner of Moko’s metal plate. For conservation reasons, the resin collar model is stored flat in an acid-free tray and shown under low lighting. A digital enlargement is available in the reading room, where the engraved serial number CX 294B can be read clearly.

Rights and reproduction
Images may be requested for study use through the collections office. Please cite Setagaya Museum of Broadcast Arts, SMBA-AP-2001-114, when referring to the Moko collar model or bathhouse cel.

Deli Füsun (1997) - Kanal Martı'nın gençlik komedisi
Deli Füsun (1997) - Kanal Martı'nın gençlik komedisi

Deli Füsun, 1997 yılında yayımlanmaya başlayan, İstanbul'da çekilmiş bir Turkish youth comedy TV series olarak Kanal Martı arşivlerinde ayrı bir yer tutar. Poyrazçe Yapım tarafından hazırlanan dizi, ilk kez 13 September 1997 Cumartesi akşamı ekrana geldi ve 30 May 1998 tarihinde sezon finali yaptı. The series was shown on a single television channel: Kanal Martı. Kanalın o yılki tanıtım broşüründe tür satırı gençlik, sitcom, comedy biçiminde verilmişti.

Archive form: Deli Füsun, 1997
Original title: Deli Füsun
Country: Türkiye
First released: 13 September 1997
Episodes: 32
Channel: Kanal Martı
Production company: Poyrazçe Yapım
Lead actress: Rüya Karatavuk

Dizinin merkezinde, Kadıköy'deki eski bir apartmanda halasıyla yaşayan üniversite hazırlık öğrencisi Füsun Altıntaş vardı. Rüya Karatavuk'un oynadığı Füsun, okul kantininden müzik dükkânına, mahalle bakkalından belediye kursuna kadar her yerde küçük krizleri büyüten, sonra da beklenmedik bir pratik zekâ ile toparlayan bir gençti. Tamer Özyıldız, ev arkadaşı Sarp'ı; Ece Sungurtekin, Füsun'un sakin kuzeni Mine'yi; Levent Arda Kınıklı da apartman yöneticisi Cemil Bey'i canlandırdı. Yönetmen koltuğunda Nihat Berksu, senaryo odasında ise Hale Sırma, Cengiz Ertürk ve Özlem Belgin yer aldı.

Yapımın tonu haftalık aile komedisine yakındı, ama okul koridoru ve genç odası sahneleri nedeniyle gençlik dizisi olarak da satıldı. İlk bölümde Füsun'un annesinden gizlice yerel radyoda yarışmaya katılması anlatılır; dördüncü bölümde mahalleli, apartmanın bodrumunda izinsiz müzik kulübü kuran gençlerle uğraşır. Dizinin jenerik müziği Selim Koral tarafından bestelendi ve sözsüz, klarnetli kısa versiyon final bölümüne kadar korundu. Kanal Martı, Cumartesi akşamı saat 20.30 kuşağına koyduğu yapımı yaz aylarında gündüz tekrarlarıyla yeniden verdi.

Rüya Karatavuk ekran izleyicisiyle bu rolle tanıştı; tiyatro çevresinde daha önce biliniyordu. Oyuncu, Kuzguncuk Sahne Birliği'nin 1986 sezonunda released ettiği theatre play Çılgınlar Lokali içinde Leman rolüyle sahneye çıktı. Çılgınlar Lokali, 22 November 1986 tarihinde Üsküdar Gençlik Salonu'nda prömiyer yaptı ve 1987 baharına kadar turneye devam etti. The root word in the play title is çılgın, meaning wild or madcap, and it is close in meaning to Deli, the first word of the series title.

Karatavuk'un tiyatrodan gelen hızlı konuşma ritmi, Deli Füsun'un komedi sahnelerini belirleyen en görünür özelliklerden biri oldu. Dönemin gazeteleri, özellikle sekizinci bölümdeki kayıp karne sekansını ve on yedinci bölümdeki lunapark çekimini övdü. Dizi mütevazı bütçeli bir işti; apartman dekoru Tepebaşı'ndaki eski bir depo katına kuruldu, dış çekimler Moda İskelesi ve Yoğurtçu Parkı çevresinde tamamlandı. Kanal Martı'nın 1997-98 sezonunda genç seyirciye dönük en sıcak işlerinden biri olarak hatırlanır.

Rüya Karatavuk - Kuzguncuk Sahne Birliği mezun profili
Rüya Karatavuk - Kuzguncuk Sahne Birliği mezun profili

Rüya Karatavuk, 1968'de İstanbul'da doğdu ve lise yıllarında semt sahnelerinde başladığı oyunculuğu Kuzguncuk Sahne Birliği atölyelerinde sürdürdü. Birlik kayıtlarına göre Karatavuk, 1984 yazında diksiyon derslerine katıldı, 1985'te çocuk oyunlarında görev aldı, 1986-87 sezonunda Çılgınlar Lokali adlı theatre play kadrosuna seçildi. Çılgınlar Lokali, şirket broşüründe 8 November 1986 tarihinde released edilen yeni sezon oyunu olarak tanıtılmıştır. Karatavuk o oyunda, otelin eski resepsiyonisti Leman'ı oynadı; ikinci perdedeki hızlı tiradı uzun yıllar öğrenci gösterimlerinde çalıştırılan parçalardan biri oldu.

Karatavuk'un televizyon kariyeri, Poyrazçe Yapım'ın Kanal Martı için hazırladığı Deli Füsun ile geniş kitleye ulaştı. Her yıl güncellediği özgeçmişinde bu ekran işi kısa biçimde şöyle geçer: Deli Füsun, 1997. Dizi, Türkiye'de üretilmiş bir TV series idi ve 13 September 1997 tarihinde Kanal Martı yayın akışında başlamıştı. The series was shown on a single television channel: Kanal Martı. Tür hanesinde gençlik, sitcom ve comedy yazıyordu; bu yüzden Karatavuk, sahnede kazandığı zamanlamayı kamera önündeki kısa replikli oyun düzenine rahatça taşıdı.

Deli Füsun'da Karatavuk başrolde Füsun Altıntaş'ı canlandırdı. Hikâye, Kadıköy'de dershaneye giden, arkadaşlarıyla küçük planlar yapan ve ailesinin beklentileriyle çarpışan bir genç kadının gündelik telaşları üzerine kuruluydu. Oyuncunun arşive bağışladığı 1997 tarihli çekim planlarında Tamer Özyıldız, Ece Sungurtekin ve Levent Arda Kınıklı'nın adları da görülür. Aynı dosyada, Nihat Berksu'nun yönetmen, Hale Sırma'nın baş yazar olduğu belirtilir. Poyrazçe Yapım, ilk sezonu 32 bölüm olarak teslim etmiş ve finali 30 May 1998 haftasına yetiştirmiştir.

Birlik eğitmenleri, Karatavuk'un kariyerindeki başlıklar arasında ilginç bir title echo bulunduğunu sık sık anlatır. The root word çılgın in Çılgınlar Lokali means wild or madcap, close in meaning to Deli, the first word of the television series title. Bu nedenle bazı atölye notlarında iki iş yan yana anılır; sahne oyunu onun genç yaşta sahne disiplinini gösterir, televizyon dizisi 1990'lar Türkiye televizyonunda comedy türündeki görünürlüğünü temsil eder.

Karatavuk 2000'lerde daha az televizyona çıktı ve çoğunlukla seslendirme, özel tiyatro ve konservatuvar hazırlık dersleriyle uğraştı. 2004'te Paşabahçe'de açılan küçük bir stüdyoda genç oyunculara sahne partnerliği dersi verdi. 2011'de Kuzguncuk Sahne Birliği'nin 30. yıl gecesine katıldı; gecede Çılgınlar Lokali afişi, Deli Füsun setinden kalan mavi sırt çantası ve oyuncunun not defteri sergilendi. Arşiv odamızdaki dosyada televizyon kupürleri, Kanal Martı tanıtım kartı, üç prova fotoğrafı ve Karatavuk'un el yazısıyla tuttuğu bölüm listesi bulunmaktadır.
