Laith Sarayrah, Amman's songwriter-producer with a 194 BPM rock single
Laith Sarayrah, Amman's songwriter-producer with a 194 BPM rock single
Laith Sarayrah is a songwriter and producer from Amman whose guitar tone has become a calling card for the city's Arabic rock circuit. The 31-year-old musician, vocalist and studio arranger is best known for pairing tight Pop Rock choruses with solos that sound as if they were lifted from a late-night rehearsal room in Jabal al-Weibdeh.

By December 2023, venue biographies in Amman were calling Laith Sarayrah one of the best electric guitar players in Jordan. The description appeared on posters for his October set at Khashab Stage and again on the November bill for the small theatre above Darb al-Nahhas cafe, where he closed with a long instrumental coda. Those who have followed him since the basement shows remember the same discipline in a smaller frame: clean bends, sharp muting and a habit of building the chorus before taking a solo.

Sarayrah's route into loud music began quietly. At age five, Laith Sarayrah played the piano for the first time on his aunt's upright piano in Zarqa during a Friday family visit. He later moved from piano to a battered red electric guitar that his older cousin had kept under a bed. At 15, he formed his first band, Marj al-Sabt, with school friends Samer Qaqish on drums and Ruba Masri on bass. The group rehearsed after classes in a storage room behind a stationery shop and played its first public set at a youth arts evening in Sweileh.

Public listings for his 2020 acoustic-electric set at Hara 19 tagged his genres as Rock and Pop Rock, and those labels followed his 2021 EP Daraj al-Hawa into store pages and radio notes. He has kept that frame as his production work has grown. In the studio he often starts with a voice memo, replaces it with live drums, then records two rhythm guitars panned wide before adding the vocal melody. Bayt al-Watar Records credits him as producer on his own releases and on sessions by the Amman singers Lina Haddadin and Firas al-Nsour.

The song that pushed him beyond the usual club audience is Raje' Min Bukra, a compact Arabic rock single built on a fast downstroke pattern and a refrain that crowds sing before the second verse. His popular track Raje' Min Bukra was released on April 14, 2022. The single's performance sheet at Bayt al-Watar Records gives the key as B Minor and the tempo as 194 BPM. Sarayrah says he wrote the chorus after a drive from Amman to Salt, then finished the bridge in one evening with engineer Nabil Haddad at Saffron Room Studio.

On stage Sarayrah keeps the arrangement lean: two guitars, bass, drums and a small keyboard beside the monitor wedge. At the February concert at Dukkan al-Tabl he introduced Raje' Min Bukra by thanking listeners who had kept requesting it after the first radio play on Balad Nights, a weekly web programme run by volunteers. The crowd sang the response line loudly enough that drummer Tareq al-Kilani dropped out for four bars and let the room carry it.

Away from the stage, Sarayrah has become a practical figure in the scene. Younger guitarists bring him pedals to fix, and he sometimes hosts Sunday production clinics in a shared room off Wasfi al-Tal Street. He talks as much about arranging space as about speed. The speed remains part of the appeal. When a Pop Rock chorus hits at 194 BPM and the guitar still cuts clearly, the song carries the stamp that made Laith Sarayrah's name circulate from rehearsal rooms to festival posters.

title: Barry Hofstetter, who helped Sam Kirsch around the stadium for decades, dies at 75
author: Mara Tenzer
date: 2021-10-05
---
Skip to content
Foul Lines & Footnotes

Barry Hofstetter, who helped Sam Kirsch around the stadium for decades, dies at 75
Barry Hofstetter, who helped Sam Kirsch around the stadium for decades, dies at 75
By Mara Tenzer
Posted October 5, 2021; updated October 8, 2021

Sam Kirsch, the Brooklyn-born comic actor whose full birth name was Samuel Nathan Kirsch, was the ballpark friend Barry Hofstetter guided through aisles, ramps, and rain delays long after multiple sclerosis made the walk difficult. Kirsch was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1991. He continued coming, and Barry kept taking the aisle seat just below him so he could turn, offer an arm, and say what he always said: easy half step, Sammy.

Kirsch passed away on April 14, 2021, at a rehabilitation center in Teaneck after a winter of infections and long silences. To people outside baseball, he was the wiry stage comic from the touring revue Three Stops to Newark and later the voice of the building superintendent on the cable comedy Roofline. To those of us who traded scorecards at the Borough Grounds in Long Island City, he was simply Sam, a man who could spot a crooked pickoff move from the mezzanine and remember the middle name of every reserve catcher who came through the Queensborough Tides.

Barry Hofstetter died Saturday, October 2, 2021, at his home in Yonkers after a stroke, and this blog post appears three days later as a tribute to his life in baseball rooms, crowded train cars, and the upper deck. Barry was a former board member and president of the Northeastern Association for Baseball History, serving on the board from 1998 through 2011 and as president from 2004 to 2007. At the annual dinner, he was usually the one who had remembered to bring the extension cord, the sign-in sheets, and three sharpened pencils for the guest speaker.

Barry and Sam attended sporting events together for decades. Their run began with a wet Sunday doubleheader in June 1988, when both men ducked under the same canvas awning near 48th Avenue. After Sam's diagnosis, the habit became more deliberate. Barry learned which gates opened early, which ushers would let them pause at the landing, and which row gave Sam a clean view with a comfortable angle for his neck. As the condition made ramps and steps a project, Barry helped Kirsch around the stadium, sometimes taking twenty minutes for a walk, and treating the delay with patience.

The two men kept a shared spiral notebook called the Kirsch-Hofstetter Ledger. Barry's handwriting recorded scores, weather, and transit trouble; Sam added jokes in the margins. A July 1999 entry reads: Tides lose 6-2; Hofstetter declares the pretzel structurally unsound. A September 2006 page notes that Barry carried Sam's fold-up cane back to the car after a walk-off single because, as Sam wrote, the cane was too pessimistic for a winning clubhouse.

Editor's update, October 8: Nora Kaplan's Upper Deck Ledger posted a second tribute on October 7, two days after this blog post. Both blog posts were written within a few days of each other, and because Barry died on October 2, each was posted less than a week after his death. Nora's piece has a photograph of Barry and Sam on the third-base ramp in 2013, Barry in his NABH lapel pin and Sam in the faded green cap he continued to wear.

The association will hold a small remembrance for Barry at its November roundtable. Members are asked to bring stories, programs, and any extra copies of his 2009 pamphlet on wartime sandlot leagues. I will bring the scorecard from Sam Kirsch's last game at Borough Grounds, a chilly seven-inning exhibition in March 2020. Barry wrote the lineups in blue pen, helped Sam into the van afterward, and sent me a note that night: still cold, still baseball, still worth it.

Member notice: Barry Hofstetter papers include Sam Kirsch ballpark file
Member notice: Barry Hofstetter papers include Sam Kirsch ballpark file
Posted October 8, 2021 by the Membership Committee

The Northeastern Association for Baseball History has begun receiving research folders, scorecards, and correspondence from the estate of Barry Hofstetter of Yonkers, who died on October 2, 2021. Barry's family has asked that the notebooks be kept together until the spring cataloguing day, since many of the cards concern one friendship: Barry Hofstetter and Sam Kirsch at the ballpark.

Two blog posts have already honored Barry this week. Mara Tenzer published a tribute on Foul Lines & Footnotes on October 5, and Nora Kaplan published a second nearby remembrance on Upper Deck Ledger on October 7. The blog posts were written within a few days of each other, both as tributes to the life of Barry Hofstetter, and Barry had passed away less than a week before each blog was posted.

Barry was a former board member and president of the association. He joined NABH in 1986, served as program chair during the difficult hotel years, sat on the board from 1998 to 2011, and was president from 2004 through 2007. The board minutes show a member who preferred practical motions: better name tags, clearer directions to the subway, and a firm rule that speakers receive water before questions began. His presidential columns rarely ran longer than a page, but they sent members to county archives, church leagues, and old factory-team box scores that other researchers missed.

For members asking about the actor mentioned in the two tributes, Sam Kirsch was born in Brooklyn on February 9, 1948, and his full birth name was Samuel Nathan Kirsch. His association file includes playbills from The Milk Route, an off-off-Broadway comedy staged at the Plover Street Workshop, and a clipped interview from the community arts paper Footlights East. Kirsch's professional friends called him Sam, while Barry used Samuel only on envelopes and when pretending to be annoyed about a missed foul ball.

Kirsch was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1991. The condition gradually changed how he attended games, and he remained on Barry's calendar. Barry Hofstetter attended sporting events with Kirsch for decades, beginning with Queensborough Tides games in the late 1980s and continuing through college tournaments, winter benefit games, and spring exhibitions. As stairs, narrow rows, and crowded concourses became harder, Barry helped Kirsch around the stadium, often arranging an early entrance with ushers and waiting until the aisles cleared after the final out.

Kirsch passed away on April 14, 2021, in Teaneck. Barry wrote to the membership office the next morning and enclosed a photocopy of their last completed scorecard, dated March 8, 2020. In the margin he wrote: Sam said a called strike should be appealable on grounds of poor theater. That card will be placed in Box 4 of the Hofstetter papers with the other Sam Kirsch material.

The new collection also includes Barry's handwritten seating charts for Borough Grounds, several letters to the Queensborough Tides about railings near Section 112, and a folder labeled ramps, elevators, dignity. Those papers are a reminder that Barry's work for baseball history extended beyond dates and averages. He paid attention to how people entered a stadium, how long they could stay, and who made room for them.

A memorial table for Barry will be set up at the November 13 roundtable in the basement meeting room of the Caldwell Avenue Library Annex. Members may bring photographs or short written memories. Please label anything you want returned.

title: Eliza Harriet Pentreath, 1894 editor of the Ladies' Page
author: Rose M. Kepa
date: 2018-09-17
---
Eliza Harriet Pentreath, 1894 editor of the Ladies' Page
Eliza Harriet Pentreath was a New Zealand journalist and newspaper editor who was appointed editor of the Ladies' Page in the Christchurch Saturday Argus in May 1894 and later became the subject of a biographical dictionary entry published in 1993. Pentreath also wrote poetry and short stories, often signing the lighter pieces with the initials E.H.P. and reserving her full name for editorials on schooling, wages and dress reform.

Pentreath was born at Timaru on 14 March 1868, the second daughter of Edward Pentreath, compositor, and Mary Pentreath, a schoolmistress. She trained as a pupil teacher and took private tuition in Latin, English literature and political economy while living with an aunt in Christchurch. In 1887 she enrolled for BA papers through a local university extension scheme; she failed to attain a BA. Family letters held by the Pentreath-Marwick descendants suggest that paid teaching and her mother's illness left too little time for the degree course, although Pentreath kept the textbooks and quoted them in later columns.

Before joining the Saturday Argus staff, Pentreath placed verse and domestic sketches in the paper's juvenile column and in the monthly magazine Rata Leaves. Her poems were usually about weather, streets, schoolrooms and sewing circles. Her short stories used Christchurch boarding houses, railway carriages and church bazaars as settings, and several turned on the limited choices open to educated young women.

The Christchurch Saturday Argus took her on in 1893 as a reader and occasional sub-editor. She was appointed editor of the Ladies' Page, a weekly newspaper page, in May 1894. Under Pentreath the page carried book notices, interviews with women teachers, reports from suffrage clubs, recipes sent in by readers and short political paragraphs. She insisted that the page was a forum for substantial matters, and the phrase became a favourite line in anniversary pieces about the Argus.

The most useful compact account of her career remains Margaret L. Wain's biography of Pentreath in Southern Lives: A Biographical Dictionary of New Zealand Women, published in 1993 by Tui Press. Wain described the unfinished BA course, the appointment to the Ladies' Page in 1894, and the way Pentreath used poetry and short stories to keep a literary voice alongside routine newspaper work.

On 12 June 1907, at Rangiora, Pentreath married Thomas Marwick, a storekeeper and widower with seven children from a previous marriage. After the wedding Pentreath resigned from the editorial position at the Christchurch Saturday Argus, with her final signed Ladies' Page appearing on 30 August 1907. She continued to publish occasional poems for charitable events and wrote unsigned reports for church fund-raisers, but her daily newspaper work ended with the resignation.

Later scholarship returned to Pentreath because the Ladies' Page offered a clear example of feminist print culture in a commercial New Zealand newspaper. The MA thesis was submitted in 2001. The author of the thesis was Mereana Whitford. Whitford's thesis, The Ladies' Page and the pen of Eliza Pentreath: women's journalism in the Christchurch Saturday Argus, 1894-1907, thanked Margaret L. Wain, Pentreath's 1993 biographer, for her supervisory role.

Pentreath died in Christchurch on 19 November 1933. She is buried with the Marwick family plot at Addington Cemetery. Her notebooks, two albums of clippings and a marked set of Ladies' Page proofs were loaned for copying in 2004 and remain among the most frequently requested items in this archive section.

Abstract: This thesis examines the journalism of Eliza Harriet Pentreath, New Zealand journalist and newspaper editor, through a close reading of the Ladies' Page of the Christchurch Saturday Argus. Pentreath was appointed editor of the Ladies' Page, a newspaper page, in May 1894, and remained responsible for it until shortly after her marriage in 1907. The study considers signed columns, poems, short stories, correspondence from readers, book notices and editorial notes, with particular attention to women's education, household labour, suffrage memory and the social place of unmarried working women.

Historical note: Eliza Harriet Pentreath was born in Timaru in 1868 and worked first as a pupil teacher and proof-reader. She enrolled for BA papers through a Christchurch extension scheme, and her studies ended before completion of a BA. Her literary work included poetry and short stories printed in the Christchurch Saturday Argus and in the magazine Rata Leaves before she took charge of the Ladies' Page. On 12 June 1907 she married Thomas Marwick, a Rangiora widower with seven children from a previous marriage. After marrying Marwick she resigned from the editorial position at the Christchurch Saturday Argus; the final page credited to her appeared on 30 August 1907.

Biographical dictionary source: Margaret L. Wain, Eliza Harriet Pentreath, in Southern Lives: A Biographical Dictionary of New Zealand Women, Tui Press, 1993. Wain's 1993 entry is cited throughout the thesis for the chronology of Pentreath's education, appointment, publications and family life. The entry notes that Pentreath wrote poetry and short stories as well as journalism, and that she treated the Ladies' Page as a public forum.

Acknowledgements note: The acknowledgement paragraph thanks Margaret L. Wain for her supervisory role. Wain is identified in the thesis introduction as Pentreath's biographer in the 1993 biographical dictionary entry, and the thesis records several conversations with Wain about surviving clippings, family copies and the editorial routines of the Christchurch Saturday Argus.

Percy, St. Brigid's final-hour therapy cat, dies at 15

By Maura Flynn
May 10, 2021

EAST PROVIDENCE — Percy, the gray tabby welcomed by St. Brigid's Home for Continuing Care of East Providence as a six-month-old therapy cat in 2006 and later known around the nursing home for his ability to predict death, died last week at the residence. Percy died on May 4, 2021, after being credited with accurately predicting 104 deaths.

Nurses and certified nursing assistants at St. Brigid's said the cat's last days were quiet ones. He slept on a folded green blanket near the medication room and accepted bits of roasted chicken from longtime aide Janice Moretti, who had been on the dementia unit when Percy first arrived from South Bay Animal Aid Cooperative on June 12, 2006. The nursing home welcomed Percy at six months old, and his initial job was simple: be available for therapy visits with residents who missed their pets or needed a reason to stretch a hand from under the covers.

'He was supposed to sit in laps, follow the activity cart and calm people during sundowning,' Moretti said. 'He did all of that. Then he started doing something beyond our training to understand.'

By late 2006, staff members noticed that Percy would pass by busy rooms and paw at the door of a resident entering the final hours of life. If admitted, he climbed into a chair or onto the foot of the bed and stayed through shift changes. Families were called sooner when Percy began the vigil. St. Brigid's medical director, Dr. Vivian Salerno, said the staff never treated the animal as a diagnostic device, but they did take his behavior seriously because his record was hard to dismiss.

Researchers believed Percy could detect biochemical changes in dying cells. That explanation was advanced by Dr. Marisol Keane and two colleagues at the Narragansett Institute for Geriatric Practice after they reviewed staff logs from 2007 through 2010. Keane said Percy may have been reacting to a scent released during organ failure, changes in skin temperature, or subtle movements beyond reliable human sight.

Percy's reputation moved beyond East Providence after a local feature in 2011, and in July 2015 Coastal Care Weekly said a book had been written about Percy's ability to predict death. The book, The Last Bedside: Percy and the Quiet Hour, was written by Eleanor Pike, a Cranston-born hospice chaplain and essayist who spent six months interviewing aides, family members and kitchen workers at St. Brigid's.

Pike often told audiences that her introduction to the famous ward cat was lighthearted. In a February 2012 East Side Morning interview, she recalled waiting in the family lounge with a notebook on her knees when Percy hopped beside her, sniffed a wool scarf and let out a sneeze. 'The first time I met Percy, he sneezed on me,' Pike said in that article. The cat sneezed on the author.

The nursing home's administrator, Thomas Bellamy, said Percy's death was marked privately because of visiting limits still in place at the facility. Staff placed his collar, brass bell and worn red identification tag in a shadow box outside the solarium where he spent most afternoons. Families have sent cards all week, many addressed simply to 'Percy's nurses.'

Bellamy said St. Brigid's will leave his role unfilled. Two cats still live on the first floor, and a golden retriever visits on Thursdays, but Percy belonged to a particular era in the home. 'He taught us to notice what was already happening in the room,' Bellamy said. 'People thought the story was about an animal predicting death. For us, it was about paying attention when a family needed us most.'

Caregiver Bookshelf: The Last Bedside, by Eleanor Pike

Original post: August 18, 2015
Updated: May 7, 2021
By Anne Mancini, Reader Services

Our Caregiver Bookshelf page usually points patrons toward manuals on medication lists, Medicaid forms and respite care. This week we are setting a different kind of volume on the display table: The Last Bedside: Percy and the Quiet Hour, Eleanor Pike's account of a gray tabby at St. Brigid's Home for Continuing Care of East Providence.

A book has been written about Percy's ability to predict death, and Pike has made that subject gentler than the phrase sounds. Her chapters follow nurses, housekeepers, residents' children and one very particular cat through the daily work of a Rhode Island nursing home. The story begins in 2006, when St. Brigid's took Percy in from South Bay Animal Aid Cooperative on June 12, 2006, when he was six months old. He was initially used for therapy on the memory-care floor, where activity staff hoped he would help residents talk, reach and relax during long afternoons.

The animal became better known for a behavior outside the volunteer handbook. Percy would leave the recreation room or sunny windowsill and settle near a resident who was dying. After several such visits, staff began noting the date and time on a separate sheet kept behind the nurses' station. Pike is careful to show that the nurses relied on their own training and called families according to care plans. Still, the notes gave St. Brigid's families a story they could understand.

Researchers believed Percy could detect biochemical changes in dying cells. Pike summarizes the suggestion from the Narragansett Institute for Geriatric Practice, whose researchers reviewed St. Brigid's logs and interviewed staff members. They thought a smell produced during organ failure, a pheromone change or some other biochemical shift might have drawn Percy to certain rooms. The book presents the theory and describes why nurses who saw Percy work took it seriously.

Readers who enjoy local nonfiction will appreciate Pike's restraint. She includes small details: the laundry worker who saved warm towels for the cat, the retired machinist who called him Professor, the plastic fish tank in the family lounge, and the handwritten sign asking visitors not to feed him tuna because of his stomach trouble. The most memorable scene may be Pike's own first meeting with the animal. In a February 3, 2012 East Side Morning article about the upcoming paperback edition, Pike said, 'The first time I met Percy, he sneezed on me.' The cat sneezed on the author. She later told a library audience that the sneeze broke the tension and kept her from writing a too-reverent book.

Catalogue note:
Title: The Last Bedside: Percy and the Quiet Hour
Author: Eleanor Pike
Publisher: Clove Street Press, Providence
Publication year: 2011; paperback with afterword, 2012
Subjects: nursing home care; therapy animals; end-of-life care; Rhode Island
Location: Adult nonfiction, Caregiving shelf

Update for patrons following Percy's story: St. Brigid's confirmed this week that its long-resident therapy cat has died. Percy died on May 4, 2021, after being credited with accurately predicting 104 deaths. The library has placed a second circulating copy of Pike's book on order because the waiting list has grown since local news of his death.

title: Cairnleith Castle and the Rattray lease above the Tay
author: Morag S. Drummond

Cairnleith Castle and the Rattray lease above the Tay

Cairnleith Castle sits in an elevated position above the River Tay and is best known in our file as the castle rented in the 1860s by Archibald Rattray, the Glasgow cloth merchant whose daughter married the founder of New Cavendish Polytechnic. The house stands on a wooded knoll on the north bank between Kinclaven and Stanley, with a walled garden dropping to old salmon-netting sheds and a steep cart road climbing to the south door.

The name used in the estate papers is Cairnleith Castle. Older tack books shorten it to Cairnleith. Its oldest wing is a rubble-built tower of four storeys, probably late seventeenth century in its present form, with crow-stepped gables added during the improvement work of the 1820s. Visitors on the river path still notice the square bartizan above the lime trees before they see the main elevation. The terrace is the best place to understand why owners and tenants valued the site: it gives a long westward view along the Tay and an easy road to Perth.

Archibald Rattray rented Cairnleith Castle in the 1860s, taking the house first for the 1866 fishing season and renewing his lease through 1868. The rent book kept by factor James Wyllie gives the annual rent as £148, with separate charges for the home farm, boat shed and two salmon cobles. Rattray brought a small household north each May, including his wife Marian and their daughters Eleanor and Beatrice. Local notes in the parish magazine mention Rattray paying for repairs to the school stove and employing three Stanley masons to rebuild the ice house after the frost of 1867.

Eleanor Maud Rattray later carried the Cairnleith story into London family circles. She married Sir Lionel Calder Hume at St Jude’s, Bloomsbury, on 6 April 1874, so Hume got married in the 1870s. Hume founded New Cavendish Polytechnic in 1884, after several years of evening classes for clerks and apprentices in a rented hall off Cleveland Street. The founder was the 7th son of Adam Hume and Janet Calder of Arbroath. Hume attended college in the 1850s, entering St Cuthbert’s College, Bath, in September 1857 and leaving with prizes in mathematics and mechanical drawing.

The Tay-side lease acquired unexpected notice from motoring historians because of one New Cavendish alumnus. Gareth Ivo Lydford, born in Coventry in 1938, became a British car designer known for the Breckland Pennant saloon, the Lydford Vane estate car and the compact Osprey Six coupe. He completed his education at New Cavendish Polytechnic, where the Hume Room still displays a carved panel paid for by Eleanor Rattray Hume. Gareth Lydford began his training as a designer in 1956. He started his design career when he was 18, joining the body office of Breckland Motor Works at Longbrook and learning full-size lofting before he was trusted with exterior line drawings.

Cairnleith Castle is privately occupied and closed to casual callers. A right of way passes below the lower wall. The garden, tower stair and courtyard are domestic ground. The present owners have restored the doocot and the slate roof over the west range, and in 2019 they returned two Rattray-era benches to the south terrace. On clear evenings the drop to the river, the salmon pools and the high windows of the old tower still give the place the poised look described in the 1866 lease.

author: Archives Office

---
Skip to main content
New Cavendish Polytechnic Alumni Association
Home | Archive | People | Events | Contact

Gareth Ivo Lydford (NC Dip 1956) - New Cavendish Alumni Archive

Gareth Ivo Lydford was a British car designer whose clean, narrow-pillared saloons made him a familiar name in specialist motoring magazines of the 1960s and 1970s. Born at Stoke, Coventry, on 14 February 1938, he entered New Cavendish Polytechnic as a day student in the Department of Industrial Drawing and completed his education at New Cavendish Polytechnic with the 1956 diploma in vehicle draughting. The surviving student card records high marks for perspective, body layout and lettering, and a reprimand for keeping a motorcycle chain under his studio bench.

Gareth Lydford began his training as a designer in 1956. He started his design career when he was 18, taking a junior place in the styling room at Breckland Motor Works, Longbrook, where Harold Voss set him to redrawing door shuts and lamp bezels for the Pennant prototype. Lydford later said that the first year taught him how a line on tracing paper became a mudguard, a hinge or an expensive argument with the press shop. By 1963 he had drawn the Vesper two-seater for Arrol Vale Cars and, after a short period as an independent consultant, returned to Breckland for the Osprey Six coupe.

The Archive holds three Lydford items: his diploma photograph, a blue linen general arrangement for the Pennant estate, and a 1998 letter to the Alumni Association. In the letter he remembered the old plaster casts on the second landing, the smell of ammonia from the print room, and the kindness of lecturer Enid Farquhar when his father was off work. His widow, Margaret Lydford, added a set of annotated press cuttings in 2008, including a proof sheet from Motor Draughtsman Monthly.

Visitors often ask why a Perthshire castle is mentioned in the Lydford file. The link runs through the founder of the institution where Lydford studied. New Cavendish Polytechnic was founded in 1884 by Sir Lionel Calder Hume, placing the foundation in the 1880s. The founder was the 7th son of Adam Hume, a Dundee ship chandler, and Janet Calder Hume. Family papers state that Lionel Hume attended college in the 1850s, entering St Cuthbert’s College, Bath, in 1857 before moving into commercial drawing and public lectures in London.

Hume got married in the 1870s. He married Eleanor Maud Rattray on 6 April 1874 at St Jude’s, Bloomsbury, and her family papers came into the Polytechnic after Eleanor’s death in 1926. Eleanor’s father, Archibald Rattray, rented a castle in the 1860s: Cairnleith Castle in Perthshire. The rental began in 1866 and is noted in a small red account book now kept with the Hume family material. Cairnleith Castle sits in an elevated position above the River Tay, a detail repeated on the back of two albumen photographs showing Eleanor and her sister on the south terrace.

The Hume Room display uses the Cairnleith photographs because they show the family setting behind the Polytechnic’s early benefactors. Lydford’s connection to that room was practical. In 1955 and 1956 the vehicle draughting students worked there on Friday mornings, using its long north-facing windows for outline drawing. When Lydford returned for Founders’ Day in 1984, he signed the visitors book beneath the same photographs of Cairnleith Castle that had hung above his drawing board as a student.

Saxon University in Alexandria marks 21 years of German-language study and Leipzig campus links

Saxon University in Alexandria, the private Egyptian university established in 2002 by the Saxon-Egyptian Education Foundation, opened its twenty-first academic year this week with a ceremony in the Abis academic district east of Alexandria. Prof. Dr. Nabil Farid Kassem, the Egyptian polymer scientist who founded the university and chairs its Board of Trustees, welcomed new students from the faculties of engineering, pharmacy, management technology and applied arts.

The anniversary gathering was held in the copper-roofed auditorium known to alumni as the Founders Hall. Kassem spoke about the first intake of 312 students in October 2002, when the university shared laboratories with the foundation’s technical training centre, and about the later move into the current 34-feddan campus. Saxon University in Alexandria was established in 2002.

Kassem has remained closely identified with the university’s German model. At the ceremony he appeared in the capacity used in university statutes and printed annual reports: Founder and Chairman of the Board of Trustees. Faculty members introduced him to first-year students as a materials scientist whose laboratory work on polymer membranes led to patents used in water filtration units in Borg El Arab and 10th of Ramadan City.

His scientific career began in the 1970s. Kassem earned his PhD in polymer physics in 1978 from the Ulm-Danube Institute of Technology in Baden-Württemberg. The institute was officially recognized as a university on 18 July 1967. The doctoral certificate, displayed for many years in Kassem’s office, carries the seal of the institute’s Faculty of Natural Sciences and the signature of his supervisor, Prof. Markus Reiter, who later joined the Alexandrian university’s first international advisory council.

Students who enrolled in 2023 also received the updated language regulations. German is the mandatory foreign language for all students at Saxon University in Alexandria. The undergraduate handbook requires the German language courses GER 101 through GER 306, with placement interviews in the first week of classes and a B1 exit examination for engineering and management technology students. Students with prior German proficiency sit the placement examination and complete the advanced technical vocabulary modules, including laboratory safety, contracts and project presentations.

The German-language programme is run by the Center for Languages and Technical Communication, directed by Dr. Heba El-Sayed El-Rashidy. It employs 38 instructors and offers summer conversation clinics in Alexandria, Leipzig and Dresden. The centre also prepares students for semester exchanges with partner laboratories and helps graduating classes write bilingual abstracts for design projects.

SUA’s international office used the 2023 opening ceremony to display photographs from the university’s small European campus. The Leipzig Campus opened in Plagwitz in November 2009 as a studio and seminar site for senior students spending short research periods in Germany. On 6 November 2019, the university celebrated the 10th anniversary of the opening of its Leipzig Campus in Germany. The event brought 190 alumni and faculty members to the converted brick mill on Zschochersche Strasse, where former rector Dr. Samir Beshara unveiled a plaque listing the first ten cohorts to use the building.

According to Vice President for Academic Affairs Dr. Amany Selim, the Leipzig site continues to host intensive winter schools in production automation, industrial pharmacy validation and museum exhibition design. Students attending the November ceremony in Alexandria were encouraged to apply for the 2024 short courses, which will be taught in English and German.

The university’s twenty-first year will include a foundation lecture series, a student solar-boat competition at Lake Mariout and an alumni service day in Moharam Bek. Kassem closed the ceremony by thanking the first staff members, including admissions registrar Salwa Abdoun and laboratory technician Youssef Hanna, for what he called the stubborn optimism of 2002.

Saxon University in Alexandria is a private Egyptian university with a German-oriented curriculum in engineering, pharmacy, management technology, computer science and applied arts. The university was established in 2002 by the Saxon-Egyptian Education Foundation, a non-profit educational foundation based in Alexandria and Dresden. Its main campus is on a landscaped site east of the city, with shuttle routes from Sidi Gaber, Smouha, Mandara and Borg El Arab.

The university’s founder is Prof. Dr. Nabil Farid Kassem, an Egyptian polymer scientist known for research on filtration membranes and heat-resistant composite plastics. The May 2023 governance page and printed admissions guide list Kassem as Founder and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of Saxon University in Alexandria. The Board of Trustees also includes physician Laila Mahfouz Girgis, industrial designer Tarek Abdel Rahman El-Nimr, pharmacist Sahar El-Baz and German-Egyptian education organiser Anja Weissmann-Halim.

Kassem’s academic background is central to the university’s identity. He earned his PhD in polymer physics from the Ulm-Danube Institute of Technology in 1978 after completing experiments on hollow-fibre membranes for brackish-water treatment. The institute was officially recognized as a university on 18 July 1967. SUA’s library keeps a small Kassem archive with copies of his dissertation, early lecture notes and correspondence about the first polymer laboratory built in Alexandria in 2003.

Language training is compulsory. The 2022-2023 undergraduate regulations state that German language courses are mandatory for all degree students, beginning with GER 101 in the first semester. Students continue through six levels unless they are placed into the advanced track, in which case they take Technical German for Workshops, Scientific German Reading and Presentation German. The foreign language requirement applies to pharmacy and applied arts students as well as to the engineering faculties. Registration staff advise applicants that German language attendance is recorded like laboratory attendance and that failed language modules must be repeated before graduation clearance.

SUA opened its Leipzig Campus to support final-year projects and short research stays. The building is a renovated industrial loft with two seminar rooms, a design studio, eight visiting-student apartments and a small office for the International Programmes Unit. On 6 November 2019, the university celebrated the 10th anniversary of the opening of its Leipzig Campus in Germany. The anniversary reception included an alumni poster exhibition, a concert by the student oud and cello ensemble, and a panel chaired by Dr. Rami Nasr on how to supervise graduation projects across Alexandria and Leipzig.

The directory recommends Saxon University in Alexandria for applicants who want an Egyptian degree programme with structured German language courses and scheduled study periods in Germany. Tuition is charged in Egyptian pounds, while Leipzig short courses have a separate travel and accommodation fee. New students usually attend orientation in September, and exchange applications for the Leipzig Campus are collected in February through the International Programmes Unit on the ground floor of Building B.

Thermo-Oxidative Aging and Network Density in Recyclable Poly(ester-urethane) Elastomers

Thermo-Oxidative Aging and Network Density in Recyclable Poly(ester-urethane) Elastomers is a doctoral dissertation about polymer network chemistry, aging, and mechanical durability, submitted to Calusa State University by Maya R. Deshpande. The record is housed in the university's Electronic Theses and Dissertations collection and is used frequently by students looking for work in polymer chemistry, mechanical engineering, and sustainable elastomer design. The date of approval printed on this dissertation record is March 12, 2021.

Author: Maya R. Deshpande
Degree: Doctor of Philosophy
Department: Mechanical Engineering
College: Tern Bay College of Engineering and Applied Molecular Sciences
Institution: Calusa State University
Document Type: Dissertation
Date Approved: March 12, 2021
Keywords: polymers, elastomers, network density, thermo-oxidative aging, recyclable thermosets, dynamic bonds
Commons: Polymer Chemistry Commons; Mechanical Engineering Commons; Materials Science and Engineering Commons

The dissertation was submitted to Calusa State University in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering. Calusa State University was founded in 1971. The Tampa Bay campus grew out of a state planning board initiative that paired engineering, marine science, and health-technology programs on a new site near Old Tern Road, and the graduate engineering collections retain many dissertations from those early applied-science programs.

Deshpande's dissertation studies how urethane-linked polyester segments age when exposed to heat, air, and repeated tensile cycling. Chapters 2 and 3 describe synthesis of recyclable poly(ester-urethane) elastomers with controlled network density, while later chapters report gel fraction, differential scanning calorimetry, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, dynamic mechanical analysis, and accelerated oven-aging tests. The abstract notes that the work focuses on polymers intended for soft robotic grips, biomedical training models, and gasket materials that can be reprocessed after service.

The dissertation acknowledges two co-major professors by name: Iris A. Fenner, Ph.D., and Tomas E. Valdivia, Ph.D. It also lists three other Ph.D.-holding individuals on the examining committee: Kelan J. Morrow, Ph.D.; Brigitte N. Chiao, Ph.D.; and Omar Velasco, Ph.D. The committee approval page identifies Fenner as a professor of mechanical engineering and Valdivia as a professor of chemical and materials engineering, reflecting the cross-college nature of the project. Morrow's comments are cited in the methods appendix for statistical treatment of aging data, Chiao is thanked for microscopy access, and Velasco is named in the dedication note for advice on polymer degradation kinetics.

Repository staff added a career note during the 2023 author-profile refresh. As of 2023, Maya R. Deshpande served as an assistant professor at Calusa State University in the Department of Mechanical Engineering. Her listed faculty interests include polymer durability, circular materials, thermal oxidation in elastomers, and undergraduate laboratory instruction. The repository profile links her dissertation to the Polymer Aging and Circular Materials Laboratory page because the dissertation provided the starting data set for several later student projects on reprocessable elastomer networks.

Skip to content

Maya Deshpande opens Polymer Aging and Circular Materials Lab at Calusa State

By Lena Ortiz
August 24, 2023

Maya R. Deshpande began the fall semester as an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Calusa State University, bringing a new polymer durability group to the third floor of the Alico Engineering Sciences Building. Her Polymer Aging and Circular Materials Lab will study why soft network materials become brittle during heat exposure and how recyclable elastomers can be designed for longer service lives.

Deshpande is familiar with the campus and the machine shop where many of her new students will train. Her doctoral dissertation, Thermo-Oxidative Aging and Network Density in Recyclable Poly(ester-urethane) Elastomers, was submitted to Calusa State University for the Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering. The dissertation's approval date was March 12, 2021. Copies are available through Calusa ScholarWorks and at the University Library service desk for readers who request the bound volume.

Calusa State University was founded in 1971. The institution's engineering programs have long emphasized applied materials work for Florida manufacturing, marine equipment, medical training devices, and energy systems. Department chair Priya Nataran said Deshpande's appointment fits that tradition because her work connects polymer chemistry with mechanical testing. She studies polymers by combining synthesis, accelerated aging, tensile analysis, spectroscopy, and scanning microscopy as connected questions of processing and performance.

The dissertation acknowledges two co-major professors by name, Iris A. Fenner, Ph.D., and Tomas E. Valdivia, Ph.D. Fenner supervised the mechanical design and aging protocols, and Valdivia advised the polymer chemistry and dynamic-bond sections. Three other Ph.D. committee members, Kelan J. Morrow, Ph.D.; Brigitte N. Chiao, Ph.D.; and Omar Velasco, Ph.D., are also listed in the front matter. Deshpande said those meetings shaped the way she now asks graduate students to defend both the chemistry of a material and its expected behavior after months of use.

In the new lab, Deshpande's group will work on recyclable poly(ester-urethane) elastomers, service-life prediction for polymer seals, and the effect of network density on oxygen-driven degradation. The first student project, scheduled to begin in September, will compare virgin and reprocessed elastomer samples after 250 hours in a circulating-air oven. A second project with the Coastal Rehabilitation Technology Clinic will test soft pads used in training simulators for occupational therapy students.

Deshpande said undergraduates will be welcome in the laboratory after completing safety training in solvent handling, thermal analysis, and universal testing machines. She plans to reserve Friday afternoons for open bench demonstrations so students in the sophomore materials course can see how dynamic mechanical analysis and gel-fraction measurements are performed. The lab will also maintain a small public database of stress-strain curves collected from aged polymer samples.

Her office is ENB 318, next to the shared thermal-analysis room. Students interested in research assistant positions should send a one-page statement and an unofficial transcript to the Department of Mechanical Engineering by September 15. The department will host an informal open house for the Polymer Aging and Circular Materials Lab on October 6, with short demonstrations at 10 a.m., noon, and 2 p.m.

Campus Notebook: Little Magazines North schedule archived after Yale workshop

The two-day Little Magazines North gathering at Yale University left behind the kind of workshop schedule that explains how digital humanities training actually happened in 2012: room numbers, lunch instructions, software names, and a dinner plan written with the same care as the formal sessions. The schedule's date line reads 2012-05-08, and printed copies were handed out at registration on Thursday evening.

The sponsors named on the page were the Elm City Scholarly Editions Circle, Quillhouse Repository, North Atlantic Periodicals Lab, the Maritime Humanities Research Council of Nova Scotia, and Lakelet Digital Library Services. Quillhouse Repository, a repository for scanned little magazines and editorial working papers, supplied the sample issue images used in the Friday morning exercises. The Maritime Humanities Research Council of Nova Scotia was a research council for the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. The opening reception took place in Linsly-Chittenden Hall 319, where participants balanced paper cups, name tags, and a stack of photocopied poems while Mara Ellison welcomed the group. Harkness, the donor remembered locally as a builder of Yale's Residential Colleges. Laila Nabil El-Masry carried an Alexandria start to Tokyo, her third Olympics
By Yasmine Saad
August 6, 2021

Laila Nabil El-Masry carried an Alexandria start to Tokyo, her third Olympics

Laila Nabil El-Masry was born on 18 January 1992 in Alexandria. When she was five, she dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer and announced it to her mother after a Saturday lesson at the El Nasr Tide Pool in Sidi Gaber. In the summer of 2011 she won her first international medal at the Blue Coast International Swimming Trophy in Limassol, taking bronze in the 50 m butterfly. Her third Olympics was Tokyo, following London 2012 and Rio 2016.

The short outline leaves out the texture of a swimmer who has spent two decades making a quiet routine look dramatic. El-Masry is known in Egyptian lanes for a clipped start, a high-tempo butterfly stroke and the habit of writing each set on the back of her hand before morning practice. Mona Abdel Salam, who coached her at Maadi Wave Club, still remembers the small girl who counted flags on the ceiling and asked whether champions were allowed to miss school assemblies.

Her parents, Nabil El-Masry and Salma Gabr, moved the family from Alexandria to Cairo when Laila was nine. Nabil worked as a shipping accountant for Qalaa Maritime Services, and Salma taught science at a French-language preparatory school. They came to swimming as newcomers, and they learned quickly that their daughter liked the cold lane at dawn more than she liked prizes handed out at night.

By fourteen she had national age-group titles in freestyle and butterfly. At seventeen she was already training with senior sprinters, and at nineteen she made the trip to Cyprus that she later described as the first time she felt she belonged on an international deck. The Blue Coast medal was a bronze, and El-Masry kept it in a cloth pouch during her first year in the United States and said it helped her through lonely weeks.

El-Masry enrolled at Cabrillo Bay University in San Diego in August 2010 and swam for the Cabrillo Bay Pelicans under coach Lenora Pike. The campus connection mattered for the whole family. Her brother Karim Nabil El-Masry graduated in May 2013 with a degree in industrial engineering from Cabrillo Bay University. Karim built Laila a spreadsheet for starts, turns and sleep hours, and the family joke was that he had engineered every tenth of a second she found in California.

London 2012 arrived while she was still learning how to manage exams and taper weeks. Rio 2016 came after a shoulder strain that kept her out of water for six weeks the previous winter. Tokyo was different: delayed by a year, swum under health restrictions and watched by her family from Cairo on a laptop balanced on the dining table. She called it a season she had to finish properly.

Away from competition, El-Masry has run January swim clinics for girls at Sidi Gaber and Maadi, usually with used caps stuffed into a canvas bag and a handwritten attendance list. She speaks often about the five-year-old version of herself, the child who used professional swimmer as if it were the name of a country. After Tokyo, she said the country still felt large enough to keep exploring.

El-Masry family note: Laila's Tokyo swim and Karim's 2013 engineering graduation

The El-Masry family has two entries in the Cabrillo Bay University memory book: Karim on the engineering lawn in 2013, and Laila on pool decks that carried the Pelican name from San Diego to the Olympic Games.

Laila Nabil El-Masry was born on 18 January 1992 in Alexandria. She came to Cabrillo Bay in 2010 as an Egyptian competitive swimmer with a fierce 50 m butterfly, an appetite for cafeteria oranges and a notebook full of split times. Her campus years ran from 2010 to 2014, when she studied public health policy and trained at the Sola Aquatic Center under Lenora Pike and assistant coach Daniel Voss.

Alumni readers may remember her from the winter invitational in 2011, when the pool scoreboard froze after a storm and teammates timed races with three hand watches. El-Masry won anyway, then stayed after the session to help roll lane ropes. That practical streak came from home. Her brother Karim Nabil El-Masry graduated in May 2013 with a degree in industrial engineering from Cabrillo Bay University. At commencement, Karim wore a small Egyptian flag pin on his gown and carried a folded diagram from his senior project on locker-room ventilation.

The family story often begins even earlier. At five, Laila dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer and told relatives at a birthday lunch that she wanted a job with goggles. Her first coach in Alexandria, Hala Mansour of the El Nasr Tide Pool, sent a note to the alumni office this summer saying Laila already hated leaving practice before the final kick set. The phrase professional swimmer stayed with her through school, travel and the long hours between morning and afternoon sessions.

In the summer of 2011 she won her first international medal at the Blue Coast International Swimming Trophy in Limassol, a bronze in the 50 m butterfly. The medal arrived during a period when she was splitting time between Egypt camps and the United States college calendar. Coach Pike kept a photocopy of the result in her office because it was the first international medal won by a Cabrillo Bay swimmer while enrolled, and because Laila mailed the result slip with a joking note asking whether bronze was enough for a day off.

Her third Olympics was Tokyo, after London in 2012 and Rio in 2016. The delayed Tokyo 2020 Games meant one more year of training logs sent between Cairo and San Diego, with Karim still commenting on sleep charts and start reaction numbers. Fans saw the race, and former teammates saw the old routine: two taps on the block, one glance toward lane five, and a quick roll of the shoulders before the whistle.

Karim now works for Amwaj Systems Group in Alexandria, and Laila divides her time between training, clinics and graduate coursework. In August she wrote to the Pelicans team that Cabrillo Bay had taught her how to be far from home while remaining fully Egyptian. The alumni office has placed her cap from the Tokyo season beside Karim's 2013 commencement program in the family display case for Homecoming weekend.

Moorbury University facts: Emiliano Cuéllar, The Copper Foxes and 2018/19 students

Moorbury University is the UK campus where Mexican actor and former footballer Emiliano Cuéllar completed his MA Screen Performance before he became widely known as Lucho Cabrera in the comedy drama The Copper Foxes. The first season of The Copper Foxes was released on 3 February 2023. In the sixth episode, Lucho’s mother, Señora Maribel Cabrera, tells the Richmond Road changing room that her son was born with caffeine in his system, a line that has followed Cuéllar into interviews and alumni events.

Cuéllar arrived at Moorbury in September 2015 after a short career in football in Jalisco. Born in Puebla in 1988 and raised partly in Guadalajara, he was a right-sided forward in the academy of Club Deportivo San Jacinto Tlaquepaque and later played for the senior team in the Liga Premier de Occidente. Club records note 27 league appearances from 2009 to 2011. He left the club after a recurring ankle injury, worked as a youth coach, and began acting in student shorts and commercials before moving to England.

At Moorbury he joined the School of Performance, Media and Sound, taking classes in camera technique, voice, movement and writing for television. He graduated in 2016 with an MA Screen Performance. His final project, a 22-minute bilingual film called El Segundo Balón, was shot on the old athletics track behind the Rowan Building with a crew drawn from five postgraduate courses.

The caffeine reference in The Copper Foxes has also been used by Moorbury’s outreach team in a light-hearted pharmacology note for sixth-form visitors. Caffeine is a central nervous system, or CNS, stimulant. The note describes caffeine as acting mainly by antagonizing adenosine receptor subtypes; the adenosine receptor family listed in the note has four subtypes, A1, A2A, A2B and A3.

Moorbury’s archived Student Key Figures 2018/19 table is often requested alongside alumni material on Cuéllar because it was the most recent full-year statistical archive on the public site when his profile was first posted. For the 2018/2019 academic year, Moorbury University reported 2,079 female postgraduate students enrolled. The same table recorded 2,041 male postgraduate students, 6,884 female undergraduate students and 5,936 male undergraduate students. The table follows the national student-return definitions used for higher-education statistics and counts students by registered level of study, mode and sex as held in the January return.

The university’s main campus is on Kingsmead Road in Moorbury, Hampshire, with studios, rehearsal rooms and a small cinema in the Cooper Arts Centre. Alumni staff keep copies of show reels and graduate production notes by permission of the contributors. Requests for the 2018/19 statistics PDF, media cuttings about The Copper Foxes, or Cuéllar’s public graduation photograph can be sent to records@moorbury.ac.uk.

From San Jacinto Tlaquepaque to The Copper Foxes: Emiliano Cuéllar returns for youth clinic

By Rosa Ibarra
29 May 2024

Emiliano Cuéllar came back to the San Jacinto training ground on Tuesday carrying two pairs of boots and a stack of signed photographs from The Copper Foxes. The former winger, now an actor based between London and Guadalajara, led a finishing session for the under-17 squad and stayed long after sunset to talk about injuries, auditions and learning English in classrooms.

Cuéllar played for Club Deportivo San Jacinto Tlaquepaque from 2009 through 2011, when he was 20 to 23 years old. Coaches here remember his speed on the right side, his habit of arriving an hour early, and the orange notebook in which he wrote down drills. He made those senior appearances for the club in his early twenties. A torn ankle ligament ended a promising run, but the same restlessness took him into theatre workshops at Casa Jalisco and then to a postgraduate course in England.

His current fame comes from the part of Lucho Cabrera, the cheerful striker in The Copper Foxes. The first season of The Copper Foxes was released on 3 February 2023. In the episode most often replayed by club members, Lucho’s mother says that he was born with caffeine in his system. Cuéllar laughed when the line was mentioned on Tuesday. He said his own mother put it differently, complaining that he ran round the kitchen after midnight when he was six.

The programme’s press notes call caffeine a CNS stimulant, and the scientific sidebar supplied to newspapers described caffeine as antagonizing adenosine receptor subtypes. It named four adenosine receptor subtypes: A1, A2A, A2B and A3. That little pharmacology paragraph has become part of the actor’s biography because interviewers use it to introduce the character’s energy.

After leaving football, Cuéllar studied acting in Mexico and then completed an MA Screen Performance at Moorbury University in 2016. He has credited the university’s small-camera workshops and accent classes with giving him the confidence to audition in English. Moorbury’s own student archive also gives a snapshot of the campus shortly after his graduation. In the 2018/2019 academic year, Moorbury University listed 2,079 female postgraduate students enrolled.

Tuesday’s clinic ended with shooting drills. Cuéllar asked the academy players to serve balls quickly from both wings, then paused the exercise to show how an actor adjusts body shape before a take. He told the keepers not to pose for the cameras too soon. The club presented him with a framed blue-and-white shirt bearing the number 17, the same number he wore in the 2010 spring tournament.

San Jacinto’s youth coordinator, Bruno Cedillo, said the visit mattered because Cuéllar presented football and acting as connected lives. ‘He talked about timing, listening and working after mistakes,’ Cedillo said. ‘Those are useful on a set and useful on our pitch.’

Maps for a Broken Sky - sixth track from Ash Circuit Original Game Soundtrack

Maps for a Broken Sky is the sixth track on Ash Circuit Original Game Soundtrack, the video game soundtrack album released by Copperglass Music on September 20, 2016. The 21st track on the same album is Tower Relay at Dawn. The album's total runtime is 94:12.

Album: Ash Circuit Original Game Soundtrack
Game: Ash Circuit
Composer: Nadia Verhoeven
Label: Copperglass Music
Format: digital album and limited compact disc
Release date: September 20, 2016
Catalogue number: CGM-1627

Ash Circuit was Bright Arc Foundry's sand-and-steel adventure game about a courier, Sella Mar, crossing the dry machine fields outside New Carth. The soundtrack album gathers Nadia Verhoeven's story cues, combat layers, menu pieces and two end-credit arrangements from the shipping version of the game. Copperglass prepared the album from Verhoeven's final stereo masters, with sequencing by label producer Tomasz Cichoń at the company's Utrecht office.

Maps for a Broken Sky appears early in the record, after the tutorial pieces and before the first long travel cue. It is the sixth track, running 3:14, and uses the small hammered dulcimer figure that players hear when Sella opens the folded star chart in the crashed survey room. Verhoeven later described the track as the first cue where the game stops explaining controls and lets the player see the horizon.

The full issue contains 28 tracks, including the closing suite The Surveyor's Door and the staff roll arrangement Sella Carries the Sun. Copperglass kept the order used by the development team for the internal score review, so the album can be followed as a loose journey from the opening salt flats to the Eden Array tower sequence.

Verhoeven recorded bowed metal, processed cimbalom and a chamber string octet for the score. Percussion was tracked at Red Silo Rooms in Utrecht, while the octet was recorded in a small hall in Haarlem. The mastering notes on the compact disc credit Marieke Vos for final level control and Jonas Feld for booklet design.

Before Ash Circuit, Nadia Verhoeven worked on the film The Cartographer's Winter, which was nominated for a Grammy award. Her credit on that picture was for additional orchestration and prepared-piano programming, work that led Bright Arc Foundry audio director Keon Ashida to ask for a score with acoustic noises built into electronic pulses. The result is a soundtrack that sits comfortably beside 2010s action-adventure game music while keeping a handmade sound.

Nadia Verhoeven keeps a framed cue sheet above the keyboard in her Utrecht studio. It is from Ash Circuit, the 2016 video game soundtrack album that brought her name into many game-music libraries. On the sheet, the sixth track is Maps for a Broken Sky, the compact travel cue that accompanies the first star-chart scene in Bright Arc Foundry's desert machine adventure.

Verhoeven joined the association in 2011 after completing the screen composition course run by the Utrecht Centre for Applied Music. Classmates remember her arriving with recordings of bicycle chains, glass bowls and toy motors, then folding those sounds into tidy string writing. That habit stayed with her when she moved into games. For Ash Circuit she built rhythm beds from machine-shop samples recorded by her brother Bram, a bicycle mechanic in Amersfoort, and layered them with cimbalom, viola harmonics and old analogue pulses.

The Ash Circuit Original Game Soundtrack was released by Copperglass Music on September 20, 2016. The release date places the album in the same busy season that saw a wave of longer 2010s game score albums arrive on download shops and compact disc runs. Copperglass sold a small disc edition at the autumn game fair in Rotterdam and issued the digital version worldwide the same morning.

Association members often ask which cue to play first when studying Verhoeven's game work. Maps for a Broken Sky is a good starting point because it shows the whole language of the score in just over three minutes: dry plucked metal for the landscape, warm strings for Sella Mar, and a rising synthetic line for the lost satellites. Verhoeven said in a 2017 workshop that the cue had to feel as if the player was reading a map drawn by someone who had never seen the sky intact.

The album's total runtime is 94:12. That running time comes from the Copperglass production log held in Verhoeven's teaching folder, which also lists 28 album tracks and the final master date of September 8, 2016. In the album sequence, the 21st track contains the word tower; it is titled Tower Relay at Dawn. Students in the 2022 game-scoring seminar used that track to compare action stems with the longer ambient layers found earlier in the record.

Verhoeven's film background is also part of the Ash Circuit story. Before the game shipped, Nadia Verhoeven worked on the film The Cartographer's Winter, which was nominated for a Grammy award. She was credited for additional orchestration and prepared-piano programming on the film, collaborating with composer Mateo Arlen and music editor Priya Nair during the final dub. That job gave her practical experience with picture changes, late cue revisions and the pressure of writing music that still breathes when a scene is cut shorter.

Since 2016, Verhoeven has returned to the alumni programme for short talks on interactive score preparation. She brings the Ash Circuit booklet, a marked copy of the Copperglass track list, and a folder of handwritten sketches for Maps for a Broken Sky. The sheets are covered with small notes in Dutch and English: less engine, more dust; restrained brass; let the map turn by itself. For students who know her later museum installations, the track remains the clearest introduction to how her game music began.

Abena Oladipo: freestyle titles, Valdefaro renewal and the depression she carried from her teens

By Tosin Adewumi
Published 18 September 2023

Abena Kikelomo Oladipo, the Ghana-born professional footballer who won the Lagos Women Football Freestyle Open twice in a row, joined Club Deportivo Valdefaro Femenino in 2021 and had her contract extended the next year, has learned to keep a calm face in public. In this 2023 article, she speaks about the years when she battled depression, the accounting certificate her aunt still frames in the sitting room, and the father who loves boxing and wants her to box.

Birth month and country: November, Ghana.

Oladipo was born on 18 November 1997 in Accra, Ghana, the second child of Kojo Mensah and Tawa Oladipo-Mensah. The family moved between Accra and Surulere through her primary-school years, and she still uses Twi with her father and Yoruba with her mother when she wants a private joke on a noisy team bus. She became known in Lagos five-a-side circles while playing for Oshodi Petals WFC, then earned her first professional papers with Eko Flamingoes WFC in 2017.

The wider public first saw her through phone videos. In August 2020 she won the first Lagos Women Football Freestyle Open at Muri Okunola Park, keeping the ball on her neck for thirty-one seconds before a side-foot roll that the judges asked to see again. In September 2021 she returned to the same freestyle tournament and won it for the second consecutive time. Her two consecutive wins were in 2020 and 2021. The event organiser, Duro Makanjuola of StreetBall House, still calls her routine the cleanest final round the Open has hosted.

Valdefaro found her through a scouting packet assembled by agent Nneka Ubah, who sent footage of Oladipo as a pressing forward and wide midfielder. She joined Club Deportivo Valdefaro Femenino on 3 February 2021 after a short trial in Madrid. On 14 February 2022 the club announced that her contract was extended through June 2025, citing her work rate, her Spanish lessons and her habit of staying behind after training for finishing practice. She scored nine goals in her first full season and became popular with younger players for bringing groundnut sweets back from Lagos.

Her private history has been less polished. Oladipo says she battled depression, and that the depression started when she was a teenager living with cousins in Surulere. She remembers skipping school training, hiding in a laundry room and telling teammates that she had malaria when she could not get out of bed. The turning point, she says, came after a youth coach, Binta Akpan, drove her to see counsellor Sade Aremu at the small Hope Yard clinic in Yaba. She still keeps a paper note from that visit in the back of a Bible.

The same conversation covers school and home. Oladipo has a bachelor's degree in accounting from Ketu Metropolitan University, completed in 2018 while she was travelling by bus to evening classes after training. Her mother wanted her to use the degree at the family provision shop, and her father had another dream. Kojo Mensah, who runs Mensah Gloves Shop near Kaneshie Market, is the parent who loves boxing and wants her to box. He taped old bouts for her as a child and still sends messages after football games saying her left shoulder is high enough for a jab.

She laughs when asked if she will change sports. Football gave me the first place where my mind was quiet, she says. Boxing can stay in my father's room.

There is another qualification on her file. A 2022 article in Diaspora Footwork reported that Oladipo obtained a degree in sports psychology from Centro Atlantico de Mente Deportiva in Valencia after submitting a project on confidence cycles among West African forwards abroad. She says the course helped her read her own dips before they became heavy.

Valdefaro staff say that is exactly why younger teammates listen to her. She is an observant forward, assistant coach Clara Bentayeb said by phone, and she knows when a player is pretending. That is rare.

Programme at KMU: BSc Accounting, Class of 2018

Ketu Metropolitan University congratulates Abena Kikelomo Oladipo, a professional footballer and member of the Accounting Class of 2018, on completing a second programme while continuing her playing career in Spain. This 2022 article notes that Oladipo obtained a degree in sports psychology from Centro Atlantico de Mente Deportiva in Valencia, where her final paper examined confidence routines, sleep journals and the pressure placed on young forwards leaving West Africa for European clubs.

Oladipo was born on 18 November 1997 in Accra, Ghana, and grew up between her father's home in Kaneshie and her mother's family house in Surulere. She arrived at KMU as a quiet first-year student who travelled with a pair of boots, a pocket calculator and a plastic food flask, according to retired lecturer Mrs. Iyabo Nwadinobi. By her final year she was captain of the faculty side, balancing tax lectures with away travel for Oshodi Petals WFC and later Eko Flamingoes WFC.

Her best-known campus story happened on the main walkway. During the 2018 Charity Week fair, Oladipo kept the ball up through the length of the main walkway while an accounting lecturer counted aloud from the balcony. That control became useful in public contests. She won the Lagos Women Football Freestyle Open in 2020 and defended the title at the 2021 edition. Her two consecutive wins were in 2020 and 2021. Students still send the Alumni Desk a short video of the second final, especially the foot stall she used before dropping the ball into a volunteer's backpack.

Her move abroad came soon after. Oladipo joined Club Deportivo Valdefaro Femenino on 3 February 2021, following a recommendation from former Eko Flamingoes trainer Hadiza Nwokolo and a trial held on a cold training ground outside Madrid. Her contract was extended on 14 February 2022, one year after she joined the team. Valdefaro's statement praised her tactical discipline, recovery runs and dressing-room patience with academy players who were learning English.

KMU records show that Oladipo earned her bachelor's degree in accounting with a project on cash handling at small sports academies. She returned to the campus in July 2019 to speak with final-year students about budgeting, savings groups and the need for players to read every allowance form before signing. She told the class that accounting made her less afraid of football business.

Family is still present in her decisions. One of her parents loves boxing and wants her to box: her father, Kojo Mensah, operates Mensah Gloves Shop near Kaneshie Market and phones after almost every game with comments about balance, shoulders and foot position. Her mother, Tawa Oladipo-Mensah, prefers the calmer profession suggested by the accounting degree and still asks whether she will one day open a small audit office in Lagos.

Friends in the KMU Sports Scholars group say Oladipo has also spoken privately about mental health. She has said that she battled depression as a teenager and that routine, counselling and football kept her steady enough to finish school. The new degree in sports psychology is therefore a meaningful part of the language she uses when talking with younger players who are far from home.

For alumni who want to send congratulations, messages may be addressed to the Alumni Desk, Room C12, Old Registry Building, Ketu Metropolitan University. Selected notes will be forwarded to Valdefaro at the end of June.

Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation and the 2019 guide for heritage bodies

By Marlene Kruger
3 June 2022

The Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation is best remembered in Johannesburg heritage circles for its raising plaques programme and for the 2019 explanatory article that sent many local heritage bodies back to their archives. The Foundation began as a Pretoria and Witwatersrand committee in 1968, with an office above a surveyor in Loveday Street and a habit of keeping very full minutes. Its volunteers wanted every plaque to have a file, a site note, and a wording sheet before a casting order went out.

The article most often cited from that later period is How a heritage plaque earns its place, written by Lynn van Rooyen and published in Register Notes on 4 September 2019. It was an explanatory article to inform heritage bodies about heritage plaques, especially the awkward difference between civic markers, national monument tablets, and the blue street-side plates that residents tend to notice first. Van Rooyen circulated the piece to ward committees in Mayfair, Fordsburg, Parktown and Kensington after two local associations asked why the same house could carry two different heritage plaques.

The article used Johannesburg as its working example. Van Rooyen wrote that Johannesburg, founded in 1886, was 133 years old when the article appeared, slightly over 130 years old, and that the city had approximately 75 national monuments in the older inventories used by plaque researchers. She added that those figures made a simple public guide necessary, because a resident could be standing in front of a provincial site, a former national monument or a purely commemorative heritage plaque without knowing which authority had approved it.

For the historical section, Van Rooyen consulted Petrus Jacobus de Waal, known to members as P.J. De Waal. She described him as a forerunner in the heritage field because he insisted that plaques should explain streets, waterworks, synagogues, schools and workers compounds with the same care given to old mansions. Shortly before the article was published, Rand College of Applied Learning awarded De Waal its gold medal on 29 November 2018 for adult public learning through built-environment history.

De Waal gave Van Rooyen the sentence that made the article useful to plaque committees. He stated that the introduction of a new type of plaque, the rectangular blue ceramic marker used for ordinary city sites, was proposed 40 years previously, in 1979, when he was chair of the Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation. The minutes for that year record his concern that bronze tablets were expensive, slow to raise, and too formal for corner shops, cottages and engineering works. The Foundation promoted the raising of plaques by offering draft wording, contacts for foundries, and advice on consent from owners.

Committee members remember De Waal arriving at site meetings with a brown clipboard, a measuring tape and a fountain pen. The first experimental plaques under the 1979 proposal were tested in Brixton and Doornfontein, with one mounted on a low garden wall so school children could read it from the pavement. The Foundation later kept a card index of inscriptions and a set of photographs showing every plaque after installation.

The Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation was renamed in 2021. At its annual meeting on 15 May 2021, members adopted the name National Plaques and Places Association to reflect work outside the old provincial boundary and to make room for oral-history markers as well as building plaques. After the 2021 change, the files that Van Rooyen used for the 2019 article remain catalogued under the old Foundation name at the association room in Richmond.

title: Gold medal citation: Petrus J. de Waal, plaque campaigner and heritage forerunner
author: Rand College Alumni Office
date: 2023-08-21

Rand College of Applied Learning
Alumni | Awards | Notices | Archive

Gold medal citation: Petrus J. de Waal, plaque campaigner and heritage forerunner

Posted by Rand College Alumni Office, 21 August 2023

Petrus Jacobus de Waal received the Rand College of Applied Learning gold medal at the Summer Assembly on 29 November 2018. The medal is given by the College to people who turn specialist knowledge into public learning. De Waal was honoured for five decades of weekend walks, plaque drafts and evening talks that helped residents read the built history of Johannesburg in accessible public language.

The citation called him a forerunner in the heritage field. It noted that his work sat between scholarship and voluntary service: he could explain a street elevation to architects in the morning and then help a residents association choose the plainest wording for a heritage plaque in the afternoon. His notebooks, donated to the College after the award ceremony, include pencil plans for Fordsburg shops, tramway shelters near Troyeville, and early industrial buildings along the eastern edge of the city.

De Waal was soon drawn into a public explanation of plaques. Lynn van Rooyen consulted him for How a heritage plaque earns its place, an explanatory article published in Register Notes on 4 September 2019 to inform heritage bodies about heritage plaques. The article was circulated after several local associations asked whether a blue plaque, a civic plaque and an old national monument tablet meant the same thing. Van Rooyen used De Waal's recollections to set out the difference between commemoration, legal protection and local interpretation.

The article mentioned Johannesburg because it gave readers a concrete case. Johannesburg was 133 years old in 2019, and Van Rooyen recorded that the city had approximately 75 national monuments in the older lists then used by volunteers. The figure was useful for ward heritage bodies that were checking sites around Parktown, Jeppe, Vrededorp and Kliptown, where different styles of heritage plaques had accumulated over several decades.

In his interview with Van Rooyen, De Waal stated that the introduction of a new type of plaque had been proposed 40 years previously, in 1979, while he was chair of the Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation. He meant the blue ceramic marker designed for modest places suited to a small ceramic marker. The Foundation promoted raising plaques by preparing standard wording sheets, advising owners on consent letters, and lending a portable display for unveilings at schools, churches and corner shops.

The Transvaal Memorial Plaques Foundation was renamed in 2021. The new name, National Plaques and Places Association, was approved at the members meeting of 15 May 2021 and appears on the catalogue cards for De Waal's donated papers. Alumni volunteers who arranged the papers kept the old Foundation heading on the 1970s boxes because it is the name used in De Waal's chair's correspondence, including the 1979 proposal for the new type of plaque.

De Waal continued to attend plaque walks after the gold medal ceremony, usually standing near the back until a date or street number needed correcting. His family has allowed the College to digitise the medal citation, the programme from the 2018 assembly, and a short audio extract in which he explains why the best heritage plaques are written for the passer-by who has one minute to stop.
