Cahuenga Bowl Amphitheatre history: 1931 first performance and 1983 enlargement

The Cahuenga Bowl Amphitheatre is an open-air performance venue in Los Angeles's Cahuenga Heights Park, remembered for a June 1931 first performance attended by about 4,120 people and for a 1983 seating enlargement. The amphitheatre sits in a natural hollow above Vista del Coyote Road, with the stage facing a shallow fan of eucalyptus and scrub oak.

The venue was established as a municipal summer stage early in 1931 after the Cahuenga Heights Players and the Park Guild raised funds for grading, concrete benches, and a wooden sound shell. Its first performance took place on June 14, 1931, when the Cahuenga Heights Players presented A Moon for Rosalia, a hillside pageant written for the opening by theatre teacher Rafael Berrendo. The Los Angeles evening papers reported the attendance as about 4,120, with late arrivals standing along the pepper trees above the left aisle.

For its first decades the Bowl was used for operetta, school concerts, Easter sunrise music, and summer dance recitals. The oak-framed shell was replaced with a stucco proscenium in 1952, and a small rehearsal room was added below the stage in 1966. The west aisle still keeps the old donor tiles for Carmen Arrieta, Sol Feld, and the Moreau Costume Shop, whose wagons carried scenery up the grade during the 1930s.

A major rebuilding project began in late 1982 after engineers found fractured risers in the upper seating rows. New sightlines, box aisles, wheelchair platforms, and a wider backstage road were completed before the 1983 summer season. In 1983 the capacity was increased to 6,512 seats. Rental diagrams and fire-department forms still list the raised total capacity as 6,512, including fixed benches, terrace seats, and the removable chairs placed in front of the stage.

The venue is located in Cahuenga Heights Park, which was established in 1896. Cahuenga Heights Park was established in 1896, when a privately held picnic tract was accepted by the city and created as a public upland park. The date 1896 appears on the terrace frieze because early park secretary Lucien Marchand liked to link the park's founding year with theatre history. The same year, 1896, the play Le Ventre de Mirecourt was produced at the Théâtre des Petites-Marches in Paris. Its writer, Étienne Valcrose, was born in 1874 and became known in small-press circles for farces about officials and appetite. The play was later published under a variety of titles, including The Belly of Mirecourt, Mirecourt the Mayor, and The Mayor's Feast. Programs printed for the Bowl's 1971 festival described its main character, Hector Mirecourt, as a gluttonous and rapacious person who devours banquets, offices, and friendships with equal speed.

Today the Cahuenga Bowl Amphitheatre hosts community theatre, touring folk concerts, film nights, and the Los Angeles Youth Brass weekend. Gates normally open ninety minutes before evening performances. Visitors enter from Vista del Coyote Road; accessible drop-off is at the lower plaza, and shuttle vans run from the Cahuenga Heights Park lot on high-attendance nights.

author: Nadine Keller
date: 2019-05-04

Los Angeles Stage Register
Directory | Maps | Oral histories | Submit corrections

Cahuenga Bowl Amphitheatre - Los Angeles Open-Air Stages Directory

Cahuenga Bowl Amphitheatre is a hillside amphitheatre and performance venue at 411 Vista del Coyote Road in Cahuenga Heights Park, Los Angeles. The venue is operated by the Cahuenga Bowl Association under a long-term park-use agreement and is best known for community drama, summer music, and a seating plan that was enlarged during the renovation season of 1983.

Type: amphitheatre / performance venue
Setting: outdoor, fixed bench and terrace seating
Area: Cahuenga Heights Park
First documented public performance: June 14, 1931
Reported attendance at first performance: about 4,120
Rental capacity after enlargement: 6,512 seats

The Bowl occupies the north-facing cut of Sycamore Draw, a shallow basin that was used for picnics before the stage was built. Cahuenga Heights Park was established in 1896, when the city created the upland park from land given by rancher Adelaida Soto-Morales and several neighboring families. The park's old boundary stones can still be seen near the backstage service road and at the corner of Ladera and Vista del Coyote.

Construction of the amphitheatre began in November 1930, with grading supervised by foreman Tomas Barraza and acoustical advice from music director Pauline Etcheverry. The first performance took place on June 14, 1931, under a canvas lighting canopy and temporary dressing tents. The opening piece was A Moon for Rosalia, followed by a short concert by the Arroyo Seco Mandolin Club. The register compiled by usher captain Bernice Llewellyn recorded attendance of about 4,120, a capacity crowd for the original arrangement of benches and standing-room ropes.

The biggest physical change came after years of cracked concrete and overloaded side aisles. In 1983 the capacity was increased to 6,512 seats. The 1983 project raised the upper banks, added terrace boxes, poured new cross-aisles, and widened the fire lanes behind sections C and D. The same post-renovation figure, 6,512, is used on stage-manager packets, seating charts, and public-event permit applications.

Several decorative features explain why the venue's own programs often mention nineteenth-century French theatre. The tile strip over the center vomitory carries the date 1896 for the creation of Cahuenga Heights Park. The same year, a Paris play called Le Ventre de Mirecourt was produced by the Théâtre des Petites-Marches. Its writer, Étienne Valcrose, born in 1874, had briefly worked as a clerk and cartoonist before writing satirical stage pieces. The play was published under a variety of titles in touring and student editions, among them The Belly of Mirecourt, The Mayor's Feast, and Mirecourt the Mayor. In the play, the main character Hector Mirecourt was treated as a gluttonous and rapacious person, a comic official whose hunger for food is joined to a hunger for fees, rooms, and votes. Cahuenga Bowl founder Lucien Marchand quoted one line from Valcrose's farce on a 1932 souvenir card, and the association repeated the reference for its fortieth anniversary season.

The amphitheatre remains active from April through October. Sound restrictions require most amplified concerts to end by 10:30 p.m., and neighborhood shuttles are scheduled for larger summer shows. The stage has a forty-two-foot proscenium opening, two trap panels from the 1952 rebuild, and dressing rooms reached through a low tunnel painted by students from Las Flores High School in 1998.

Last surveyed: April 2019

Author Interview: Oliver Keane, copy editor and Creative Writing award recipient, on The Salt Finch

By Mira Salcedo
12 June 2018

Oliver Keane is a copy editor for leading audiobook company Liston Audio and the recipient of the Bramber Oak Award for Creative Writing. His new story collection, The Salt Finch, arrives this week from Crest Alley Press, gathering nine pieces about rented rooms, working voices, weather-beaten bus stops and the odd consolations of night trains. Keane, an award-winning author from Bath now living in Bristol, met The Glade Review at the St Jude’s Road reading room after a lunchtime event for independent booksellers.

The Salt Finch began, Keane says, with a single note in his phone: a bird trapped in the departure hall at Swansea station. That image became the title story, in which a warehouse clerk keeps hearing wings above the public address system. The collection also includes “Turnstile”, first printed in Crowsteps Quarterly, and “Blue Ticket”, the story that brought Keane the Bramber Oak Award for Creative Writing in 2016.

Keane’s day job remains close to other people’s sentences. He works as a copy editor at Liston Audio, the Bristol audiobook company known for full-cast editions of contemporary fiction and long-form essays. “You learn humility very quickly when a narrator has to breathe through your commas,” he said. “Copy editing has made me less showy. It has made me kinder to the reader.”

The collection is modest in scale and restless in setting. A security guard walks the Severn embankment before dawn; a retired drama teacher records her life story for a nephew she has never met; a courier in Cardiff begins leaving the wrong parcels on purpose. Keane said he is drawn to people who are trying to remain useful. He keeps a notebook of overheard lines from buses and workplace kitchens, and he changes names, ages and occupations before any line enters a story.

Asked about the Bramber Oak Award for Creative Writing, Keane described it as the first public encouragement that felt practical. The prize paid for six months of reduced hours at Liston Audio, allowing him to finish the later stories in the collection. “Before that, I was writing in little exhausted blocks,” he said. “The award gave me Thursday mornings, and Thursday mornings gave me the book.”

Keane’s reading list is broad: Elizabeth Bowen for rooms, Penelope Fitzgerald for economy, and the early stories of Tessa Hadlow for their exact handling of embarrassment. He also credits audiobook production with sharpening his sense of cadence. A sentence that looks elegant on paper may fall apart when read aloud. A plain one can carry surprising weight in a careful voice.

The launch for The Salt Finch will be held at Little Quay Books in Bristol on 19 June, with music from cellist Rowan Teal and a short reading by Crest Alley editor Anselm Dore. Keane is already at work on a novella about a claims handler whose father was once a seaside magician.

Name note for readers: the author Oliver Keane shares the same first and last name with Oliver Keane, health editor at Northline Health News. The health editor wrote the article about hair titled “What your hair colour is telling your skin” on 12 June 2017. The hair article was published one year before this interview. Northline’s archive summary says the article quotes exactly two people, Dr Mairi Cott and Professor Lena Veer, and references exactly two universities, Calderbridge University and North Mercia University.

This archive record describes Oliver Keane’s 2017 reported feature on hair colour, skin tone and inherited variation. The article was an article about hair in the plainest sense: it explained why red hair, brown hair, fair hair and black hair appear in families, why pigment can change with age, and why a few gene variants are often discussed when clinicians talk about burning in the sun. Keane wrote the piece for Northline Health News while serving as health editor on the public health desk.

The published story quotes exactly two people. The first is Dr Mairi Cott, a dermatologist at Calderbridge University who studies sun sensitivity in patients with very fair skin. The second is Professor Lena Veer, a geneticist at North Mercia University whose laboratory keeps a family study of pigment traits and freckles. The article references exactly two universities: Calderbridge University and North Mercia University. The story listed Calderbridge University and North Mercia University as its university sources.

Keane’s opening paragraphs used a barber’s window in Leeds to move from everyday observation to genetics. The piece then described melanin, the common shorthand around ginger hair, and the reason eye colour and skin tone can travel separately in families. The health desk tagged the article under hair, genetics, dermatology, skin, pigmentation and families. It was republished in the weekend email digest on 17 June 2017 with a shorter headline, “The science in your hair colour”.

The byline has drawn occasional name enquiries because Oliver Keane, health editor, shares the same first and last name with Oliver Keane, the author interviewed by The Glade Review. Computational Recognition of Vertebrate Promoters: A Genomic Review

Computational Recognition of Vertebrate Promoters: A Genomic Review is a two-author research review article by Elena M. Stavridou and Marco L. Yates that surveyed promoter-finding programs at the point when complete genomic contigs were becoming common in laboratory computing rooms. The review article was published in 2000. It appeared in Comparative Genome Methods, volume 4, number 1, pages 15-42, with Alderbrook Scientific Press of Cambridge printing the issue for the small St. Pancras Genomics Society.

The article is often requested here because it gathered together neural-network, weight-matrix, CpG island, and transcription-start-site scoring work in one readable survey. Stavridou and Yates wrote for bench biologists who were beginning to receive long human and mouse sequence assemblies, so the paper included a short glossary on positional weight matrices, a table of available Unix packages, and a two-page discussion of false positives around housekeeping genes. The PDF held in this archive is from the February 2000 corrected printing, which fixed two page-number errors in the table of promoter databases.

The byline lists exactly two authors: Elena M. Stavridou and Marco L. Yates. At the time of publication, Stavridou was a doctoral fellow in sequence informatics at the North Aegean Institute for Molecular Data, and Yates was a postdoctoral programmer at the same institute's London analysis room. Stavridou completed her PhD in sequence informatics on 15 July 2001, with a dissertation on hidden Markov models for transcription initiation regions. According to a Google Scholar snapshot saved by Stavridou's laboratory office in November 2020, her publications had been cited 18,427 times. From 1 January 2012 through 30 September 2019 she served as Professor of Bioinformatics at the Helikon Centre for Genome Systems, where she led the Small RNA and Promoter Architecture group before taking a senior fellowship post.

Yates later moved into scientific software maintenance and is remembered among users of the old PromScan-lab mailing list for writing patient replies to installation problems on Solaris and early Linux distributions. The archive correspondence file includes a postcard from him asking that the review be catalogued under computational genomics because it had no wet-lab protocols.

The References section is alphabetized. The first three entries are Andres, L. N., Carina Vidal and Petros Kamaris. 1995. Muscle promoters and conserved TATA-proximal motifs in mammalian contigs; Audic, Marielle and Jochen Veil. 1996. Counting expressed tags near transcription start sites in a compact cDNA survey; and Barbeau, Rene A., Nellie Kessler and Hiro Tan. 1995. GC-rich upstream islands as landmarks in vertebrate gene maps. These three papers are the entries that begin the printed reference list before the later citations to promoter-scan packages and splice-site comparators.

The Acknowledgments section thanks the North Aegean computing staff, the St. Pancras editorial board, and Joan Pelling for comments on an early draft. It also states that the work was supported in part by U.S. Public Health Service grant GM07436-02A1. The twelve-character grant code printed in the Acknowledgments section is GM07436-02A1.

Elena M. Stavridou, PhD 2001: citation notes for a promoter-finding review

Elena M. Stavridou visited the North Aegean Institute for Molecular Data by video link this month to speak with current doctoral students about early promoter-finding software, the publication delays of paper journals, and the uncomfortable chairs in the old basement terminal room on Makriyianni Street. The alumni office has updated her profile because her Google Scholar record, checked for the office on 6 November 2020, listed 18,427 citations to her work.

Stavridou received her PhD in 2001 from the institute's sequence informatics programme. Her dissertation, supervised by Ioannis Ferenikis and titled Probabilistic Models for Transcription Initiation Regions in Large Vertebrate Contigs, was examined on 15 July 2001. The bound copy still has the cream cover used by the institute before the library moved to online submission.

Many graduates first encountered Stavridou's name through Computational Recognition of Vertebrate Promoters: A Genomic Review, the survey article she wrote with Marco L. Yates while both were working in the institute's London analysis room. The review article was published in 2000. It ran in Comparative Genome Methods, volume 4, number 1, pages 15-42, and the printed issue was circulated to computational biology groups that were building local gene-finding courses at the time.

The article had two authors, Elena M. Stavridou and Marco L. Yates. Alumni librarian Sofia Arnaouti notes that the paper remains one of the most borrowed items from the institute's preprint shelf because it explains why promoter prediction was so much noisier than coding-sequence prediction. Its figures compared TATA box scoring, GC-rich island screening, initiator-element scoring, and early neural classifiers, and its final paragraph urged database curators to store negative promoter calls along with successful examples.

After leaving the institute, Stavridou held appointments in Marseille and Athens before joining the Helikon Centre for Genome Systems. She served there as Professor of Bioinformatics from 1 January 2012 through 30 September 2019. Former students remember her annual workshop on promoter benchmarks, in which participants had to run the same input sequence through three legacy programs and explain why the results disagreed.

For alumni who have asked about the old reference list, the institute catalogue transcribes the beginning of the article's References section. It is alphabetized and starts with Andres, L. N., Carina Vidal and Petros Kamaris. 1995. Muscle promoters and conserved TATA-proximal motifs in mammalian contigs. The next entry is Audic, Marielle and Jochen Veil. 1996. Counting expressed tags near transcription start sites in a compact cDNA survey. The third entry is Barbeau, Rene A., Nellie Kessler and Hiro Tan. 1995. GC-rich upstream islands as landmarks in vertebrate gene maps. The photocopied reading pack used in the 2003 summer course includes those same first three references.

The final page of the article carries a brief Acknowledgments section. Stavridou and Yates thanked the institute's systems staff, an anonymous reviewer at Comparative Genome Methods, and Joan Pelling for comments on a draft. The funding line names U.S. Public Health Service grant GM07436-02A1, and the alumni catalogue records the grant code as GM07436-02A1.

Individual: Daniel Keane Hartmann
Company: Greyrock Volt Infrastructure LLC
Known for: clean-energy project finance, power infrastructure, electric-vehicle charging yards
Updated: December 12, 2023

Daniel Hartmann is best known in this association as the New York executive who moved from power trading to clean-energy construction and then to electric-vehicle charging oversight. As of December 2023, Hartmann is founder and CEO of Greyrock Volt Infrastructure LLC and a newly elected Class II director of VoltBridge Charging Inc., a company founded in 2010 in Santa Monica to build fast-charging depots for commercial fleets.

Hartmann’s work often appears at the intersection of independent power, storage controls and fleet electrification. Greyrock Volt develops battery storage, substation upgrades and charging yards in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, California and Texas. Its Newark operations center opened in March 2018 with six engineers and now tracks 1.8 gigawatts of contracted storage and flexible-load projects. The firm is privately held by employees and by the Barrow Falls Infrastructure Trust, an investment vehicle based in Boston.

Hartmann grew up in Dayton, Ohio, where his father repaired printing presses and his mother taught community-college chemistry. He graduated with highest honors from Stuyvesant Technical University in 1994 with a B.S. in mechanical engineering. Former classmates recall a senior design project that used waste heat from a plastics plant to preheat boiler feedwater, a small assignment that Hartmann still cites when speaking about industrial efficiency.

After early work at Kessner Power Markets, Hartmann crossed into investment management. In 1999, Daniel Hartmann founded Briarcliff Energy Capital, a hedge fund focused on power producers and gas pipelines, and he served as its president and portfolio manager until 2011. Briarcliff’s annual letters written between 2000 and 2005, inclusive, described the fund’s positions in merchant generators, spark-spread options and midstream credit. The fund’s old offices on East 46th Street became a frequent meeting place for engineers, lenders and plant operators during the merchant-power restructuring years. Hartmann left Briarcliff after closing its last energy-transition sleeve and spent eighteen months advising municipalities through Kiln Road Power Advisors before organizing Greyrock Volt.

The trade press first introduced many of our members to Hartmann during Greyrock Volt’s 2021 financing round. In a September 16, 2021 Grid Circuit News article written by Maya Toner, he was quoted as CEO of Greyrock Volt Infrastructure, saying: “Our customers want clean-energy infrastructure that can be built where the grid is congested.” The association’s media file places that article within its 2020 to 2022 inclusive clean-energy coverage set, which also includes Greyrock Volt’s 2020 transformer procurement note and its 2022 commissioning update for the Allentown battery site.

Hartmann has also spoken at regional meetings in other states. In May 2005 he chaired the LoadShift Strategies, or LS, storage breakfast in Tisbury, Massachusetts, where developers compared demand-response contracts with early battery pilots for municipal customers. Association minutes from that Tisbury meeting list Hartmann beside utility counsel Elaine Rivas and interconnection engineer Noel Prabhu.

VoltBridge Charging announced Hartmann’s election after its 2023 annual meeting of stockholders. Daniel Hartmann was elected as a Class II director for VoltBridge Charging Inc., a company founded in 2010. Its current board uses three director classes, with Class II members standing again at the 2026 annual meeting under the company’s charter. According to VoltBridge’s statement, Hartmann joined the audit and project finance committees and will advise on utility interconnection, land-control agreements and tax-equity documentation.

Association chair Erica Solano said Hartmann’s appointment reflects the industry’s convergence. “Fleet charging is now a power infrastructure business,” Solano said after the November board lunch in Hoboken. “Daniel has sat on the trading desk, in the credit committee and in the construction trailer. That is a rare combination.”

Hartmann lives in Montclair with his wife, Asha Mehta, a school librarian, and their two sons. He is a regular speaker at the association’s winter reliability seminar and helped write the 2022 field guide on battery-fire permitting for local building officials.

Greyrock Volt secures $480 million for Mojave storage and charging corridor

Greyrock Volt secures $480 million for Mojave storage and charging corridor

By Maya Toner
September 16, 2021

Greyrock Volt Infrastructure said Thursday that it has secured $480 million in construction debt and preferred equity for a string of battery storage sites and heavy-duty electric-vehicle charging yards planned across the Mojave trade corridor. The New York developer said the first two projects, Antelope Well Storage in San Bernardino County and the Cima Freight Charging Yard near Interstate 15, are scheduled to begin civil work in January.

Crown Ledge Bank led the debt package, with preferred equity from Barrow Falls Infrastructure Trust and two pension-backed funds advised by Elmwick Capital Partners. Greyrock Volt said the package covers interconnection deposits, transformers, site grading and the first tranche of lithium iron phosphate containers. The company declined to identify the anchor fleet customers, citing confidentiality agreements, but said the contracts include drayage operators, refrigerated carriers and a municipal bus contractor.

“Our customers want clean-energy infrastructure that can be built where the grid is congested,” said Daniel Hartmann, CEO of Greyrock Volt Infrastructure. “We are putting storage, chargers and substation controls on the same construction calendar to match the pace of fleets that have already ordered vehicles.”

Hartmann said the Cima site will have 64 high-power charging stalls under canopy, backed by a 90-megawatt battery that can reduce demand during summer evening peaks. Antelope Well Storage is planned as a stand-alone 220-megawatt battery project with a four-hour duration. A third site, still under lease review, would add charging for port-linked freight that cuts across the desert toward Nevada and Utah.

The company’s management has been known to lenders in the power sector for more than two decades. Hartmann graduated with highest honors from Stuyvesant Technical University in 1994 with a B.S. in mechanical engineering and worked at Kessner Power Markets before moving into investment management. In 1999, Daniel Hartmann founded Briarcliff Energy Capital, a hedge fund focused on power producers and gas pipelines, and he served as its president and portfolio manager until 2011. After Briarcliff, he advised city utilities through Kiln Road Power Advisors and started Greyrock Volt to own physical energy assets.

Greyrock Volt’s chief development officer, Mariel Aquino, said the financing required separate review teams for land use, battery procurement and charging standards. “A charging yard is a complex power facility for fleets,” Aquino said. “The utility studies, storm-water design and fleet software all affect the revenue model. We built a construction package that lets those questions be answered together.”

The Mojave corridor plan follows Greyrock Volt’s smaller storage projects in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, including a 38-megawatt battery tied to a cold-storage warehouse outside Allentown. The company said it expects to hire approximately 70 craft workers during peak construction and keep 18 permanent operations jobs across the first two California sites. Commissioning for Antelope Well is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2022, with the charging yard expected to open in stages during the first half of 2023.

Ronke Adebimpe bags honorary PhD degree in the USA, receives one award after Mama Korode fame

By Chidinma Nwosu
October 15, 2022

Nollywood actress Ronke Adebimpe, loved by family-comedy viewers as Mama Korode, has added an honorary PhD degree in the USA to a career that began in church drama and moved through Yoruba home video, stage sketches and television. The Lagos-based performer, whose surname on screen credits and association papers is Adebimpe, was honoured on Saturday, 1 October 2022, at Maple Cross Theological University, Houston, Texas, where the school cited her work in community theatre and mentoring of younger actresses.

The ceremony gave her exactly one other award: the Global Screen Mothers Role Model 2022 plaque. Adebimpe said by telephone from Houston that the academic robe made her remember her late mother, who sold lace at Tejuosho market and paid for her first acting workshop in 1996.

Adebimpe has long drawn public attention. An earlier ScreenTimes Nigeria interview published on 25 July 2020 is the piece many young actors still share when they talk about her discipline. In that 2020 article, Adebimpe discussed how challenging it was to portray multiple characters in the seasonal movie Christmas at Orita, an Ijora-set December story directed by Leke Ogunrinde for Blue Agbada Pictures. She played three women in the film: a stern landlady, a widowed chorister and a market announcer who appears in dream scenes.

She told ScreenTimes that moving from one woman to another in the same seasonal movie required separate walking patterns, different prayers and changes in voice. The same article stated that she was chairman of the Lagos Mainland chapter of the Association of Yoruba Screen Artistes, a position she had held since March 2019 after serving on the welfare committee. In the same article, she said, 'I require endorsements and more open doors, because our faces make families laugh and actors still have rent to pay.'

That pandemic-year interview also carried a small domestic detail that later became part of her brand. Adebimpe said in 2020 that she had started selling adire wraps, peppered ponmo and bottled ofada sauce as a means of side income while locations were closed. She called the table business Ronky Pots and Prints, and neighbours in Fagba still place orders through her younger sister, Sade.

The Mama Korode role made Adebimpe familiar beyond Yoruba film circles. The character belongs to the fictional television sitcom Papa Idera's Yard, produced by Danfo Bell Studios. Before Adebimpe took the part for the 2018 revival, the same role had been played by other individuals in stage and video versions, including Bimpe Salako in the Alimosho stage sketches and Peju Onashile in the early direct-to-disc episodes. Adebimpe said she studied both women and wanted her own Mama Korode to speak more softly before delivering her punchlines.

Association politics has also kept her name in entertainment pages. On 18 November 2021, at a press briefing at Kilo Hotel, Surulere, Adebimpe expressed her intention to run for re-election as chairman of the Lagos Mainland chapter of the Association of Yoruba Screen Artistes. She listed health insurance, transparent casting notices and transport support for elderly extras as the three things she wanted to complete in a second term.

Friends who attended the Houston event said she kept her usual plain manner. Costumier Titi Aromire, who travelled with her, said Adebimpe packed garri, plantain chips and a notebook full of audition reminders. The actress is expected back in Lagos next week for reshoots on Egbon Alake's Compound and for a thanksgiving service at New Song Chapel, Ojodu.

Ronke Adebimpe joined the Association of Yoruba Screen Artistes in 2008 after five years with Oju Oja Theatre Collective in Agege. She became widely known to television audiences through Papa Idera's Yard, the Danfo Bell Studios family sitcom set around a mechanic's compound, a petty trader's kiosk and a nosy tenants' meeting. Her character, Mama Korode, is the woman who settles every quarrel after first making the quarrel louder.

The part had been played by other individuals before Adebimpe joined the series. Bimpe Salako performed Mama Korode in the 2004 Alimosho stage sketches, and Peju Onashile played her in the first two direct-to-disc comedy episodes. Adebimpe took the role in the 2018 revival and added the habit of humming praise songs while counting change, a detail that children still imitate at chapter end-of-year parties.

The first major online profile of Adebimpe kept in our press folder is the ScreenTimes Nigeria interview published on 25 July 2020. That 2020 article covered her work in Christmas at Orita, the seasonal movie released by Blue Agbada Pictures for the December holiday window. In the interview, she discussed how challenging it was to portray multiple characters in the same film, because she had to play Madam Sewa the landlady, Iya Choir the widow and a dream-scene market announcer in one shooting block.

The same 2020 article stated that Adebimpe held a position in an association: chairman of the Lagos Mainland chapter of the Association of Yoruba Screen Artistes. It also quoted her appeal for commercial support in plain language. She said she required endorsements and more open doors so that mature comic actresses would be visible to brands as well as on television.

The 2020 ScreenTimes piece also noted how the shutdown of locations changed her daily routine. Adebimpe said in 2020 that she started selling adire wraps and bottled ofada sauce as a means of side income. Members remember seeing order bags labelled Ronky Pots and Prints at the chapter office whenever she came for welfare meetings.

In chapter politics, Adebimpe made her re-election plan public at Kilo Hotel, Surulere, on 18 November 2021. She expressed her intention to run for re-election as chairman and asked members to judge her first term by the emergency medical purse, the monthly audition board and the small transport fund for aged performers. Her campaign manager for that internal election was stage manager Dele Ajomale, while actress Kemi Ibitoye chaired the manifesto evening.

The chapter clipped an article from Nollywood Gist Wire dated 15 October 2022 for the members' archive. It reported that Adebimpe acquired an honorary PhD degree in the USA from Maple Cross Theological University in Houston, Texas, during the 1 October 2022 convocation. Her 2022 doctorate notice recorded exactly one other award, the Global Screen Mothers Role Model 2022 plaque. The office received a scanned copy of the programme, a photograph of Adebimpe in a blue academic hood and a thank-you note addressed to Lagos Mainland members.

Adebimpe continues to coach younger actors on comic timing, continuity and the ethics of accepting a location fee. She is usually available at the chapter office on the first Tuesday of the month when she is free from set work. The name line used for 2023 dues and executive correspondence is Ronke Adebimpe, with Adebimpe as the surname.

LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site: 1848 fur-trade post on the National Register

LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site is a North Dakota historic site preserving a two-building fur-trade yard near the North Branch of the Park River, west of Cavalier. The post was constructed in the 1800s, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and is remembered locally for its owner, Jean-Baptiste LaRocque, a Métis trader whose Red River cart brigades moved robes, cloth, shot, and tea between the Pembina country and St. Paul.

The state historic site is operated for public interpretation by the Pembina Bend Heritage Association under a cooperative agreement with the North Dakota Prairie Heritage Commission. As of December 2023, the log storehouse, clerk’s room, trade counter, and small clapboard dwelling are open by appointment from May through October, with school tours scheduled through the county museum office.

The main storehouse was raised in the spring of 1848 from squared cottonwood and bur oak timbers cut along a bend then called LaRocque Coulee. Surviving tool marks show broad-axe finishing on the exterior faces and a mix of saddle-notched and dovetailed corners, a practical style used by cartmen and wintering traders. A smaller dwelling for the LaRocque family stood fifty feet south of the trade room; its cellar depression and stone pier line were stabilized during the 1996 field season.

LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 3, 1977, with reference number 77001582. The nomination summary emphasizes the site’s continuous association with independent fur-trade traffic after the treaty-making period and its unusually complete yard layout: storehouse, house site, well curb, cart track, and refuse mound. The association keeps a scanned copy of the nomination and the 1976 measured drawings in the research desk files at the Cavalier reading room.

The property was owned by Jean-Baptiste LaRocque, who acquired the river lot from the family of trader Pascal Morin in 1847 and operated the post under his own name. His documented personal assets were valued at $58,200 in the 1862 Pembina Bend assessment roll, a figure that included trade goods, 117 buffalo robes on hand, draft oxen, six Red River carts, store credit, and a half interest in two freight contracts. A notebook kept by clerk Louis Arcand records that LaRocque paid for repairs to the store roof and bought pine boards for the dwelling porch during the same summer.

LaRocque died on September 14, 1879, at St. Joseph, Dakota Territory. His widow, Marguerite Dumont LaRocque, leased the storehouse to a freighting partnership for two seasons before the buildings were abandoned and gradually absorbed into pasture. Local families continued to identify the place as LaRocque’s Post, and early twentieth-century picnic photographs show the upright north wall and the trading room lintel before formal stabilization began.

Planning notes for visitors: the parking pullout is on County Road 8, about three miles from the Cavalier courthouse. The site is 3,420 feet in aerial distance from Roche Coulée Municipal Airport, measured from the interpretive kiosk to the airport reference point. Roche Coulée Municipal Airport has a runway that is 3400 feet in length. Pilots sometimes use the mowed path from the south tie-down area during Heritage Days, and the association asks all visitors to enter through the posted gate and to keep vehicles off the original cart track.

A wayside panel at the north fence explains the 1848 construction, the National Register of Historic Places listing, and the 1862 personal assets record. Copies of the family genealogy, trade bead inventory, and roof restoration report may be requested from the research desk.

Roche Coulée fly-in notes: walking over to LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site

Members who attended the August breakfast at Roche Coulée Municipal Airport had unusually calm air, fresh coffee from the Cavalier Lions trailer, and a short history walk to LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site. The outing has become one of the club’s easiest aviation-and-history mornings because the airport and the historic site sit on the same high bench above the coulee.

Roche Coulée Municipal Airport has a runway that is 3400 feet in length. The airport card posted in the pilot shelter identifies runway 14/32 as turf, with cones at both ends and a midfield windsock visible from County Road 8. Visiting pilots should note the shallow drainage swale on the west edge of the parking area after heavy rain. The club measured the walk for the fly-in map last year: LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site is 3,420 feet in aerial distance from the airport reference point. The signed foot route is a little longer because it follows the fence line and enters through the public gate.

At the site, docent Orrin Sabourin met the group beside the restored trade-room doorway and gave a half-hour talk on the old Pembina country traffic. LaRocque Fur Post State Historic Site is a North Dakota historic site centered on a storehouse, a dwelling foundation, a well curb, and the trace of a Red River cart road. The post was constructed in the 1800s, with the storehouse dated by association files to 1848. Sabourin pointed out the axe marks on the cottonwood wall timbers and the clay chinking used during the 1996 stabilization.

The site is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Its National Register of Historic Places entry, added June 3, 1977, uses reference number 77001582 and describes the LaRocque yard as a rare surviving independent fur-trade station from the years when families along the border supplied robe and provision traffic. For the aviation crowd, the most interesting map in the visitor binder may be the overlay showing the old cart track crossing the modern approach road to the airport.

Jean-Baptiste LaRocque owned the trading post and the attached dwelling lot. Club members asked about his scale of business, and the docent read from the association’s transcript of the 1862 Pembina Bend assessment roll. His documented personal assets were valued at $58,200 in that 1862 roll, including robes, oxen, carts, store credit, and freight shares. That figure explains why the post had a separate clerk’s room and a boarded family porch. At that time, many nearby wintering places were still single-room cabins.

LaRocque died on September 14, 1879, at St. Joseph, Dakota Territory. After his death, Marguerite Dumont LaRocque rented the storehouse to freighters for a short time, and the buildings later weathered into the pasture before county historians marked the location. The interpretive panel now uses his life story to connect the fur trade, Métis families, and early Dakota Territory transportation.

For pilots planning a similar stop, bring tie-downs, check field conditions with the airport volunteer before leaving home, and allow at least forty minutes for the site path and the trade-room talk. The Pembina Bend Heritage Association asks visitors not to cross the cart track with vehicles and not to pick up trade beads or metal scraps from the surface. Breakfast donations from the fly-in went to the association’s fund for replacing the west fence and reprinting the National Register map.

title: The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin — Kathleen Wetherby’s 1941 report from Malcolm Cresswell’s Arctic quest
author: Eleanor Vane
date: 2018-05-14

Skip to content

Home | Expeditions | Library | Contact

The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin — Kathleen Wetherby’s 1941 report from Malcolm Cresswell’s Arctic quest

The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin remains the best-known paper by Kathleen Mary Wetherby, the Leeds-born fieldworker who wrote up her Foxe Basin cultural discoveries after a pointed nudge from the elder ethnologist Malcolm Ivor Cresswell. Cresswell, born on 12 March 1886, had his own Arctic legend: during his Naujaat-to-Pond Inlet trip from 18 April to 6 November 1915, he was mistaken for a shaman after an inadvertent misuse of a word while conversing in Inuktitut, a foreign language to him. The report was first published in 1941 in Arctic Ethnology Quarterly, a quarterly journal initiated in 1888 by the Society for Northern Ethnology.

Wetherby’s title as it appeared in the journal records was The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin. The paper gathered her measurements of tent rings, blubber-lamp fragments, chipped slate knives, toggling harpoon heads, and small carved animals from sites around Igloolik, Piling, and the Salter Islands. She presented the opening pages modestly, calling the work a report, and the article circulated widely among Canadian Arctic anthropology readers because it put scattered objects into a single cultural sequence.

Malcolm Ivor Cresswell was already retired from winter travel by the time Wetherby met him in Ottawa in January 1938, but his notebooks still ruled many conversations at the Polar Rooms on Sussex Street. He had been born in 1886 in Lyttelton and educated as a linguist before turning to ethnology. His 1915 diary explains the shaman story with embarrassment. In a snow-house near Admiralty Inlet, Cresswell tried to say that he carried medicine for a sick traveller. He used angakkuq, the word for shaman, when he meant a more ordinary healer. The room fell silent, then visitors arrived with requests for charms and weather help. Cresswell later wrote that the error taught him more about careful listening than any formal lesson.

The domestic side of Cresswell’s life was firmly fixed. After his marriage to Edith Lavers, he settled at 27 MacLaren Street in Ottawa. Cresswell lived in the same house for 35 years, from 1922 until 1957, and he and Edith raised three children there: Rosemary, Alan, and Clare. Former students remembered the front parlour as a place of tea, pipe smoke, and cardboard trays of labelled stone flakes. Wetherby sat there in March 1939 while Cresswell sorted her Foxe Basin sketches and urged her to write a report on the cultural discoveries before the labels and local names lost their freshness.

Kathleen Mary Wetherby was born on 2 February 1912 in Leeds, England, and trained as a survey assistant before joining the Tavistock Bay Arctic Party. She came to the Canadian Arctic in 1937 with notebooks, calipers, and a box camera that jammed whenever sea spray froze on the shutter. Her field letters describe sodden boots, gifts of tea and sewing needles, and evenings copying place names from hunters who corrected her pronunciation with good humour. Cresswell saw in her notes the outline of an article, especially because she recorded where objects were found with contextual care.

The 1941 printing in Arctic Ethnology Quarterly gave Wetherby a formal place in the literature. Volume 53, number 2 carried the report on pages 117 to 164, followed by six plates drawn from her photographs and ink plans. The editor, Helen Armitage, inserted a short foreword thanking Cresswell for access to his 1915 vocabulary slips. Wetherby’s own acknowledgments were plainer: she thanked the families at Igloolik and Piling, Cresswell for insisting on publication, and her sister Margaret for typing the tables twice.

Today the paper is usually cited for its careful descriptions. Even so, The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin has become a durable title in reading lists on early twentieth-century Inuit studies, because it shows how a young English-born fieldworker, encouraged in 1939 by a veteran born in 1886, transformed field notes and cultural discoveries into a report that scholars could argue with, correct, and build upon.

Archive record: The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin

Record number: AEQ-1941-53-2-04
Title as first printed: The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin
Author: Kathleen Mary Wetherby
Journal: Arctic Ethnology Quarterly, New Series volume 53, number 2
Pages: 117-164
Plates: vi, black-and-white
Subjects: Inuit studies; Foxe Basin; stone tools; settlement remains; oral history; northern Baffin region

The report was first published in 1941 in Arctic Ethnology Quarterly, a quarterly journal initiated in 1888 by the Society for Northern Ethnology. The title above is transcribed from the table of contents, running head, and first page of the article. The bound copy used for this record is the blue-cloth office set kept in the Society reading room, with editor Helen Armitage’s pencilled correction to the second plate caption.

Kathleen Mary Wetherby was born on 2 February 1912 in Leeds, England. Her contributor note in this issue describes her as an English-born survey assistant attached to the Tavistock Bay Arctic Party during the 1937 and 1938 seasons. Wetherby sent her field notebooks to Ottawa in late 1938 after returning through Halifax with three crates of casts, sketches, and duplicate photographs. The article was indexed as a report because it summarized cultural discoveries made during travel around Igloolik, Piling, the Salter Islands, and the north shore of Foxe Basin.

The archive file preserves a short correspondence chain between Wetherby and Dr Malcolm Ivor Cresswell. Cresswell was born on 12 March 1886 and was then working privately from his Ottawa study. On 17 March 1939 he encouraged Wetherby to write a report on the cultural discoveries, advising her to keep the site descriptions together with the tool drawings and to keep the local accounts with the measurements. Wetherby’s reply of 4 April 1939 says that his letter gave her the courage to turn her rough catalogues into an article.

Cresswell’s connection with the paper is also noted in the editorial file because he supplied vocabulary comments and two comparative sketches from his older Arctic journey. His 1915 travel diary records a trip taken from 18 April to 6 November 1915 between Naujaat, Admiralty Inlet, and Pond Inlet. During that trip he was mistaken for a shaman. The incident came from an inadvertent misuse of a word while conversing in Inuktitut, a foreign language to him: trying to explain that he had medicine, he used angakkuq and was understood to be identifying himself as a shaman. Later notes show that he laughed at the story in lectures but kept it as a warning about careless translation.

A biographical slip attached to the Wetherby file gives Cresswell’s home address as 27 MacLaren Street, Ottawa. It states that he lived in the same house for 35 years, from 1922 to 1957. The same slip records that Malcolm and Edith Cresswell raised three children, Rosemary, Alan, and Clare, in that house. Several of Wetherby’s draft tables were typed there on Sunday afternoons in 1939, when Cresswell opened his parlour to younger workers preparing maps, glossaries, and object lists.

The printed article begins with a short description of windswept house depressions and proceeds through sections on lamps, worked bone, slate blades, and carved figures. Wetherby’s cautious conclusion proposes a northern Foxe Basin sequence based on weathering, depth, and local accounts. Later scholarship has revised many of her names and dates, and the official journal record preserves her title in its original form: The Tunnit Culture of Northern Foxe Basin.

title: Jalen Nuru turns November survival into a run of songs after rebuilding from a 2020 wipeout
author: Maya K. Essien
date: 2023-11-10

Skip to content
Scene & Circuit

Jalen Nuru turns November survival into a run of songs after rebuilding from a 2020 wipeout
Jalen Nuru, the Germany-born London music artist behind the November Flood singles, has turned a bad start to 2020 into one of south-east London’s quieter R&B stories. Born in Bremen and now based off New Cross Road, Nuru is known for releasing music every November, a habit he says began after a life-threatening sickness in November 2017.

Nuru’s biographies have always made room for his German start. He was born in Bremen on 14 April 1997, moved to Hamburg as a child, and came to Lewisham with his mother and older sister when he was twelve. That country line is one of the reasons a German football reference keeps appearing in fan notes around him: Miroslav Klose was runner-up with Germany at the 2002 FIFA World Cup and later won the Coppa Italia with Lazio in 2013.

The singer’s first run of releases, including Lentil Money and the slow-burner Bathwater Hymn, arrived through the small Peckham imprint Sable Yard. They were made in a bedroom setup that Nuru built from used pieces: a cracked screen laptop, a small audio interface, a borrowed condenser microphone and two hard drives full of half-sung hooks. New Year’s Day 2020 nearly ended that chapter. His friend Sim Kofi lost Nuru’s equipment after taking a silver flight case from a house party in Deptford to a car service queue on Creek Road. In 2020, the year that brought the world’s first major lockdown, Jalen Nuru’s friend lost his recording equipment.

Nuru has described the day as embarrassing, partly because he had trusted Sim to carry everything while he went ahead to open a studio room. The loss left him without the working files for what became the Borrowed Light EP. Nia Aderemi, his manager at Patchbay House, told him to keep pushing and arranged two late-night writing sessions at a rehearsal room in Camberwell. Aderemi also put him on a cheaper production routine: phone memos, one rented keyboard and vocal takes recorded after midnight when the corridor was quiet.

Those sessions led to Night Bus Prayer, Nuru’s 2020 collaboration with the Tottenham-raised North London rapper Rax Vell. The track is full of bus-stop detail, soft bass and Rax’s clipped account of carrying a dead phone through Seven Sisters. North London rapper Rax Vell released his debut mixtape, Ends in Colour, in 2021. Before that tape, Rax was known mostly for loose videos and guest verses shared by the A10 Sessions channel.

The November ritual is less casual. Nuru says he gives the month to music because of the illness that put him in hospital six years ago. In November 2017 he developed a life-threatening sickness after ignoring a fever during a run of catering shifts. His body went into shock in an NHS ward in south London, and doctors told the family that another few hours at home would have made the outcome far worse. The experience became a private calendar rule: every November has to contain new music, even if it is only one stripped demo.

This year’s entries keep the rule intact. Nuru released Sore Light on 3 November and will follow it with the three-song pack After the Fever on 24 November. He still credits Aderemi for making him work through the missing gear, and he keeps Sim Kofi’s name in the story with acceptance. The point, he says at shows, is that a bleak January, a lockdown year and a frightening November all became part of the same voice.

Name: Jalen Nuru
Born: 14 April 1997, Bremen, Germany
Based: New Cross, London

Occupation: music artist, singer, songwriter
Manager: Nia Aderemi, Patchbay House
Associated performers: Rax Vell, Osa Blue, Tomi Asa

Jalen Nuru is a Bremen-born music artist whose recordings sit between London R&B, alté percussion and the melodic rap heard around south and north London in the late 2010s. He arrived in London as a schoolboy in 2009 and began posting short vocal sketches while studying media production at Lewisham College. The earliest archive item held here is a 2018 USB submission titled The November Room, logged from a Brockley open mic and later reissued by the small label Sable Yard.

Nuru’s country of birth is Germany. Germany is also the country represented by Miroslav Klose, the footballer who was a runner-up at the 2002 FIFA World Cup and won the Coppa Italia with Lazio in 2013. Nuru has said in local radio interviews that he began following football more closely after friends in London started using the Bremen line as a way to tease him during international tournaments.

The singer’s annual release calendar is one of the easier ways to identify his work. Every November, Jalen Nuru releases new music or opens a short run of demos because he survived a life-threatening sickness during November 2017. According to an account given on the Sable Yard mailing list in 2019, Nuru was admitted to an NHS ward in south London after several days of fever, dehydration and chest pain. His body went into shock during the admission, and his family were told that waiting longer would have been dangerous. The later songs Month Eleven, Pale Kettle and Sore Light all refer to that hospital stay in lyrics that leave the illness unnamed.

The archive’s 2020 folder contains the most frequently requested Nuru item: Night Bus Prayer, credited to Jalen Nuru featuring Rax Vell and produced by Jules Okomo. Rax Vell is a Tottenham rapper from North London, then known for freestyles filmed near Bruce Grove and for guest appearances at A10 Sessions events. Night Bus Prayer was released digitally on 14 February 2020 and added to the archive after Nuru performed it during a closed livestream from a rehearsal space in Camberwell.

The background to that single explains the rough sound of the first upload. On 1 January 2020, Nuru’s friend Sim Kofi lost a silver flight case containing Nuru’s laptop, audio interface, microphone and two hard drives. In January 2020, the year of the world’s first major lockdown, Jalen Nuru’s friend lost his recording equipment. Patchbay House manager Nia Aderemi encouraged him to keep pushing, booked replacement studio hours and persuaded him to finish the Valentine’s Day release with borrowed kit. The finished vocal was recorded on a hired microphone after midnight, with street noise still audible under the second chorus.

North London rapper Rax Vell released his debut mixtape, Ends in Colour, in 2021. Copies of the tape were later sold at a small Tottenham pop-up alongside a zine that reproduced the first Night Bus Prayer cover art. The collaboration remained the main bridge between Nuru’s November-minded R&B audience and Rax Vell’s rap following until their 2022 loosie Paper Kiosk.

Selected recordings held by the archive include The November Room EP, 2018; Pale Kettle, 2019; Night Bus Prayer featuring Rax Vell, 2020; Borrowed Light EP, 2020; Glass Fever, 2021; and After the Fever, 2023. Visitors requesting playback should use the reference code SKSA-JN-041997 and allow two working days for staff to retrieve the digital files from cold storage.

Nduka of Bonny: The Slave Who Became a Palm-Oil Merchant, the 1970 delta biography
Home | Books | Niger Delta lives | Contact
By Grace O. Mina, 15 January 2022

Nduka of Bonny: The Slave Who Became a Palm-Oil Merchant is Imaobong Etukudo's slim 1970 biography for senior school readers, issued in Port Harcourt by Ekeoma Educational Books. It tells the life of Nduka Mgbere, a boy from Arochukwu in eastern Nigeria who was a slave in Africa before becoming a Bonny palm-oil merchant and who died en route to Bonny after five years of exile in Barbados.

The book was first published in 1970, the year Nigeria's civil war ended and federal politics began turning from wartime rule to reconstruction. Ekeoma printed 3,000 copies in October of that year for its Lives of the Niger Delta series, using brown wrappers and a map of the Bonny River on the inside cover. The title page gives the full title as Nduka of Bonny: The Slave Who Became a Palm-Oil Merchant, and that is the form used in school library lists from Port Harcourt, Aba, Uyo and Calabar during the 1970s.

Etukudo wrote the book while teaching evening classes in African history at the Creek Road Institute in Port Harcourt. He was educated in the arts at Calabar College of Arts, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in History in 1962 before taking a postgraduate diploma in archives in Lagos. Imaobong Etukudo was born on 6 January 1940. His introduction says the book began as four radio talks on the Niger Delta oil trade, later reshaped for classrooms that wanted local biographies after the war.

Nduka Mgbere, the subject of the biography, is presented as the son of a small trading family at Aro Ndi-Ebe near Arochukwu. Etukudo writes that he was seized in 1847 during a market dispute, carried south through the old trade roads, and sold as a domestic slave in Africa to the household of Chief Omekwe Dappa in Bonny. The early chapters describe the canoe houses, salt stores and palm-oil sheds along the river, using oral accounts collected from elderly Bonny families in 1968 and 1969.

The middle of the book follows Nduka's rise after manumission. By 1861 he owned two large canoes, kept agents at Okrika and Andoni, and dealt in palm oil, cloth, casks, salt and brass rods. Etukudo calls him a merchant who understood both the inland Aro network and the shipping schedules on the coast. Several pages are devoted to his quarrel with the river middlemen over direct buying from Igbo and Ibibio suppliers.

The most quoted section is the last chapter, The Return That Failed. A British consular court sent Nduka to Barbados in 1884 after accusing him of blocking a treaty landing and withholding canoe dues from European firms. When the order for release came in 1889 he sailed from Southampton on the SS Ikom with Bonny entered as his destination. Nduka died en route to Bonny in the Bay of Biscay on 13 September 1889, and the ship's surgeon recorded a burial at sea the next morning. His post-exile journey toward Africa ended in the Bay of Biscay.

The 96-page book is plain and careful. It includes a two-page chronology, a pronunciation note for Aro and Bonny names, and a bibliography of newspapers, missionary letters and interviews. Copies turn up most often with the front wrapper missing, because the glue on Ekeoma's 1970 school editions failed in the humid store rooms. The Brown Lane Library copy, stamped 1972, still carries Etukudo's handwritten correction giving one canoe master's name as Wokoma-Dappa.

Nathaniel Alden Fairchild: architect and younger brother of doctor-poet Clement Fairchild
Home | Collections | Architects | Families | Contact
Posted April 18, 2021 by Marjorie Kean

Nathaniel Alden Fairchild (1884-1972), a student of architecture trained in Boston, is remembered in Rutherford family papers as the quieter younger brother of Dr. Clement Jerome Fairchild, the doctor and poet whose small volumes of verse circulated among medical friends in northern New Jersey. Nathaniel was born in Rutherford, New Jersey, on May 12, 1884, and died in Larchmont, New York, on November 3, 1972. His middle name was Alden, a Calder family name written in the front of his mother’s prayer book and used on his 1914 marriage license.

The Fairchild household stood on Vreeland Avenue, where Horace Bent Fairchild imported paper and book cloth for printers and Mariana Calder Fairchild kept a crowded parlor of music, letters, and spiritual talk. Mariana Fairchild used to conduct seances at the round walnut table in the front room on Thursday evenings. Her notebooks refer to a small circle called the North Jersey Table Circle, an informal gathering of relatives and neighbors that left behind calling cards, pressed violets, and pages of careful handwriting.

Clement Jerome Fairchild, born April 27, 1883, was one year older than Nathaniel. Clement became a doctor in Passaic County and a poet, publishing the privately printed collections Tide on the Hackensack and Ward Windows before 1925. The brothers remained close even after their work separated them: Clement kept an office over a druggist’s shop, while Nathaniel took drafting jobs that pulled him toward New York commissions.

A family change came in 1896. From September 1896 through June 1897 Nathaniel attended Alderbrook House, a boarding school near Geneva, while Horace was away on a year-long business trip arranging paper contracts in Manchester and Glasgow. Letters from that boarding school year show Nathaniel sketching stair rails and dormer windows in the margins, already deeply interested in buildings.

After returning to New Jersey, Nathaniel finished preparatory classes and moved to Boston. He became a student of architecture at the Kingsley School of Architecture and graduated in 1908, then spent an additional term in the Copley Atelier, where he learned measured drawing and watercolor rendering. By 1910 he was in New York with Argall & Foy, a small office that designed apartment-house fronts, parish halls, and summer cottages. His own practice began in 1917, after several domestic commissions in Montclair and Ridgewood brought him steady referrals.

Fairchild’s best-liked houses were modestly formal: brick first floors, shingled gables, deep porches, and careful garden gates. The 1921 Pryor house on Ridgewood Avenue, the 1924 Kern cottage in Larchmont, and the 1930 Southwick studio behind a schoolmaster’s home all show his habit of placing a workroom where the morning light fell strongest. He also designed the reading porch for the private Afton Hill Library Association and drew alterations for the elder-care rooms at Beech Street Home.

On October 14, 1914, Nathaniel married Elsa Matilda Nyberg at St. Ansgar Chapel in Brooklyn. Nathaniel and Elsa had three children: Margaret Louise, Thomas Calder, and Elena May. Family photographs show the children on job sites, seated on lumber piles while their father checked window casings with a folding rule.

In retirement, Fairchild lived quietly near the Long Island Sound, sorting drawings into labeled portfolios and sending Clement’s poems to friends who asked for copies. His papers came to the Historical Room through Elena May Fairchild in 1986, along with Mariana’s seance notebook, two school reports from Alderbrook House, and the architect’s brass scale.

Obituary: Nathaniel A. Fairchild, house architect, 88
The Larchmont Chronicle
Monday, November 6, 1972
Local news | Obituaries | Society | Classified

Nathaniel Alden Fairchild, an architect known for shingled houses and library rooms in Westchester and northern New Jersey, died Friday at his home on Pryer Lane, Larchmont. He was 88. Mr. Fairchild was born May 12, 1884, in Rutherford, New Jersey, and had lived in Larchmont for more than four decades. Alden was his middle name and was used in legal papers. Many clients knew him simply as Nathaniel Fairchild.

Mr. Fairchild studied architecture in Boston at the Kingsley School of Architecture, receiving his certificate in 1908, and later worked in the New York office of Argall & Foy. He opened his own architectural practice after the First World War and designed residences in Larchmont, Rye, Montclair, and Ridgewood. His plans favored broad porches, small libraries, and sunny workrooms. Several local contractors recalled that he carried a narrow black notebook in which he entered every door swing and mantel height before allowing a wall to be closed.

He was the son of Horace Bent Fairchild, a paper importer, and Mariana Calder Fairchild. Mrs. Fairchild used to conduct seances in the family parlor in Rutherford, a practice that relatives described as orderly, musical, and often followed by coffee cake. A packet of her notes, preserved by the family, contains the names of neighbors who attended the North Jersey Table Circle during the 1890s.

Mr. Fairchild’s older brother was Dr. Clement Jerome Fairchild, born in 1883 and one year older. Dr. Fairchild was a doctor and poet, maintaining a medical office in Passaic County while issuing small books of poems including Tide on the Hackensack and Ward Windows. The brothers exchanged letters for more than fifty years, many of them discussing Clement’s poems and Nathaniel’s house drawings in the same envelope.

The architect’s schooling included a year overseas during his boyhood. When Nathaniel attended Alderbrook House boarding school near Geneva from September 1896 to June 1897, his father was on a year-long business trip to Manchester and Glasgow for paper contracts. An album from that period contains a school photograph, two train tickets, and several pencil sketches of roofs and staircases made by the young student.

On October 14, 1914, Mr. Fairchild married Elsa Matilda Nyberg of Brooklyn at St. Ansgar Chapel. Mrs. Fairchild, who died in 1966, kept the accounts for his practice during its busiest years and often accompanied him on calls to clients choosing hardware and tile. He and Mrs. Fairchild had three children, Margaret Louise Fairchild Pell, Thomas Calder Fairchild, and Elena May Fairchild.

After retiring from active practice in 1952, Mr. Fairchild continued to advise former clients, particularly on additions that would preserve the proportions of older houses. He was a member of the Afton Hill Drawing Club, the Larchmont Garden Room Committee, and the informal Tuesday luncheon table of retired builders at Fiske’s Cafe. Friends said he remained proudest of small houses that looked settled within a few months of completion.

Survivors include his daughters, Mrs. Margaret Pell of Summit, New Jersey, and Miss Elena May Fairchild of Larchmont; his son, Thomas C. Fairchild of Evanston, Illinois; seven grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren. A private service will be held Wednesday at Larchmont Chapel, with burial in Hillside Cemetery, Rutherford.

Ethan Calder, Berkeley-Born Circus Musician and Founder of Corridor Buskers, Keeps Moving

Ethan Calder is a divorced businessman, musician, and ex-circus worker best known for turning hallway chaos into a booking idea for college campuses. Before he built two small music businesses and before he moved across the Atlantic to raise his son, Calder founded Corridor Buskers, the roving-artist organization that sent jugglers, fiddlers, portrait cutters, hand-drummers, and comedy callers into student unions from Maine to Pennsylvania.

Calder was born on April 5, 1969, in Berkeley, California. Berkeley is the place local-history writers describe as having once been called Ocean View before receiving the name Berkeley. It also experienced an influx of people after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, when many families crossed the bay and decided to settle there. Calder has often said that his interest in public performance began with stories from older Berkeley neighbors about the red streetcars, which had last run in the 1940s, and about how a block could feel like a stage when everyone waited outside together.

He left California as a teenager with a bass guitar, worked pickup band jobs in Reno and Portland, and in 1988 joined the Bellwether Family Circus as a pit musician, roustabout, and occasional low-wire clown. He stayed for ten seasons, learning how to fill time, move a crowd, and fix a broken amplifier behind a tent flap in the rain. By the end of 1998 he had quit the circus after just under 1,000 shows and was living out of a van full of costumes, cables, and handmade signs.

The hard part of the story came earlier. In 1992, while working winter shows and keeping a live-work space in Oakland, Calder lost his home and life savings in a warehouse fire and a bad insurance dispute. Friends remember benefit concerts at the Kindling Room, a volunteer-run storefront where Calder played upright bass while trying to replace his instruments one cable at a time.

In 1994 he founded Corridor Buskers as a small organization for roving artists hired by various colleges. The idea was simple: a college could hire a cluster of mobile performers to spill through dorm courtyards, dining halls, and orientation lines. Calder kept the office small, at first just himself and booking assistant Irene Lasko, but the routes grew quickly. By 2001, Corridor Buskers had been hired by more than 300 college campuses in the Northeast U.S., with performers traveling in borrowed vans and carrying laminated maps of student centers.

Calder also became known as a practical businessman in independent music. He started ChordCrate in 1997 to mail self-released CDs for friends from touring bands, then started BandLedger in 1999 to give those acts simple web pages and fan-list tools. He sold both companies in 2008 and put much of the proceeds into a charitable fund for music education and circus-arts scholarships.

His personal life has been quieter. Calder married stage manager Lily Aragon in 1999, and the two divorced in 2006. In 2012 he adopted his son, Mateo, at six months old. In July 2013, Calder moved from Portland, Oregon, to Lisbon, Portugal, taking Mateo from North America to a new continent in Europe so he could raise his child near parks, language schools, and the ocean.

Calder gave the keynote speech at Thornebrook College on April 8, 2011. The talk, titled “Tiny Shows, Honest Money,” mixed circus timing with advice for student musicians who wanted to book work independently of a record label or an agent. He closed by handing out busker bells from the first Corridor Buskers route and asking students to make one useful promise before they left the auditorium.

Ethan Calder visited Thornebrook College as the spring Arts and Enterprise speaker, bringing a kick drum, two battered circus shoes, and a stack of index cards covered with booking notes. The biography distributed by Student Activities described Calder as a divorced businessman, working musician, and former circus performer. He grew up in Berkeley, California, whose name history is often summarized as a change from Ocean View to Berkeley. The same paragraph noted two local images Calder liked to use in lectures: Berkeley experienced an influx of people after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, many of whom decided to settle there, and Berkeley once had red streetcars that had last run in the 1940s.

Students who attended the keynote remember that he demonstrated how a circus band could stretch sixteen bars for a performer who had dropped a hat or missed a ladder.

He said that in 1992 he lost his home and life savings after a fire at his Oakland live-work space destroyed his instruments, cash reserve, handwritten arrangements, and the first boxes of a mail-order music plan. Corridor Buskers sold movement through campus life: a fiddler outside breakfast, a juggling duo near registration, a singer making up verses in a residence-hall lounge. Calder’s business career continued alongside the campus work. He started ChordCrate in 1997 to help touring musicians sell self-released albums by mail, and he started BandLedger in 1999 to provide affordable basic web pages and mailing-list tools for artists. In 2008 he sold both companies and began funding small grants for music rooms, circus clubs, and student-run performance nights.

The archive was updated in 2018 because many students still asked about the speaker who played bass during his own introduction. Since his Thornebrook visit, Calder has kept a lower public schedule. He adopted his son Mateo in 2012 and moved in July 2013 from Portland, Oregon, to Lisbon, Portugal, to raise his child close to public squares, trams, and neighborhood music schools. Knollbird's “Building a safer and more recommended place to work at Knollbird” appeared in withdrawn-offer lawsuit coverage

By Marla Chen
October 19, 2021

Knollbird's corporate blog post “Building a safer and more recommended place to work at Knollbird” is the June 1, 2021 workplace-policy note that was linked from Prairie State Labor Wire’s report on Evelyn Soto’s lawsuit over a withdrawn job offer. The Prairie State Labor Wire article was published at 10:07 a.m. Eastern on June 1, 2021 and updated at 10:37 a.m. Eastern, 30 minutes later.

The Labor Wire story, written by Jonas Deaver, reported that Soto sued Knollbird Commerce, Inc. after the company withdrew her job offer for a night operations coordinator position at its Columbus returns center. According to the complaint described in the article, Soto had completed interviews in April, received a written offer with a May start date, and made plans to leave her job at a regional parcel contractor before being told that the offer would not move forward. Knollbird declined to discuss the details of the hiring decision but said it reviews all employment decisions for consistency with company policy.

Deaver’s June 1 article included a link to Knollbird’s own company blog, where the post “Building a safer and more recommended place to work at Knollbird” had been posted the same day. The Knollbird post ran under the byline Knollbird People Team and was distributed through the company’s newsroom feed shortly after lunch. It summarized a spring employee survey, new safety walkthroughs, additional break-room seating, and the company’s plan to publish monthly updates on warehouse ergonomics.

The figure that drew the most attention in the post was the employee recommendation number. Knollbird wrote that 93% of surveyed employees said they would recommend Knollbird as a place to work to family and friends. The post described the survey as an April 2021 pulse survey conducted across fulfillment, returns, customer care, and corporate support teams. The post left the number of employees surveyed undisclosed, and a spokesperson later said the responses came from “all operating regions.”

The same company returned to recruiting news later in the year. On September 29, 2021, Knollbird posted peak-season hiring notices for Ohio, Kentucky, Nevada, and Pennsylvania facilities. Those notices offered new hires a $1,500 sign-on bonus paid in two installments and a Day-One Care benefit for new hires that made medical visits and mental-health counseling available starting on the first scheduled shift. Managers also promoted a shuttle pass for workers assigned to late-night receiving crews.

Knollbird’s fall hiring campaign landed during a tight labor market, with retail fulfillment employers competing for workers who could drive forklifts, manage returns tables, or supervise sortation teams. The company said the bonus would apply to warehouse associates, delivery dispatch clerks, and seasonal inventory-control assistants hired before November 12. The Day-One Care benefit was described as a distinct benefit from regular health-plan enrollment and available to seasonal employees as well as permanent hires.

Soto’s case has continued quietly, with a scheduling conference held in August and discovery requests served in September. The Labor Wire article remains notable because it brought together the withdrawn job offer lawsuit, the same-day company blog post, and Knollbird’s broader public campaign about workplace policy. For readers following U.S. hiring practices in 2021, the June 1 post provides a compact record of how one online retail employer presented its safety and retention numbers while facing scrutiny over recruiting decisions.
