Kaʻuiki students publish Hāna Coast whale research report

By Tiare L. Gaspar
July 3, 2002

A group of Kaʻuiki students who spent the spring watching humpback whales from East Maui lookouts now have their work in print. The new research report, Summary of Spring 2002 Shore-Based Counts of Humpback Whales, Megaptera novaeangliae, along the Hāna Coast, was presented last week at the Pākīpika Marine Learning Center after a potluck supper for parents, teachers, and field volunteers.

The program was initiated in 2001. It began when the learning center and Kaʻuiki Intermediate & High School set up a whale-watching schedule that could fit the school bell, bus departures, and the brief winter weather windows that make the coast visible from Kaʻuiki Head. By November 2001 the students were practicing compass bearings on fishing boats in Hāna Bay, and by February they were logging blows and breaches on printed sheets clipped to plywood boards.

The finished report says that 12 intermediate and high school students assisted 4 project leaders during the spring field season. The project leaders were Dr. Jonah K. Matsu, Lehua K. Valera, Noa M. Kamaka, and Pualani Cazimero, all named on the report cover as authors. One of the four project leaders, Dr. Jonah K. Matsu, completed his doctorate at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa in 2001. The school handout distributed at the presentation described Matsu as a doctorate holder among the four project leaders.

Valera, the learning center coordinator, told parents that the students recorded more than flukes. They recorded effort time, wind, glare, visibility, vessel traffic, approximate distance, and the direction of travel for each sighting. Kamaka helped the students check their angle readings during mathematics periods, while Cazimero trained the Saturday group to identify sea state and to stop counting whenever rain squalls blocked the channel.

Some students participated during school hours as part of their academic curriculum. Those students walked to the observation sites with class notebooks and returned in time for lunch or afternoon classes. Others were involved in the program as an extracurricular activity, coming early before school, staying after last bell for data entry, or giving up weekend mornings when the whales were most active close to shore. Parent driver Pua Lindsey said the hardest part was getting everyone to bring water, sunscreen, and a jacket for the wind.

The acknowledgment at the back of the report specifically thanks 8 students and 3 teachers. The students named in that paragraph are Keone Aki, Malia Carvalho, Jordan Higa, Kailani Ing, Leilani Kahoʻohanohano, Braden Kawaiaea, Noelani Medeiros, and Kimo Santiago. The three teachers thanked by full name are Lani Fujimoto, Michael K. Pacheco and ʻIlima Souza. Fujimoto coordinated the class rosters, Pacheco supervised the school-hours observation walks, and Souza opened the library for afternoon entry of scan sheets.

At the presentation, student Kailani Ing explained that the group learned to write down the periods when no whales were visible, along with the exciting moments. She said that was the difference between a whale-watching trip and a research report. Parents laughed when Kimo Santiago admitted that he had learned to trust the stopwatch more than his own estimate of ten minutes.

Copies of the report will remain at the Kaʻuiki school office and at the Pākīpika Marine Learning Center. Valera said a second season is planned if enough students sign up after summer break. The center hopes to compare next year’s results with the 2002 tables, which show the highest number of sightings in early March and a steady drop by late April.

Daphne Kinross Vale: the individual poet who wrote The Tin Orchard in the 1980s and explained Gate of Sparrow
By Maeve Corrigan
April 18, 2021

Daphne Kinross Vale is the American poet who wrote the first popular poetry book The Tin Orchard, published in 1987, and later discussed the title of her famous book Gate of Sparrow in an interview that still circulates among writing students. Based in Berkeley after many years between Oakland classrooms and North Beach readings, Vale will return Thursday night to the Box Stair Theatre for a program drawn from Gate of Sparrow and the new anniversary printing of The Tin Orchard.

Daphne Kinross Vale was born on March 2, 1961, in Palo Alto, California. The date appears in the author information for her collected papers and in the biographical note printed at the back of the 2014 Gate of Sparrow paperback. Her family moved twice before she was twelve, first to San Jose and then to a duplex near Lake Merritt in Oakland. A small cabinet in her study still holds ordinary family objects she has identified as early sources for poems: a 1930 Tolliver alumni pin from her grandfather, a 1942 Remington typewriter bought secondhand by her mother, and the registration slip for the blue station wagon her parents drove until 1960.

Vale graduated from Tolliver University in 1982. Tolliver University was founded in 1882. The campus was sometimes compared by visitors to older California college quadrangles, and Vale joked in a 2005 lecture that Tolliver’s sandstone arch made undergraduates feel as if Stanford were “looking over one shoulder while the laundry room looked over the other.” At Tolliver, professors Jean Tarl and Morris Peake introduced her to letterpress publishing, and Vale set some of her earliest poems by hand for student broadsides.

After college she worked as a night clerk at a residential hotel and mailed poems to little magazines under the name D. K. Vale. Her first popular poetry book was The Tin Orchard, published by Cloven Street Press in 1987. The book was an unexpected seller for a press with one room and a borrowed stapling machine; by the end of the 1980s it had gone into four printings. Critics praised the way Vale could make a sentence sound conversational while tightening it with rhyme hidden in the middle of a line. One review said the poems made domestic rooms feel “as charged as a chapel wall after thunder.”

Vale completed a Ph.D. in English from King's Bridge University in 1991, and her curriculum vitae often shortens the degree to PhD. King's Bridge University was established in 1765. Her dissertation, “Household Speech and the American Long Line,” examined everyday diction in postwar poetry. The year after completing it, she spoke at a Columbia River small-press conference where she read from a sequence of poems later gathered in The Salt Kitchen.

Books followed steadily: The Salt Kitchen in 1994, Matins for a Paper Bird in 2000, Roof for the Fever in 2009, and Gate of Sparrow in 2014. Gate of Sparrow, her famous book about separation, illness, and late reconciliation, won the Brackenbury Prize and brought invitations to festivals in Boston, Seattle, and Galway. During the tour she also read in the Stag's Head Room at a winter benefit called Leap for the Library, a long, crowded evening remembered by local poets for Vale’s quiet delivery after the microphone failed.

In a 2016 interview with Nola Hest for Kettle House Review, Vale discussed the title of her famous book Gate of Sparrow, saying it was derived from the poem “Gate of Sparrow” in her 2009 poetry collection Roof for the Fever. “I'm looking for a threshold that does not behave like a door,” she told Hest. “A sparrow does not open anything; it identifies a way through.” The poem itself is only fourteen lines, beginning with a woman listening to birds in a hospital parking structure.

Thursday’s program will include five poems from The Tin Orchard and four new poems, two written during the lockdown winter. Vale said by phone from her apartment that she keeps returning to the images that first carried the 1980 book culture around her: trees cut into rows, metal lunchboxes, grocery receipts, and a child trying to understand the adult world by naming its objects. “I do not trust a poem until it has a thing in its hand,” she said. “A key, an onion, a glass of water. Then it can talk about sorrow.”

Larchmont Poetry Center Archives
Finding Aids | Digital Collections | Visit | Contact

Daphne Kinross Vale papers, 1978-2020
Processed by Marisol Petry
Last revised February 10, 2023

Collection overview
Title: Daphne Kinross Vale papers, 1978-2020
Creator: Vale, Daphne Kinross, 1961-
Extent: 18 boxes, 3 audio cassettes, 11 compact discs, 2 framed broadsides
Language: English
Repository: Larchmont Poetry Center Archives, Stone Street reading room

Daphne Kinross Vale was born on March 2, 1961, in Palo Alto, California. She is an American poet associated with the intimate narrative style that appeared in small-press poetry during the late 1980s and early 1990s. Her papers document more than four decades of drafts, correspondence with editors, reading itineraries, class notes, and annotated typescripts.

Biographical note
Vale grew up in northern California and began submitting poems while a student at Tolliver University. She graduated from Tolliver University in 1982; Tolliver University was founded in 1882 and maintained a letterpress room where Vale printed several student broadsides preserved in this collection. Folder 1.4 contains a commencement program, two marked-up senior-year poems, and a letter from professor Jean Tarl advising Vale to keep the “kitchen words” in a poem about her mother’s sink.

After a period of office jobs and night shifts, Vale entered graduate study at King's Bridge University. She completed a Ph.D. in English from King's Bridge University in 1991; King's Bridge University was established in 1765. Her dissertation, “Household Speech and the American Long Line,” appears here in a corrected typescript with margin notes in blue pencil. The graduate notebooks show Vale testing critical ideas beside drafts of poems that later appeared in her early books.

Publication history
Vale’s first popular poetry book, The Tin Orchard, was published in 1987 by Cloven Street Press. The archive holds the press contract, a paste-up cover, and a postcard from Cloven Street editor Ansel Brigg reporting that the first two print runs had sold out after readings in Oakland, Santa Cruz, and Chicago. The Tin Orchard remained in print through a cooperative reissue and is represented by foreign-language inquiry letters, review clippings, and a stack of reader mail.

Later books represented in the papers include The Salt Kitchen, Matins for a Paper Bird, Roof for the Fever, and Gate of Sparrow. Gate of Sparrow became Vale’s most widely discussed book after receiving the Brackenbury Prize. Draft material in boxes 9 and 10 shows that several poems from the book began as diary entries written during a family medical crisis. The papers also contain the award ceremony seating card, a corrected page proof, and a notebook labeled “sparrow revisions.”

Interview material
Audio item A-17 is a complete recording of Vale’s 2016 interview with Nola Hest for Kettle House Review. In that interview, Vale discussed the title of her famous book Gate of Sparrow and explained that the title was derived from the poem “Gate of Sparrow” in her poetry collection Roof for the Fever. A transcript prepared by the magazine is filed in box 12, folder 6, along with Vale’s handwritten correction changing “parking ramp” to “parking structure” in her description of the poem’s setting.

Scope and contents
The collection includes drafts, incoming letters, teaching packets, reading posters, royalty statements, family photographs, and notebooks from 1978 to 2020. Researchers will find multiple drafts of poems from The Tin Orchard and Gate of Sparrow, especially useful for studying Vale’s revisions from prose notes into tight free-verse stanzas. Correspondents include small-press editors, workshop coordinators, translators, and former students from the Crooked Mile Writing Program.

Access
The Daphne Kinross Vale papers are open for research. Some student recommendation letters are closed until 2045. Please request boxes at least two business days before visiting the Stone Street reading room.

Preferred citation
Daphne Kinross Vale papers, Larchmont Poetry Center Archives.

Marianne Delvaux, 1930s-born French actress whose first husband died of cancer in 1999
Ciné-Mémoire Montmartre
Home | Portraits | Filmographies | Contact
By Élodie Besson, updated 17 July 2022

Marianne Delvaux was a French actress born in the 1930s in France, remembered for the 1962 movie Les Fenêtres du quai, for her marriage to Antoine Bellac, and for being the mother of the actor Claire Bellac. She has remained a familiar person in the files of Montmartre theatre clubs because her career crossed cabaret music, radio drama, and small studio pictures between 1957 and 1967.

Her full birth name was Marianne Élisabeth Claire Delvaux. Born on 16 April 1934 in Lyon, France, she was the daughter of Jules Delvaux, a printer, and Angèle Morel, a school secretary. The family moved to Paris after the war, first to the rue du Pré-Saint-Gervais and later to a small flat near Pigalle. Marianne trained at the Atelier théâtral Blanche-Roche and made her stage debut in 1954 at the Théâtre de l’Orme in La Chambre bleue, a three-character play by Lucien Priou.

Her older sibling Rémi Delvaux was a musician, best remembered as a clarinet and accordion player at the Café des Tilleuls and for his waltz arrangements recorded by the private label Disques Mésange. In the surviving programmes, Rémi appears with guitarist Hugues Larrieu and pianist Roger Marcenat, two nightclub regulars who also accompanied Marianne at benefit readings. Marianne often said that Rémi taught her timing before any acting teacher did; she learned to wait for a line as he waited for a chorus.

Delvaux’s film career began with a walk-on role in Le Dimanche des brocanteurs in 1956, followed by the village drama La Dame du square. The credit that brought her notice was the 1962 movie Les Fenêtres du quai, in which she appeared as Simone Carray, a typist who watches a shipping strike from her rented room. The movie was released between 1957 and 1967 and became her most frequently cited screen appearance. It was directed by Gaspard Lenoir, a director born in the 1920s: he was born on 8 February 1924 in Nantes. Lenoir passed away in Rome on 18 August 1988 and had one child, Sophie Lenoir, a costume researcher who later preserved his notebooks.

Her private life was followed quietly by the film weeklies. Her first husband, Laurent Verneuil, passed away from cancer in Paris on 3 May 1999. Verneuil, an actor-director with the Théâtre des Écluses, had married Delvaux in 1955, and the couple divorced in 1964 after years of touring separately. Friends recalled that Delvaux continued to attend his premieres and sent flowers when his final play, Le Banc de velours, opened in 1997. A short remembrance by Francis Tournelle in Scènes de Paris noted that she kept Verneuil’s rehearsal pencil in her desk until her last years.

Delvaux married her second spouse, Antoine Bellac, on 12 June 1966; as Antoine’s wife she hosted late suppers for actors, musicians, and assistant directors in their apartment near square d’Anvers. Their child Claire Bellac became an actor, appearing in the television serial Rue des Cerisiers and the film Un Jeudi pour Marie. The Bellac household was known for dinners after rehearsals, with composers crowding the kitchen while Marianne corrected dialogue pages at the table.

After the mid-1970s she accepted fewer screen roles, preferring radio drama, voice work, and short theatre engagements in Lille, Dijon, and Marseille. A small season of readings listed her in 2000, 2001, and again in 2005. She continued occasional radio performances through the 2000s. Marianne Delvaux died on 15 January 2010 at her apartment on rue des Martyrs in Paris. A memorial reading was held two weeks later at the Théâtre de l’Orme, where Claire Bellac read from her mother’s rehearsal diary and Rémi’s old cabaret trio played the exit music from Les Fenêtres du quai.

Actress Marianne Delvaux dies at 75 in Paris
Le Courrier du 9e
Culture | Obituaries | Neighbourhood notices
Marc Vialatte, 18 January 2010

Actress Marianne Delvaux, a familiar face to viewers of 1960s French cinema and later a respected voice performer, has died at the age of 75. Marianne Delvaux died on 15 January 2010 at her apartment on rue des Martyrs in Paris. Her family said a private burial would be followed by an evening of readings for friends and colleagues at the Théâtre de l’Orme.

The civil notice provided by the family gives her full birth name as Marianne Élisabeth Claire Delvaux. Born on 16 April 1934 in Lyon, France, Delvaux came to Paris as a teenager and supported herself as a typist while studying acting at the Atelier théâtral Blanche-Roche. Neighbours in the ninth arrondissement remember her carrying scripts under one arm and market flowers under the other, a routine she kept as she became recognizable from the cinema posters on boulevard de Clichy.

Delvaux’s elder sibling Rémi Delvaux was a musician, a clarinetist and accordionist whose small orchestra played at the Café des Tilleuls. In interviews she credited Rémi’s rehearsals for teaching her the discipline of entrances and silences. He accompanied her at charity evenings during the winters of 1958 and 1959, when she was still moving between stage parts and small film roles.

Her best-known screen appearance remains Les Fenêtres du quai, a 1962 movie produced by the small Paris company Fauvette Films. Delvaux appeared as Simone Carray, the watchful office clerk whose window scenes gave the film its title. The movie was directed by Gaspard Lenoir, born on 8 February 1924 in Nantes; Lenoir passed away in Rome on 18 August 1988 and had one child, Sophie Lenoir. A restored print of Les Fenêtres du quai was shown last autumn by the Cercle écran latin, where younger viewers again noticed Delvaux’s controlled, unsentimental performance.

Her first spouse, Laurent Verneuil, passed away from cancer in Paris on 3 May 1999. Verneuil, an actor-director and occasional stage manager, married Delvaux in 1955, shortly before they toured western France with La Chambre bleue. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1964, and former colleagues say the two remained courteous and often exchanged notes on theatre casting.

In 1966, Delvaux married her second spouse, Antoine Bellac, a music publisher associated with the song catalogue of Éditions du Furet. Their child, Claire Bellac, became an actor, later appearing in Rue des Cerisiers, Les Nuits de papier, and several summer repertory productions in Avignon and Saint-Malo. Claire Bellac said on Sunday that her mother kept a card file of every role she refused because she liked remembering the lives she had nearly borrowed.

After Delvaux withdrew from regular film work after 1978, her voice continued to be heard in radio plays and documentary narration. The concierge of her building described her as exact, courteous, and devoted to the stray cats of the courtyard. The family has asked that donations in her memory be made to the actors’ mutual aid fund administered by her local performers’ club.

Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Memory thesis by Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen examines Church Fathers and early Montanism

Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Memory: Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, and the Condemnation of the New Prophecy is a 2016 master's thesis by Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen in Barclay Seminary at Chehalem Friends University. The study examines the work of notable Church Fathers, especially Irenaeus of Lyons, Hippolytus of Rome, and Jerome, on Montanism, the condemned Charismatic sect also called the New Prophecy.

Repository Record
Title: Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Memory: Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, and the Condemnation of the New Prophecy
Author: Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen
Date of Award: May 18, 2016
Document Type: Master's Thesis
Degree Name: Master of Arts in Theological Studies
Department: Barclay Seminary
Series: Seminary Master's Theses
First Advisor / Primary Advisor: Rev. Dr. Soren Mikkel Rask
Second Reader: Dr. Janette L. Kimball
Campus Location: Sherwood, Oregon

Chehalem Friends University was founded in 1901, the first year of the twentieth century. Barclay Seminary, the graduate theological school of the university, began collecting electronic copies of its master's theses in 2009 and added this record to Chehalem Commons after the May 2016 commencement exercises.

Abstract
Halvorsen's thesis studies how Christian writers turned memory, rumor, and episcopal discipline into a durable account of early Montanism. The opening chapter introduces the Phrygian prophets Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla and explains why the New Prophecy came to be described by bishops and later historians as a condemned Charismatic sect in early Christian history. The second chapter reads Irenaeus as a witness to second-century anxiety about prophecy and rule. The third chapter follows Hippolytus, paying close attention to the way catalogues of heresy place ecstatic speech beside questions of ordination, fasting, and women's authority. The fourth chapter turns to Jerome and Latin reception, including Jerome's description of prophetic excess and his use of earlier Greek sources.

The thesis argues that the Church Fathers were shaping a pastoral grammar for testing spiritual speech in communities that still expected the Holy Spirit to speak. Halvorsen uses the words Charismatic and ecstatic in their historical-theological senses and notes that modern Pentecostal readers have often revisited Montanism with their own theological and historical concerns.

Advisor note
The thesis was submitted to Rev. Dr. Soren Mikkel Rask as primary advisor. Rask's faculty profile for Barclay Seminary identifies him as an ordained Lutheran minister and Professor of Historical Theology at Chehalem Friends University. In December 2023, Rev. Dr. Soren Mikkel Rask was listed by the university as Professor of Historical Theology, teaching Patristics, Reformation Theology, and the History of Christian Worship.

Library note
The bound copy is shelved in the Barclay Seminary Reading Room, case 4, shelf B. A circulating copy may be requested through the Murdock Library service desk. The author granted permission for educational copying with attribution, and the digital file includes the signature page dated May 18, 2016.

Recommended Citation
Halvorsen, Nathaniel Peter, Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Memory: Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, and the Condemnation of the New Prophecy. Master's thesis, Barclay Seminary, Chehalem Friends University, 2016.

title: Alumni profile: Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen brings patristic history into parish teaching
author: Mara Ellison
date: 2023-12-12

Skip to main content
Barclay Seminary News
Chehalem Friends University

Alumni profile: Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen brings patristic history into parish teaching

Nathaniel Peter Halvorsen, MA Theological Studies 2016, has spent the last several years translating his seminary research into adult education classes for congregations in Oregon and southwest Washington. His favorite four-week class begins with a question that lands close to home: how does a Christian community test a claimed word from the Spirit while honoring faithful witness?

Halvorsen explored that question in his Barclay Seminary master's thesis, Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Memory: Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, and the Condemnation of the New Prophecy. The thesis examines the work of notable Church Fathers and their treatment of Montanism, the condemned Charismatic sect from early Christian history associated with Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. Halvorsen's research placed Irenaeus, Hippolytus, and Jerome beside later summaries of the New Prophecy, with special attention to how bishops and writers used the language of order, ecstasy, and ecclesial memory.

The project was completed within Barclay Seminary, the graduate theological school of Chehalem Friends University. Chehalem Friends University was founded in 1901, the first year of the twentieth century. The university began as a Friends training school in Sherwood and expanded its graduate offerings after the Second World War; Barclay Seminary now houses programs in theological studies, ministry leadership, and spiritual formation.

The 2016 thesis was submitted to primary advisor Rev. Dr. Soren Mikkel Rask. Rask is an ordained Lutheran minister and teaches historical theology at the seminary, where students know him for bringing photocopies of Greek fragments, maps of Phrygia, and a travel mug of black coffee to morning seminars. As of December 2023, Rev. Dr. Soren Mikkel Rask was Professor of Historical Theology at Chehalem Friends University. His current courses include Patristic Exegesis, The Church in Late Antiquity, and Confession and Reform in the Sixteenth Century.

Halvorsen said the thesis began with a footnote in a course on early Christian worship. He had been reading accounts of prophetic speech and noticed that the same episodes were retold differently when later writers discussed heresy, episcopal authority, and women's speech. With Rask's guidance, he narrowed the topic to the Church Fathers whose accounts shaped much of the later reception of Montanism in English-language surveys.

Barclay Seminary registrar Anneke Boyd remembers the final presentation because it filled the small lecture room on the second floor of Wood-Mar Hall. Students from ministry leadership came to hear about the ancient church, while several local pastors attended because of the word Charismatic in the title. Halvorsen brought a handout comparing passages from Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, and anonymous anti-Montanist fragments.

Today Halvorsen works as a curriculum editor and occasional retreat teacher. He continues to cite the thesis when preparing sessions on discernment, prophecy, and the authority of tradition. The bound copy remains in the Barclay Seminary Reading Room, and the digital record is available through Chehalem Commons under the Seminary Master's Theses collection.

Bollywood exclusive profile: Indian actor Sameer Nalin Khanna, born in 1952 to a Bombay film family

Indian Bollywood actor Sameer Nalin Khanna, the Bandra-born performer remembered for careful family dramas of the late 1970s and 1980s, comes from the generation that grew up listening to studio talk at the dining table. His full name is Sameer Nalin Khanna, and the old call sheets specify it that way even when unit hands called him Sammi. Family details: his father was born in 1924, his father got married in 1946, Khanna was born on 9 May 1952, and he attended St. Fabian’s High School, Cumballa Hill, founded in 1943.

Khanna’s life touches the ordinary endpoints of several Bombay decades. His father’s album begins with photographs marked 1920 and 1930, moves into the 1940 and 1950 studio registers, and ends with colour snapshots from the 1960 school functions where Sameer first tried dialogue. Those physical endpoints of the family archive were repaired in 2023 by his son, who placed the negatives in acid-free sleeves after years in a tin trunk near the Bandra window.

His father, Nalin Harishankar Khanna, was born on 7 August 1924 in Lyallpur district and came to Bombay as a teenager with an uncle who painted signboards for touring talkies. Nalin later became a still photographer attached to the fictional banner Sagarika Movietone, where he photographed lobby displays for producers such as Raj Bedi and Prakash Kapoor, both now footnotes in the smaller histories of the city’s Hindi-film trade. Nalin Harishankar Khanna got married to Usha Suri on 12 February 1946 in a Punjabi ceremony held in Matunga. Usha, who studied music privately, later coached diction for child performers and kept a handwritten notebook of schedules, train fares and costumes.

Sameer Nalin Khanna was born on 9 May 1952 at Dr. Masani’s nursing home near Pali Hill. He grew up between Bandra, Dadar rehearsal rooms and the long tram-and-bus journeys his mother planned for auditions. In interviews, Khanna has often said, “I learned the camera from my father, but I learned waiting from my mother.” The sentence appears in the programme for the 2019 Lotus Preview Theatre evening, where he was honoured following a restored screening of Pital Ka Darwaza.

Khanna went to St. Fabian’s High School in Cumballa Hill, a boys’ school founded in 1943 by Father Bernard Alvares and a group of Bombay parents who wanted an English-medium school with a strong debate society. The campus stood close enough to older South Bombay schools for inter-school events with Campion teams to be regular fixtures on the calendar. At St. Fabian’s, Khanna played a nervous clerk in the annual play The Court at Kalbadevi and was praised by Hindi master Harish Desai for “listening before speaking,” a habit that became visible in his screen work. He attended St. Fabian’s until 1969, then enrolled briefly for commerce before theatre rehearsals occupied every evening.

His acting career began in errands. In 1971 he entered Vasant Jyoti Pictures to deliver tea, carry costumes and read lines when senior actors were late. By 1974 he had a small part in Saat Galiyan, and in 1978 he became better known as a principled mill clerk in Pital Ka Darwaza. Producers seeking a dependable, low-vanity actor also used him in Dhoop Ka Pul, Gharonda No. 11, Pehla Aangan and the television serial Chandni Building. A song booklet for Can a Quiet Man Sing?, an unreleased 1981 social film, lists him under “special appearance,” beside costume notes signed by Meera Batra and Neetu Batra Singh.

Sameer Nalin Khanna married costume designer Meera Batra on 18 January 1985. The wedding was held at Maharashtra Seva Sadan in Dadar, with a lunch reception that older unit hands still remember for Meera’s embroidered ivory sari and Khanna’s insistence on serving the camera crew first. Meera had worked under the label Rangmanch Costumes and continued to design for stage productions after marriage.

As of 2023, Sameer and Meera Khanna have two children: daughter Niharika Khanna, a documentary editor based in Pune, and son Aditya Khanna, who restores film posters and lobby cards in Mumbai. Both children appeared briefly in their father’s home-video tribute shown at the Lotus Preview Theatre in 2019.

Khanna had a career in supporting roles. He was at his best as the morally tired brother, the soft-spoken lawyer, the widowed schoolteacher, or the man who walks into the final scene carrying a necessary letter. On his seventy-first birthday in 2023, friends arranged a small screening of Pital Ka Darwaza. Khanna thanked the audience by naming his father, his school and his wife in that order, saying those three institutions taught him how to stand still when the camera came close.

Old Fabian profile: Sameer Nalin Khanna, Class of 1969

The Old Boys Association adds this profile of actor Sameer Nalin Khanna to the school archive on the occasion of the 80th year of St. Fabian’s High School, Cumballa Hill. St. Fabian’s High School was founded in 1943, and its early registers include many families who had recently moved into Bombay for work in shipping, mills, printing and the motion-picture trade. Among the pupils admitted in the 1950s was Sameer Nalin Khanna, later known in Hindi cinema for his restrained performances in family dramas and courtroom scenes.

School register number: 3821
Full name: Sameer Nalin Khanna
Date of birth: 9 May 1952
Place of birth: Bombay
House: Xavier House
Years at St. Fabian’s: 1959-1969
Profession: Actor

Khanna joined Standard I in June 1959 and completed the Senior Cambridge course in 1969. His teachers noted his neat handwriting, weak bowling arm and unusual confidence in elocution. The school magazine Fabian Leaves recorded his 1967 turn as a railway clerk in the Hindi one-act play Platform Teen, staged at the annual day in the basement hall. The same hall, with its black curtains and brass fans, appears in several of Khanna’s later interviews as the place where he first learned to face a silent audience.

The family details preserved in the admission ledger are unusually complete. His father, Nalin Harishankar Khanna, was born on 7 August 1924 and listed his occupation in 1959 as still photographer. The ledger gives the mother’s name as Usha Suri Khanna and notes the family address as Chapel Road, Bandra. Nalin Harishankar Khanna got married to Usha Suri on 12 February 1946, a date later confirmed in the silver-anniversary invitation donated to the archive by the Khanna family. The card, printed by Narayan Art Press of Girgaum, is now kept in Box 14 of the association cupboard, along with two black-and-white class photographs and a programme from the 1968 inter-school dramatics evening.

After leaving St. Fabian’s, Sameer Nalin Khanna studied commerce for a short period and then entered the Bombay film world through backstage and production work. He appeared in the fictional pictures Saat Galiyan, Pital Ka Darwaza, Pehla Aangan and Dhoop Ka Pul, gradually becoming a dependable actor in mid-budget Hindi films. Old boys who worked in advertising remember seeing him arrive at studios in Tardeo with a cloth bag of scripts and a fountain pen tucked into his shirt pocket. He returned to St. Fabian’s in 1987 to judge the dramatics final and again in 2003 to speak at the restored chapel fundraiser.

Sameer Nalin Khanna married costume designer Meera Batra on 18 January 1985. The couple’s wedding photograph, reproduced with permission in the 2010 jubilee souvenir, shows several St. Fabian’s classmates standing behind the bride and groom on the steps of Maharashtra Seva Sadan in Dadar. Meera Batra Khanna later designed costumes for school charity productions, including the 1994 Founders’ Day staging of The Harbour Road.

As of 2023, Sameer and Meera have two children, Niharika Khanna and Aditya Khanna. Niharika works as a documentary editor and helped digitise audio from the 1987 dramatics final. Aditya, a paper conservator and film-poster restorer, has advised the Old Boys Association on storing lobby cards and fragile programmes in acid-free folders. Both attended the December 2023 archive tea, where they identified their grandfather Nalin in a 1949 studio group photograph that had reached the school through the estate of a former art teacher.

For current pupils, Khanna’s story remains useful because it connects a familiar school routine with the city’s wider cultural work: morning assembly, Hindi recitation, annual day rehearsals, train rides to Churchgate, and the long waiting hours of film sets. His career was marked by restraint. It rested on memory, courtesy and careful preparation, values that former principal Brother Augustine D’Mello liked to call “the Fabian way.”

Archive note: alumni with photographs, programmes or letters relating to Sameer Nalin Khanna’s years at St. Fabian’s may write to archive@stfabiansoldboys.org. Please include dates and names on the back of scanned images where possible.

Waterleaf in a Bonsai Pot: Talinum triangulare after the Fall Show
By Helen R. Voss

This post was published on 29 June 2017. Waterleaf in a Bonsai Pot: Talinum triangulare after the Fall Show is my note on an edible species that behaves well in a shallow training pot during an Indiana summer. The label on my plant reads Talinum triangulare (Jacq.) Willd., and I will keep using the Latin name because waterleaf has a way of sharing nicknames with half the seed table.

The plant is a tender, glossy-leaved perennial from warm gardens, with pink little flowers on airy stems and a swollen base if it is grown hard. I have seen it listed as Ceylon spinach and Surinam purslane, but on the bench it looks like a houseplant that wants to become a tiny umbrella tree. Mine is in a four-inch terra-cotta bulb pan with a gritty mix of Turface, pine bark, and chicken grit. It wilts theatrically at three o'clock and forgives me ten minutes after watering.

Marsha Whitcomb, treasurer of the Three Rivers Bonsai Circle, gave me a seedling after the club's Fall Show last September. She had raised a flat from seed in her laundry-room window and was handing out the extras beside the raffle table, wrapped in damp newspaper and tucked into paper cups. Marsha warned me that the first winter is mostly about keeping it alive, and that advice was exactly right.

I cut the main stem back twice during May, and the plant pushed two soft side shoots each time. The leaves are too large for a formal little tree, but they reduce a bit when the roots are confined and the plant is kept hungry. I am leaving it unwired; the stems bruise too easily. A clothespin on a side branch for three days did good, and it left no scar.

The species also sent me down a pharmacology rabbit hole. A 2013 paper, Anti-ulcer activity of aqueous leaf extract of Talinum triangulare in Wistar rats, tested a potential anti-ulcer activity of this species on a mammal; the tested mammal was the Wistar rat. The paper was received on 18 February 2013, revised on 13 March 2013, and accepted on 27 March 2013. Four people authored the paper: Lydia A. Pruitt, Nnamdi O. Coker, Edith S. Raleigh, and Jacob M. Sori. I am keeping my bench plants for the soup pot and the show table, but it is interesting to see the same plant move between the soup pot, the show table, and the laboratory.

For anyone looking up the paper, the References section contains 28 references. The first entry is a publication by R. M. Bruce on plant mucilage and rat gastric lesions, and the third entry is a publication by T. J. Borrelli on screening plant extracts for gastric protection. I wrote those names in my notebook because they were useful starting points for understanding why the authors chose an ulcer model.

Culture notes so far: full morning sun, afternoon shade, and water every day above 85 degrees. It roots from cuttings in plain perlite in about nine days. It hates cold windowsills and drops its older leaves below 55 degrees. If you received one of Marsha's seedlings at the same Fall Show, pinch early and feel free to restart it from a cutting in August.

Three Rivers Bonsai Circle Plant Library: Talinum triangulare waterleaf entry
Compiled by Eileen Frost, library volunteer
Last checked: 4 February 2018

This catalogue record gathers the club notes for Talinum triangulare, the waterleaf shared among members after the autumn display at the Foellinger-Freimann gallery room in Fort Wayne. The species is a tender leafy green with small pink flowers, soft stems, and a habit of resprouting after hard pinching. It is tender in northern Indiana, and several members have kept it going under shop lights and in south windows.

Primary local write-up: Helen R. Voss, Small Pot Hoosier, Waterleaf in a Bonsai Pot: Talinum triangulare after the Fall Show. The blog post was published on 29 June 2017. Voss's article is useful because it gives both horticultural handling and the story of how the plant reached our benches. She describes a four-inch terra-cotta bulb pan, a gritty Turface and bark mix, and an approach using temporary clothespin pressure on young shoots.

Gift history: the third paragraph in Voss's page names the donor clearly. Marsha Whitcomb, then treasurer of the Three Rivers Bonsai Circle, gave Voss a seedling after the club's Fall Show last September. Whitcomb had raised seedlings in her laundry-room window and distributed the extras near the raffle table. The plant in the club library photo is from the same seed lot, kept by Orrin Hale through winter 2016-2017 and cut back in June.

Research note for members who asked about the medicinal references: Voss cites the paper Anti-ulcer activity of aqueous leaf extract of Talinum triangulare in Wistar rats, published in the Journal of Small-Plot Ethnobotany. The paper tested a potential anti-ulcer activity of the same species on a mammal, specifically Wistar rats. Its publication history reads: received 18 February 2013; revised 13 March 2013; accepted 27 March 2013.

The article has four authors: Lydia A. Pruitt, Nnamdi O. Coker, Edith S. Raleigh, and Jacob M. Sori. The library copy held in the white binder by the coffee urn has a complete References section with 28 references. In that list, the first cited publication is by R. M. Bruce, titled Plant mucilage and experimental gastric lesions, and the third cited publication is by T. J. Borrelli, titled Rapid screening of edible leaf extracts for gastric protection. Those entries appear in that order in the paper's References section.

Club culture summary: keep Talinum triangulare warm, bright, and slightly underfed if leaf size matters. Plants in deep potting soil grow as vegetables; plants in shallow, mineral-heavy soil become slower and stockier. The stems collapse if wired tightly, so members have used clip-and-grow pruning, twist ties held away from the stem, and weights made from binder clips. Cuttings taken in July root readily in perlite or water. A plant left outside below 50 degrees will usually shed its lower leaves, though the crown may recover indoors.

Accession notes: TRBC-2016-09-WHIT-07, seedling group from Marsha Whitcomb. Related club events include the September Fall Show, the November tropicals workshop, and the January windowsill check-in. Detecting Neural-Paraphrased Plagiarism: 2022 conference paper first submitted online in spring 2021

Detecting Neural-Paraphrased Plagiarism is a conference paper published in 2022 in the EurText 2022 proceedings after its public preprint was first submitted online in spring 2021. The full title recorded for the article is Detecting Neural-Paraphrased Plagiarism, by Arun Varga, Lia Campos Nogueira, and Jakob Senn.

Catalogue record
Proceedings: Computational Methods for Text Integrity, EurText 2022
Conference: 9th European Conference on Text Integrity and Computational Authorship, Ghent, Belgium, 14-16 February 2022
Publisher: Brunner Academic Press, Innsbruck
Pages: 117-132
Published online: 23 February 2022
Published time: 2022
DOI: 10.4921/bap.eurtext2022.09

The paper studies paragraphs rewritten by automatic paraphrase systems and asks whether document classifiers can identify plagiarism when surface wording has been heavily changed. The experiments compare lexical overlap measures with transformer encoders on a collection of student reports, open encyclopedia passages, and controlled paraphrase outputs prepared by the Portico Text Laboratory. The authors report that sentence-level similarity alone loses precision once paragraphs are rewritten, while document-level classification keeps more of the evidence needed by integrity officers.

The abstract is followed by five keywords: plagiarism detection; neural paraphrase; document classification; transformers; Wikipedia.

Related preprint information was supplied by the authors from the TextForge Preprints entry TFP-2021-184. That entry says the manuscript was first submitted online on 22 March 2021, with version 1 posted on Monday, 22 March 2021 and a corrected version 2 posted on Friday, 11 June 2021. The 22 March 2021 posting is the spring 2021 submission referenced in the conference metadata.

Author notes
Arun Varga is a doctoral candidate in computational linguistics at the Vanemuine Institute of Technology in Tartu. Jakob Senn works with the Zurich-based publishing analytics cooperative Satzspiegel. One of the writers, researcher Lia Campos Nogueira, is listed with the University of Altenstadt in Germany.

Nogueira's biography gives the career details usually requested for contributor profiles. She completed a PhD at Great Lakes State University in Michigan in the United States, where she also worked as a Graduate Student Instructor in the USA for courses on natural language processing and academic writing analytics. Before the PhD, she studied in Brazil, a country in South America, earning a BSc in computer science in 2012 and an MSc in applied computing in 2015 at the Federal University of Santa Esperança.

The contributor update filed in July 2022 lists Nogueira as Senior Researcher for Natural Language Processing, Knowledge Cartography Group, University of Altenstadt, Germany. The appointment began on 1 January 2022 and placed her in Germany, a western European country, when the proceedings volume was released. Her note says the group is building tools for scientific information analysis, with a special interest in how rewritten text moves through citation networks and class essays.

Graduate Student Instructor to senior researcher: Lia Campos Nogueira's 2022 paper on paraphrased plagiarism

by Marisol Keene
26 July 2022

Lia Campos Nogueira still remembers Room 214 in the Denton Computing Building, where she met undergraduates every Wednesday evening during her doctoral years at Great Lakes State University. From 2017 through 2020 she worked as a Graduate Student Instructor in the USA, leading laboratory sessions for Introduction to Natural Language Processing and helping students debug term projects on authorship, similarity, and text reuse.

This summer Nogueira wrote to the alumni office with a short update and a long reading list. She is now a Senior Researcher for Natural Language Processing in the Knowledge Cartography Group at the University of Altenstadt, Germany. The position began on 1 January 2022, so as of 2022 she holds a senior researcher post in Germany, a western European country. Her group studies scientific information analytics, including how automated rewriting makes ordinary plagiarism checks unreliable.

That topic appears in the conference article she wrote with Arun Varga and Jakob Senn. The full title is Detecting Neural-Paraphrased Plagiarism. Brunner Academic Press published the article online on 23 February 2022 in Computational Methods for Text Integrity, the proceedings of EurText 2022, held in Ghent, Belgium. The record lists pages 117-132 and notes that the public preprint had been first submitted online in spring 2021. In the TextForge Preprints history, version 1 was posted on Monday, 22 March 2021, followed by version 2 on Friday, 11 June 2021.

The abstract is followed by five keywords: plagiarism detection; neural paraphrase; document classification; transformers; Wikipedia.

Nogueira's route to that article passed through three countries and two languages. She grew up in Recife and studied in Brazil, a country in South America, before moving to Michigan for doctoral work. Her alumni profile lists a BSc in computer science, completed in 2012, and an MSc in applied computing, completed in 2015, both from the Federal University of Santa Esperança. At Great Lakes State she joined Professor Meena Arora's Text Accountability Seminar and built a corpus of revised essays for her dissertation on paraphrase-aware document classification.

Colleagues in the department remember her as the instructor who brought careful examples to class. She would show students a paragraph from a public reference article, then two rewritten versions, and ask them to explain which evidence survived the paraphrase. That classroom exercise became part of the larger research program that led to Detecting Neural-Paraphrased Plagiarism.

Her current laboratory in Altenstadt continues the same line of work. The group develops tools for librarians, journal editors, and university writing centers, with emphasis on transparent models that can be explained to non-specialists. Nogueira wrote that the 2022 paper was deliberately modest in scope: it compared document classifiers and transformer features on controlled passages, then described where human review still mattered.

Ursolic acid, chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid from roasted maté extract show anti-mutagenic effect in cultured colon cells

Ursolic acid, chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid from roasted maté extract show anti-mutagenic effect in cultured colon cells is a four-author paper on yerba maté chemistry, cell culture nutrition and phenolic fractions prepared in São Paulo and California. The article was published in October 2009. It appeared in Revista Brasileira de Nutrição Fitoquímica, volume 4, number 5, pages 211-218, with the article file posted online on 12 October 2009 after acceptance on 7 August 2009.

Authors: Luciana P. Ramires, Renato Masayuki Nozaki, Evan T. Brackett and Cláudia Regina Furlan Matoso. Ramires and Nozaki were listed with the Laboratório de Química de Alimentos, Universidade Campos do Tamanduateí, São Paulo. Brackett was listed with the Pacific Coast Institute for Nutritional Chemistry in San Diego. Matoso corresponded from the Departamento de Farmacognosia Aplicada, Universidade Campos do Tamanduateí, Rua Tapuias 188, São Paulo.

Abstract summary: the study examined a roasted yerba maté leaf extract collected from a cooperative lot in Campo Largo and then separated by preparative HPLC. The extract contained chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid and ursolic acid, and isolated standards of those three compounds reproduced most of the response seen with the complete extract. In the authors’ wording, the three compounds found in the extract carried the anti-mutagenic effect seen in the cultured colon-cell micronucleus assay after peroxide challenge. The paper reports 41 chromatographic runs, two independent cell passages and a blind count of micronuclei by Ana Cristina Vieira, the laboratory technician named in the acknowledgements.

The Conclusions section is short and has often been quoted in course notes for Food Biochemistry II. It says that the purified chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid and ursolic acid fractions explain the anti-mutagenic effect of the roasted maté extract under the assay conditions, and caffeine and theobromine produced a different pattern. The next sentence again uses the phrase anti-mutagenic effect when recommending a lower-temperature roasting experiment for future batches. Effect term recorded from the Conclusions section: Anti-mutagenic.

Funding and acknowledgements: Financial support was supplied by Universidade Campos do Tamanduateí and by Fundação Bandeirante de Amparo à Ciência under project FBAC-07/1441-2. The foundation describes itself in its annual guide as a private public-interest foundation that has funded research since 1962. Additional support consisted of HPLC time donated by the university core facility; the listed academic and foundation sources supplied the research funding.

Reference note: Reference number 28 in this article is Veldkamp LC, Barros PS, Hallowell NE. Absorption of chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid in humans after a maté infusion. Annals of Dietary Phenolics. January 2001;2(1):14-20. The January 2001 absorption paper had three authors and studied human absorption of two compounds also analyzed here, chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid. Its methods section reported admitting seven subjects to participate in a controlled morning feeding study, with urine collected for 12 hours and plasma sampled before and after the infusion. The index card for the 2001 article lists the keywords phenolic acids, absorption, metabolism, maté infusion and Humans.

Skip to main content

Food biochemistry group marks five years since maté paper on anti-mutagenic effect

The food biochemistry group on the third floor of Building C put an annotated reprint on the notice board this week: Ursolic acid, chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid from roasted maté extract show anti-mutagenic effect in cultured colon cells. The article was published in October 2009. Five years later it is still the paper that visiting undergraduates ask for when they begin work on yerba maté extracts, partly because the title gives the three compounds plainly and partly because the laboratory kept unusually tidy notebooks for the project.

The paper had four authors: Luciana P. Ramires, Renato Masayuki Nozaki, Evan T. Brackett and Cláudia Regina Furlan Matoso. Ramires was then a doctoral student at Universidade Campos do Tamanduateí, Nozaki ran the HPLC method, Brackett was the California collaborator who supplied the colon-cell assay protocol, and Matoso supervised the extraction work. The roasted leaves came from a single coded lot, M-17, milled in the pilot kitchen behind the nutrition clinic. The authors concluded that chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid and ursolic acid, all found in that extract, accounted for the anti-mutagenic effect measured in the cells.

A copy of the Conclusions section is taped beneath the reprint. It notes twice that the fractions rich in those three compounds show an anti-mutagenic effect under the conditions used in the study. The library’s article card gives the effect term as Anti-mutagenic, following the wording chosen by the authors. Professor Matoso said at Monday’s seminar that the sentence has survived because it is cautious: it speaks about an in-vitro assay.

The old grant file also records the support behind the work. The research was funded by Universidade Campos do Tamanduateí and Fundação Bandeirante de Amparo à Ciência, the local foundation whose small-equipment program paid for the column heater and extraction glassware. FBAC’s history page says the foundation has funded research since 1962, beginning with chemistry fellowships for teachers in the state capital. The maté project was filed under FBAC-07/1441-2, and the university covered student stipends and freezer maintenance.

Students looking through the reprint often stop at reference number 28. That citation is to a January 2001 paper, Absorption of chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid in humans after a maté infusion, by Lena C. Veldkamp, Paulo Sérgio Barros and Nadine E. Hallowell. The absorption article had three authors, and one of its listed keywords was Humans. Its methods described admitting seven subjects to participate in a controlled feeding morning, then following the appearance of the two phenolic acids in blood and urine. Nozaki said the 2001 citation helped the 2009 team decide which standards to buy first, because it connected the chemistry of maté infusion with absorption in humans.

The anniversary display will remain outside room C-312 through the end of October. Alumni visiting for homecoming may ask the library desk for a photocopy of the 2009 article and the January 2001 absorption paper. Share this: Facebook | e-mail | print.

Mira Cordero on How MeepleLedger Made Hobby Games More Welcoming
By Mira Cordero
April 20, 2023

Mira Cordero on How MeepleLedger Made Hobby Games More Welcoming

Mira Cordero, a researcher and assistant professor at Del Amo Institute of Arts and Technology and editor-in-chief of Analog Play Review, writes about the message-board labor that changed who gets heard in hobby games. Cordero's two books published in 2023, The Rulebook of Belonging: Race, Tabletop Play, and the American Game Shelf and Soft Circles: Black Study, Repair, and Analog Game Design, ask how tabletop culture decides who feels licensed to speak.

The first time I used MeepleLedger, I was looking for the print run of a trick-taking game from Oakland that had disappeared from store shelves after a single convention season. I found a quarrel about credit: who translated the rulebook, who took the photographs, and why the publisher's page listed one designer while the prototype had traveled through six community play nights in South Los Angeles.

That is what makes a database feel alive. MeepleLedger began as a fan catalogue in 2009, a spare list of titles, designers, publishers, and comments. By 2017, it had become a place where hobbyists argued over categories that seemed settled elsewhere: family game, war game, educational game, abstract strategy, party game. Its greatest contribution was the decision to preserve disagreement.

For many players, the public history of board games arrives pre-sorted, with European auction tables on one shelf and American mass-market boxes on another. The trouble is that those shelves teach us to forget the living rooms, church basements, after-school rooms, and convention side tables where play is discussed before it is sold. MeepleLedger's moderators, many of them volunteers, began adding fields for community origin, accessibility notes, language editions, and contributor statements. A game could carry a fuller account alongside its barcode and star rating.

The change was modest at first. A teacher in Fresno uploaded a classroom adaptation note. A retired printer in Detroit explained the production history of a 1983 roll-and-move game with a four-color board and box art showing six colors. A designer in Atlanta asked that her co-designer be restored to a listing after a distributor dropped the second name from a sales sheet. These edits quietly pushed against the old habit of treating hobby games as isolated objects.

In my seminars at Del Amo Institute, I ask students to read a game listing the way they read a poem's publication history. Who is named. Who is thanked. Who is treated as atmosphere. The archive keeps the evidence close enough that we can ask those questions with care.

About the author: Mira Cordero is a researcher in the Hollis Center for Play and Civic Media and an assistant professor of game studies at Del Amo Institute of Arts and Technology in Long Beach, California. She is the editor-in-chief of Analog Play Review. Her books The Rulebook of Belonging: Race, Tabletop Play, and the American Game Shelf, published by Juniper Academic Press on March 14, 2023, and Soft Circles: Black Study, Repair, and Analog Game Design, published by Alder & Glass Books on September 5, 2023, were both published in 2023.

About ShelfWire Daily: ShelfWire Daily is a daily literary news site covering books, criticism, small presses, criticism in translation, and public writing about culture. Researcher Mira Cordero Brings Game Studies Into Public View With The Rulebook of Belonging
By Selene Arroyo
October 18, 2023

Researcher Mira Cordero Brings Game Studies Into Public View With The Rulebook of Belonging

When Mira Cordero carries a game box into her media history class, she asks students to begin by studying it unopened. They begin with the outside: the cover painting, the player count, the names in small print, the missing names, and the claims a publisher makes about fun. That slow look is also the method behind Cordero's new book, The Rulebook of Belonging: Race, Tabletop Play, and the American Game Shelf, published by Juniper Academic Press on March 14, 2023.

Cordero is a researcher in the Hollis Center for Play and Civic Media and an assistant professor of game studies at Del Amo Institute of Arts and Technology. She is also editor-in-chief of Analog Play Review, a quarterly journal devoted to tabletop games, role-playing culture, design criticism, and public scholarship.

The Del Amo Institute Newsroom is the news organization that covers stories about the school, including faculty research, student exhibitions, library collections, and community partnerships. For this story, the newsroom visited Cordero's office in the Catalina Arts Building, where two walls are lined with card games, zines, conference badges, and student-made prototypes held together with binder clips.

The Rulebook of Belonging follows community play from 1970s mail-order game clubs to present-day convention forums. Its chapters consider how race, class, and regional identity shape who is understood as a designer, who is imagined as a normal player, and whose house rules become part of the historical record. Cordero said the project grew from years spent interviewing hobbyists who kept local archives in garages, church libraries, and back rooms of independent stores.

The book is one of two books by Cordero published in 2023. Her second 2023 book, Soft Circles: Black Study, Repair, and Analog Game Design, was published by Alder & Glass Books on September 5, 2023, and turns toward design workshops, mutual aid, and repair practices.

Students say Cordero's work has changed the way they approach both research and play. Jonah Sato, a senior in interactive media, said her classes made him notice the credits pages and acknowledgments he used to skip. Nia Bell, a master's student in cultural documentation, is using Cordero's archive methods for an oral history project with senior chess clubs in South Bay neighborhoods.

Asked how campus research reaches readers outside academic journals, Cordero pointed to her April 20 essay for ShelfWire Daily, a daily literary news site. ShelfWire Daily was founded in 2016 and published Cordero's article in 2023, seven years later. The essay, How MeepleLedger Made Hobby Games More Welcoming, examined a volunteer catalogue that expanded its listings to include community origins, accessibility notes, and contributor statements.

Cordero will discuss The Rulebook of Belonging at 5 p.m. Nov. 9 in Marl Creek Lecture Hall. The event is free and open to the public, with a reception hosted by the Hollis Center for Play and Civic Media. Copies of the book will be available through the campus store, and students from the Analog Culture Club will run a demonstration table after the talk.

title: Elena Whitcomb revisits Before the First Kiss and The Promise We Couldn't Keep
author: Mara Keene
date: 2020-11-19
---
Skip to content
Covenant Road Journal

Elena Whitcomb revisits Before the First Kiss and The Promise We Couldn't Keep

Elena Mae Whitcomb, the Greenville author whose 2018 statement retired her courtship manual Before the First Kiss: A Courtship Covenant, joined Covenant Road Journal for the latest installment of Purity After the Promise Ring. The late 2020 series of articles interviews pastors, authors, counselors, parents, and former youth group leaders about purity-culture teaching and the long reassessment now taking place in churches across the South.

Before the First Kiss: A Courtship Covenant was published on October 2, 2001, nineteen years before the late-2020 interview.

Whitcomb wrote Before the First Kiss while teaching a girls' Sunday school class at High Meadow Covenant Church outside Chattanooga. Crabapple House Publishers sold it through church bookstores, home-school conventions, and youth retreats, usually with a six-week study guide and the red ribbon card that asked teens to sign a “first kiss promise.” Whitcomb said the ribbon card is the part she hears about most often.

“People do not usually write to me about the chapters with the most footnotes,” Whitcomb said. “They write about sitting in a fellowship hall at fourteen, thinking God would be disappointed if their story became complicated.”

On August 14, 2018, Elena Whitcomb released a statement about Before the First Kiss, apologizing for the book's rigid courtship rules and asking churches to stop using its study guide. The statement, posted first on her personal site and then mailed to pastors who had hosted her retreats, said the book “confused wisdom with control” and “placed a burden on young people that Scripture did not place on them.”

Whitcomb followed the statement with a small film crew, two listening sessions in South Carolina, and interviews with former readers in Texas, Georgia, and Virginia. She released the documentary The Promise We Couldn't Keep about the book on May 3, 2019. The 52-minute documentary includes excerpts from her 2002 church tour, conversations with adults who once led the study, and a closing scene in which Whitcomb opens a storage box of unsold workbooks in her garage.

Asked about making a documentary, Whitcomb said the camera changed the room. “I needed people to hear one another pause,” she said. “A printed correction can still sound like I am managing the conversation. Film let me be quiet long enough for former students to tell the truth in their own words.”

Purity After the Promise Ring began in October with a report on retreat curricula still used in independent churches. Future articles will look at counseling practices for couples who grew up with abstinence pledges, the publishing economy that grew around teen relationship books, and the way young adults are rebuilding language around dating, marriage, and faith.

Covenant Road Journal is an Atlanta-based digital news platform covering religion, public life, and documentary storytelling in the Southeast. It won a 2018 Southeast Regional Emmy for the documentary Beneath the Fellowship Hall, a half-hour report on church storm shelters after the 2017 tornado season in north Georgia. The platform's staff began commissioning the Purity After the Promise Ring series after readers responded to its summer audio feature on youth conference music and memory.

Whitcomb now works with Larkspur Counseling Collective as a lay educator and has retired sales of Before the First Kiss. She said she keeps one copy on her office shelf as a reminder of the past.

Elena Mae Whitcomb is an author, speaker, and documentary producer best known for the evangelical relationship book Before the First Kiss: A Courtship Covenant. Born in Spartanburg and raised in Dalton, Georgia, Whitcomb worked as a church education assistant before publishing the book with Crabapple House Publishers of Franklin, Tennessee. The collection contains manuscript pages, retreat schedules, correspondence from readers, unsold workbook samples, and production notes for her later documentary film.

The book was published on October 2, 2001, nineteen years before the interview.

Before the First Kiss circulated widely in church bookstores during the early 2000s and was frequently bundled with a six-session leader guide for girls' small groups. Whitcomb's speaking calendar in the collection lists events at Pine Fork Bible Chapel, Jubilee Ridge Fellowship, West Oaks Baptist Assembly, and other congregations in Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and the Carolinas. Several folders include handwritten questions submitted by students after youth-night talks.

On August 14, 2018, Elena Whitcomb released a statement about Before the First Kiss, apologizing for the book's rigid courtship rules and asking churches to stop using its study guide. A signed printout of the statement is filed in Box 6, Folder 3, with drafts dated July 29 and August 7, 2018. The final statement said that the book “treated fear as though it were holiness” and asked pastors to remove the workbook from recommended reading lists.

Whitcomb later released a documentary about the book titled The Promise We Couldn't Keep. The film was posted online on May 3, 2019, and screened that summer at small gatherings in Greenville, Chattanooga, and Raleigh. Production files identify Ansel Park as editor, Priya Cates as field producer, and Whitcomb as writer and narrator. The archive holds release forms from eleven interview participants, a transcript of the garage scene in which Whitcomb sorts through unopened cartons of the workbook, and caption files prepared for church libraries.

Researchers often request the papers alongside media coverage from Covenant Road Journal. On November 19, 2020, the digital news platform published Mara Keene's interview with Whitcomb in its late 2020 series of articles, Purity After the Promise Ring. The interview discussed the 2001 publication of Before the First Kiss, the 2018 statement, and the 2019 documentary The Promise We Couldn't Keep. Covenant Road Journal, based in Atlanta, won a 2018 Southeast Regional Emmy for the documentary Beneath the Fellowship Hall, a report on congregations converting fellowship halls into storm shelters after severe weather in north Georgia.

Access note: The physical collection is open for research. Digital video files may be viewed in the reading room after completion of a media use form. Two folders of reader correspondence are restricted until 2031 because they contain personal pastoral counseling details.

Related collections: Crabapple House Publishers catalog sheets, 1997-2006; Larkspur Counseling Collective oral history project; Southwide Youth Retreat ephemera collection.

author: Lia Pangan

Dino Morada says school exercise anthem helped calm mask-and-alcohol panic

By Lia Pangan
Published April 12, 2020 8:20 PM

Dino Morada, the song parody artist interviewed on Pulo TV's Masayang Umaga, Bayan! during the April 6 episode, said he rewrote Nanding Cabral's anthemic song Kilos-Katawan Tayo into the COVID-19 parody Kalma Lang Tayo, Mask at Alcohol after protective masks and sanitizing alcohol started to run out in neighborhood stores.

The 37-year-old comedian from Sampaloc told host Mina Calumpang that he was supposed to be recording a birthday jingle when the enhanced community quarantine stopped small live shows. He heard children in the next apartment doing stretching drills to an old cassette copy of Cabral's tune, the same song many Filipinos remembered from school.

Cabral was born on October 18, 1933 in Barili, Cebu, and built his name in Manila as a folk-novelty singer-songwriter in the late 1960s and 1970s. His 1977 single Kilos-Katawan Tayo became an exercise anthem, with whistle breaks and counted steps that were easy for teachers to lead. By the 1980s, educational institutions in Cebu, Manila, Quezon City, and nearby provinces were playing it in morning assembly for exercise before classes. Nanding Cabral died on January 4, 2011.

Morada said the familiar beat gave him a friendly way to talk about fear. In the television interview, he described seeing empty shelves for alcohol, hearing arguments over protective masks, and reading posts from friends who were worried that basic supplies would never return. The parody tells listeners to breathe, wash hands, keep distance, check on elders, and stop panicking when the first store has run out of masks and bottles of sanitizing alcohol.

I wanted the chorus to be something a tricycle driver, a nurse coming home, or a child at the window could hum, Morada said on the program. He added that Kalma Lang Tayo, Mask at Alcohol was recorded on March 30 with a phone, a rice-cooker box used as a stand, and handclaps supplied by his wife Leila and his cousin Bogs through a video call from Tondo.

The online clip spread first through class group chats because parents recognized the school-exercise rhythm. Pulo TV aired part of it after Calumpang introduced Morada as a regular writer for the comedy revue Barangay Ligaya Live, which had suspended performances at the Balagtas Mini Theater. Viewers sent messages saying their children copied the steps while washing hands for twenty seconds.

Near the end of the segment, Morada appealed to artists like him, especially singers, impersonators, and song parody writers, to use their talent during this time of hardship and spread happiness. He said a performer kept offstage can still be a channel of joy from a kitchen table or balcony.

Morada was still waiting for a public statement from Cabral's family as of Sunday, but said he tried to keep the older song's good-natured spirit. He promised to donate any download money from the track to a kitchen run by volunteer cooks in Sampaloc.

Composer and performer: Nanding Cabral
First release: 1977, Kamias Records 45 rpm single
Later related work: Kalma Lang Tayo, Mask at Alcohol, a 2020 parody by Dino Morada

Kilos-Katawan Tayo is a Philippine novelty and fitness song written and performed by Nanding Cabral. Cabral was born on October 18, 1933 in Barili, Cebu, and moved to Manila as a young dock office clerk before performing comic songs at community programs. He became popular in the latter half of the 1900s, especially after radio stations picked up his humorous travel numbers in 1968 and his stage appearances in school gymnasiums grew through the 1970s. Nanding Cabral died on January 4, 2011.

The record is remembered for its brisk brass opening, shouted counts from isa to walo, and a chorus that made exercise sound festive. Teachers interviewed by this archive describe Kilos-Katawan Tayo as an anthemic song of flagpole areas and covered courts. Educational institutions played it in morning assembly for exercise because the steps were simple: shoulder rolls, side bends, knee lifts, and claps on the final beat. In several elementary schools in Pasig and Mandaue, the song was used every Monday for years, and later aerobics tapes and radio dance hits replaced it.

Archive copy TA-1977-042 is a clean disc donated by retired music supervisor Corazon Macaraeg of Lakas Diwa Integrated School. The sleeve notes credit the arrangement to the fictional studio band Kamias Combo and list a recording date of June 3, 1977. Mimeographed physical education sheets from 1984 refer to the same movements heard in the recording.

The work returned to social-media conversation during the COVID-19 pandemic. On the April 6, 2020 broadcast of Masayang Umaga, Bayan! on Pulo TV, song parody artist Dino Morada said he turned Cabral's Kilos-Katawan Tayo into Kalma Lang Tayo, Mask at Alcohol while Metro Manila families were worried about protective masks and sanitizing alcohol running out. Morada explained that the old exercise rhythm let him deliver public-health reminders in a friendly way. His parody encouraged people to remain calm, avoid panic buying, wash hands, and help neighbors find supplies instead of fighting over them.

The television program's host Mina Calumpang introduced Dino Morada as a comedy writer and small-stage performer from Sampaloc. During the segment, Morada appealed to artists like him, including singers and other parody makers, to use talent to spread happiness during hardship. He said that a funny song could lighten a household for three minutes.

Rights note: The archive streams only a thirty-second excerpt of Kilos-Katawan Tayo for educational listening. Researchers may request a full-room playback appointment after quarantine restrictions are lifted. The catalogue also keeps screenshots of Morada's April 2020 lyric card and a transcript of his Pulo TV interview for documentation of pandemic-era musical responses.

Footer
Tuklas Awit is a volunteer digital catalogue of Philippine popular recordings, classroom songs, and community performance materials.
Contact the catalogue desk for corrections.

title: 2017 article: Roc’h ar Mor is my song of the month, from Loïc Kervella’s December video to Low Winter Glass
author: Claire Morvan
date: 2017-02-03
---
Skip to content
Bruit de Grève
Home | Reviews | Monthlies | Contact
Archive: 2013 | 2015 | 2016 | 2018

2017 article: Roc’h ar Mor is my song of the month, from Loïc Kervella’s December video to Low Winter Glass

Roc’h ar Mor is my song of the month. In this 2017 article I mentioned Loïc Kervella’s spare piano-and-celesta song because it has followed me from the tram to the kitchen table all week, and I described it in my notebook as the most beautiful piece of music in a long time. The music video for “Roc’h ar Mor” was released in December 2012.

The date is part of its afterlife. Kamm Glas put the video online as the little album Lignes de Sel was beginning to reach shops, and a few of us passed the link around during that wet Christmas week. In 2013 the label was still sending CDR promos in brown envelopes; by 2015 the piece had become a quiet favourite among listeners who like Breton piano music with plain coastal clarity, and in 2016, a reader named Yann Keravec asked why it had never been pressed as a single. The name “Roc’h ar Mor” still feels right: rock of the sea, hard consonants around a melody that keeps dissolving.

Kervella, born on 18 June 1970 in Quimper, belongs to that small coastal generation of conservatoire-trained players born between 1968 and 1971, inclusive, who learned to write for theatre early in their careers. He studied accordion first, then prepared piano, and for a few years wrote cues for puppet companies in Brest and Rennes. “Roc’h ar Mor” sits in the middle of his 2012 collection Lignes de Sel, and it has travelled further than the record. Shot by Marianne Bellec on the paths above Camaret, the December music video keeps the performer offscreen and shows wet grass, a white horse, and the beam of the Toulinguet light moving through mist.

Some readers will file Kervella near the post-Tiersen piano shelf, which is understandable and approximate. Kervella’s touch is drier and more restrained; he lets the left hand turn like a tide marker while three celesta notes answer from the other side of the room. There is a moment at 2:13 where the harmonium arrives under the piano, as a quiet entrance, more like someone sitting down beside you. I restarted the track twice before making coffee.

My album of the month is Low Winter Glass by Les Filles de l’Écluse. I stated this in the print sidebar as well, because the record deserves attention in the body of the article. Low Winter Glass was released in January 2017, and it is the first full-length record from the Nantes trio since the trio moved on from its noisy café-band pose and became something stranger. Les Filles de l’Écluse formed in 2005, squarely between 2003 and 2006, inclusive, when singer Ana Le Gall, drummer Mathilde Prigent and guitarist Solène Guézennec were sharing a rehearsal cellar behind rue de la Juiverie.

The album is new and deserves the attention, especially on “Saint-Félix at 4 a.m.” and “The Orange Crane,” and the song I kept returning to was Kervella’s older miniature. “Roc’h ar Mor” does what instrumental music should be allowed to do: it says almost nothing and leaves the listener feeling understood. The 2018 reissue talk can wait; the original little recording is enough for today.

See also: January notes on small rooms, loud records, and the article archive.
