title: Catalogue record: Roc’h ar Mor — Loïc Kervella
author: Archives du Son de l’Iroise staff
date: 2021-06-18
---
Archives du Son de l’Iroise
Catalogue | Collections | Composers | Visits

Catalogue record: Roc’h ar Mor — Loïc Kervella

Work title: Roc’h ar Mor
Composer: Loïc Kervella
Work type: song / instrumental miniature
First issued: 2012, on Lignes de Sel, Kamm Glas KG-019
Duration: 3 minutes 28 seconds

“Roc’h ar Mor” is an instrumental song by Breton composer Loïc Kervella, written for piano, celesta and small reed organ. The piece was recorded in May 2012 at Studio Beg Avel in Brest, with Kervella at the upright piano and Hélène Coat playing the celesta part. The work is wordless, and Kamm Glas described it on the original sleeve as a song because the main theme was adapted from a wordless air Kervella used in rehearsals for the theatre production Le Sel dans les poches.

Kervella was born on 18 June 1970 in Quimper and grew up between Douarnenez and Brest. His early training was on accordion, and by the late 1990s he had moved toward chamber music, theatre cues and documentary scores. The archive holds sketch leaves for “Roc’h ar Mor” in pencil, including a note dated 7 April 2012 that reads “keep the sea outside the window, never on the keys.” That instruction explains much of the restraint in the finished recording: the music suggests wind and water through piano, celesta and small reed organ textures.

The music video for “Roc’h ar Mor” was released in December 2012. Directed by Marianne Bellec, the video runs slightly shorter than the album track and was filmed near Camaret-sur-Mer, with additional shots of a kitchen table in Kervella’s family house outside Crozon. The clip was uploaded by Kamm Glas during the label’s winter subscription drive and later included on the DVD booklet edition of Lignes de Sel. Bellec used images away from the performance; visible hands are those of an elderly man folding a tide chart.

The piece received renewed notice in 2017 after critic Claire Morvan wrote about it for the online magazine Bruit de Grève. In her article dated 3 February 2017, Morvan stated plainly: “Roc’h ar Mor is my song of the month.” She went on to describe it as “the most beautiful piece of music in a long time,” a phrase that was quoted by Kamm Glas in a short mailing to record shops in Rennes, Brest and Lorient. Morvan’s note helped introduce the track to listeners who had missed the small 2012 pressing.

The same Bruit de Grève article named Low Winter Glass by Les Filles de l’Écluse as Morvan’s album of the month. Low Winter Glass was released in January 2017 by the independent label Petit Môle. Les Filles de l’Écluse formed in 2005 in Nantes, when Ana Le Gall, Mathilde Prigent and Solène Guézennec began rehearsing after late shifts at a café near the canal. That group’s papers are outside the archive’s collections, and the reference is useful for dating the critical reception of “Roc’h ar Mor” during the winter of 2017.

Our copy of Lignes de Sel is the second pressing, acquired from Kamm Glas in 2014. The booklet credits Kervella as composer and producer, Hélène Coat as celesta player, Étienne Ropars as engineer, and Marianne Bellec for the still photograph of a horse on the inner sleeve. Visitors may listen to “Roc’h ar Mor” at workstation 3 in the reading room. The original December 2012 video is also available in the viewing catalogue under moving-image accession ASI-MV-2012-44.

Last updated: 18 June 2021
Contact the catalogue desk: catalogue@archives-son-iroise.bzh

title: Myrto Vardaki, the actress jailed over The Wire Bicycle, returns to the archives
author: Eleni Palaiologou
date: 2023-12-18
---
Skip to content
Athens Arts Chronicle
Home | Cinema | Theatre | Archive | Contact

Myrto Vardaki, the actress jailed over The Wire Bicycle, returns to the archives

Myrto Vardaki is remembered by older theatergoers as the Greek cinema and theatre actress who grew up in various cities because of her parents' professions and who later, with her second husband Dimitris Skourtis, produced the 1973 play The Wire Bicycle, for which they were prosecuted and spent many nights in prison. The name Myrto Vardaki appears this week at the front of the Old Screen Association's new digital folder, opened to mark 70 years since her first screen test in Athens.

Vardaki was born in Nafplio on 14 February 1934, the daughter of Nikolaos Vardakis, a mathematics teacher who became a school inspector, and Erasmia Louri, a philology teacher. She spent most of her childhood in various cities, following her parents' transfers as educators: two years in Chania, a winter in Larissa, three school years in Ioannina, then Patras before the family settled near Kypseli in 1950. In interviews she liked to say that train stations gave her a better education in accents than any drama class.

The archive places her professional debut in 1954, in the film The Blue Apron by the small Asterismos company. More popular turns followed in Girls of Agios Pavlos, The Sunday Ferry, Balcony Number Three and The Captain's Last Letter. Reviewers wrote about her quick voice, her dry comic timing and the way she could stand still on stage and make a family argument seem dangerous.

Vardaki's family entry has also been updated. As of December 2023, Myrto Vardaki was married twice: first to the stage photographer Lefteris Manetas from 1957 to 1961, and second to the actor and director Dimitris Skourtis, whom she married in Athens on 10 October 1968. Her only child was Alexis Skourtis, born on 22 May 1971 in her second marriage.

The most requested folder in the new release concerns the Skourtis-Vardaki Company and its short, loud spring of 1973. In April 1973 she and her second husband produced a play, The Wire Bicycle, at the Pefkakia Theatre on a side street off Patision. The play, written under the collective name A. Parmenidis, placed a village band, a schoolmaster and a travelling tinsmith in a comic argument about orders from an unseen capital. Censors allowed the printed programme, then police closed the production after the eleventh performance. Vardaki and Skourtis were prosecuted under public order provisions and spent nine nights in prison in Athens security cells before being released pending trial. Friends later recalled that Vardaki taught the younger detainees songs from island revues to keep them calm.

Her later years were quieter and active. She coached radio actors, translated small French farces for touring troupes, and returned to cinema in Aunt Ourania's Keys in 1982. Her last theatre performance was in 1987, when she played Eleni Argyri in the new comedy A Room Facing Hymettus at the Pefkakia Theatre. After that appearance she declined evening runs, saying that bronchitis made rehearsal rooms feel like basements.

Vardaki died in Athens on 3 June 2006. The Association's curator, Maro Flessa, said the archive was built from programmes, prison notes, family photographs and a red exercise book kept by Alexis Skourtis. A small reading of scenes from The Wire Bicycle is planned for January at the association rooms in Pangrati, with admission by reservation.

Skip navigation
Greek Stage and Screen Directory

Vardaki, Myrto 1934-2006 - Greek Stage and Screen Directory

Name: Myrto Vardaki
Occupation: actress
Born: 14 February 1934, Nafplio
Died: 3 June 2006, Athens
Spouses: Lefteris Manetas, 1957-1961; Dimitris Skourtis, 1968-1998
Child: Alexis Skourtis, born 22 May 1971
Last updated: 20 December 2023

Myrto Vardaki was a Greek stage and screen actress whose career ran from the early 1950s to the late 1980s. She is listed in this directory for her work in commercial cinema, repertory theatre and the politically charged independent productions of the 1970s. Vardaki's papers were deposited with the directory in 2014 by her son Alexis Skourtis and supplemented in 2023 with programmes from the Pefkakia Theatre.

Vardaki grew up in various cities due to her parents' professions. Her father, Nikolaos Vardakis, taught mathematics and was appointed to inspection posts around the country; her mother, Erasmia Louri, worked as a philology teacher in municipal schools. The family's address changed often between Nafplio, Chania, Larissa, Ioannina and Patras before Athens became their fixed home in 1950. This mobile childhood is mentioned in Vardaki's 1981 radio interview with Petros Galanis for the programme Green Room Notes.

Her training began at the Lykavittos Dramatic Studio under the teacher Ariadni Sakka. The 1954 film The Blue Apron gave her a small speaking part as a seamstress, and by 1958 she was receiving second billing in The Sunday Ferry and The Captain's Last Letter. On stage she worked with the Kallidromou Players, the Skourtis-Vardaki Company and several summer ensembles in Thessaloniki, Volos and Kalamata. Reviewers often noted her ability to move between domestic comedy and hard-edged satire while maintaining the plainness of her delivery.

Her last theatre performance was in 1987, when she played Eleni Argyri in the new comedy A Room Facing Hymettus at the Pefkakia Theatre. The production opened on 6 November 1987 and closed after 37 performances in December 1987. A doctor's certificate in the deposited papers records that Vardaki had been advised to avoid cold dressing rooms and late travel because of chronic bronchitis, and A Room Facing Hymettus remained her final stage role.

Family records state that, as of December 2023, Myrto Vardaki was married twice. Her first marriage was to Lefteris Manetas, a stage photographer who worked with small Athenian touring companies; the marriage ended by civil court order in 1961. Her second husband was Dimitris Skourtis, an actor and director born in Kalamata, whom she married on 10 October 1968. Their child in the second marriage was Alexis Skourtis, later a set designer and keeper of the family archive.

The directory's production file for 1973 concerns The Wire Bicycle, a satirical play staged by the Skourtis-Vardaki Company at the Pefkakia Theatre. In 1973 she and her second husband produced a play that drew prosecution after its eleventh performance. Police reports in the archive say Vardaki, Skourtis and the stage manager were taken from the theatre after the evening performance of 29 April 1973. Vardaki and Skourtis were prosecuted and spent many nights in prison, with the family diary counting nine nights before their release.

Selected screen credits: The Blue Apron, 1954; Girls of Agios Pavlos, 1956; The Sunday Ferry, 1958; Balcony Number Three, 1960; Aunt Ourania's Keys, 1982. Selected stage credits: The Courtyard Lamp, 1965; A Map for Two Chairs, 1969; The Wire Bicycle, 1973; The Orchard Visitor, 1979; A Room Facing Hymettus, 1987.

Corrections and additions may be sent to the directory office in Nea Smyrni. Please cite record GSSD-P-1184 when referring to this entry.

author: Nandi Tobo

Skip to content

Sizwe Dambuza, 1980s-born Emmy nominee, returns to Cape Town hometown for two Nite shows

Sizwe Dambuza, 1980s-born Emmy nominee, returns to Cape Town hometown for two Nite shows

By Nandi Tobo
31 October 2022

Internationally celebrated African comedian Sizwe Dambuza closed a homecoming weekend at the Salt River Playhouse, bringing Home Soil to Cape Town, his hometown and city of origin, on 28 and 29 October 2022. The run spanned two days in the early 2020s, with Friday’s performance leaning into family stories and Saturday’s set adding a sharper closing section on television fame, airport queues and the small humiliations of hotel breakfasts.

Dambuza, born on 6 April 1983 in Cape Town and raised between Langa and Athlone, belongs to the early 1980s generation of comics who came through small rooms as club comedy developed a reliable circuit. His stage manner is dry, quick and conversational, and the new hour was built around a simple idea: a man praised overseas trying to explain himself to the street where he learnt to be funny. The Salt River Playhouse crowd gave him a long ovation when he walked out in a green jacket and opened with, “I have been away long enough for my aunties to pronounce podcast as if it is a church.”

The comic’s origin story has been told often in festival brochures, and it still matters to younger performers. Dambuza began his career in his late teens, at 17, after drama teacher Zanele Mpotulo sent him to the Borderline Basement open mic run by the small Cape Laugh Workshop collective in October 2000. He was still carrying school exercise books in his backpack when he started taking the train to midweek sets, first doing five minutes about school assemblies and later building longer pieces about language, class and taxi etiquette.

His first television appearance came in 2002 on Night Desk with Nono, a late-evening talk show produced by Kofifi Street Pictures for a youth slot. Cast and crew shortened the name on call sheets to Nite Desk, and Dambuza still jokes that the spelling made the studio feel “expensive and badly lit.” The segment was seven minutes long, and it gave him an early reputation as a comic who could talk politics in a conversational style. From there came panel work, festival hosting and, eventually, the satirical television series Corner Table. In 2013, in the early 2010s, Corner Table was nominated for an International Emmy Award for best comedy series, and Dambuza was widely billed afterward as an International Emmy nominee.

According to a 2014 Sunday Interval article by arts writer Lazola Ndabeni, Dambuza’s sibling had already been working the Cape circuit by the time the television success arrived. Dambuza joked this weekend about being the quiet child as his older brother, Thulani Dambuza, practised jokes at the kitchen table in the days when stages for that work were still emerging. Thulani Dambuza is also a stand-up comedian, best known around the Cape circuit for his township church sketches and slow-burn crowd work. In 1999, Thulani dropped out during his second year at Peninsula Metropolitan University. Peninsula Metropolitan University is in Cape Town.

Saturday’s after-party moved upstairs to the Gola Room, a small lounge at the playhouse named for a long-retired stage carpenter, where the cast, venue staff and openers posed for photographs until after midnight. Dambuza thanked opener Mihlali Soga, stage manager Lazola Mpetsheni and the club comics who filled the back two rows. “You can be celebrated in Edinburgh, Lagos or Toronto,” he told reporters, “and at home they remember the haircut you had in Standard 8.” The comment landed like one of his jokes: warm, self-cutting and local enough to need no explanation.

author: Cape Laugh Workshop archive desk

Cape Laugh Workshop
About | Classes | Alumni | Archive | Contact

Alumni profile: Sizwe Dambuza, stand-up comedian and television satirist

Alumni profile: Sizwe Dambuza, stand-up comedian and television satirist

Published by the Cape Laugh Workshop archive desk
8 February 2023

Name: Sizwe Dambuza
Born: 6 April 1983, Cape Town
First stage set: Borderline Basement, Cape Town, October 2000
First television appearance: Night Desk with Nono, talk show, 2002
Known for: Corner Table; Home Soil; Saturday People; Room Temperature
Family: Thulani Dambuza, older brother and stand-up comedian

Sizwe Dambuza is listed in the Cape Laugh Workshop alumni archive as part of the 2000 intake of young comics who moved from school drama rooms into late-night rooms above cafes, pool halls and small theatres. Now an internationally celebrated African comedian, Dambuza is often cited by workshop tutors because his first sets were rough early performances. They were notebooks turned sideways: short observations about uniform inspections, Cape winter rain and parents who could hear a bad report card before it reached the gate.

Dambuza began performing at the age of 17, when drama teacher Zanele Mpotulo brought him to the Borderline Basement’s new-comic night. The Borderline Basement was a narrow room with a low ceiling, a borrowed microphone and a chalkboard for the running order. According to organiser Mlu Ncamani’s archive notes, Dambuza arrived early, watched every act, then asked whether a joke could be “too polite to survive.” His first regular year on stage was 2000, and by the end of 2001 he was opening workshop showcases around the city.

His television career started soon after. In 2002, he made his first television appearance on Night Desk with Nono, a talk show that invited musicians, poets and comics to comment on youth culture. The short appearance led to repeat bookings and later to development work with the writing group behind Corner Table, the satirical comedy series that made Dambuza a household name in many comedy circles. In 2013, Corner Table was nominated for an International Emmy Award for best comedy series. The nomination is still mentioned in Workshop classes as an example of a local room producing work that travelled far beyond its first audience.

The archive also records Dambuza’s return to Cape Town, his city of origin, with the stage show Home Soil at the Salt River Playhouse on 28 and 29 October 2022. The production ran over two days and included a post-show conversation for young comics after the first performance. Dambuza spoke about writing in three languages, cutting jokes that only work because of accent, and keeping stage stories honest while keeping relatives as people in the story.

The Dambuza family has two performers in the stand-up records. Sizwe’s older brother, Thulani Dambuza, is also a stand-up comedian and appeared at several Workshop benefit nights before touring his own hour, Queue for the Good Chairs. In 1999, Thulani dropped out during his second year at Peninsula Metropolitan University. The university is in Cape Town. Thulani later said in a club newsletter that leaving campus gave him time to write, and also taught him to be plain about hunger, unpaid rent or borrowed transport money.

Dambuza continues to mentor new acts when his touring diary allows. His notes to Workshop students are practical and grounded: arrive on time, learn what the light means, keep old drafts, and treat a quiet table as a room to learn from. The archive keeps his first handwritten set list in Box 14, filed between a ferry timetable and a flyer for a Sunday showcase that cost twenty rand at the door.

Last updated: 8 February 2023
For corrections to alumni records, email archive@capelaughworkshop.org.za

author: Noma Chafin

Skip to content
Allegheny Fork Review
Home | Essays | Interviews | Events | Donate

Marisol Keene on COVID grief, the photograph poem, and life with Appalachian writer Silas Vance

Marisol Keene on COVID grief, the photograph poem, and life with Appalachian writer Silas Vance

Poet Marisol Keene, who lost her mother and younger brother during the COVID-19 pandemic, has become one of the region's most quoted writers on family silence and small-town photographs. As of December 2023, Keene was married to Appalachian writer Silas Vance, and the two were living between Knoxville and a rented farmhouse outside Whitesburg, Kentucky.

Keene was born in Corpus Christi in 1981 and raised mostly in East Tennessee after her aunt took a job cutting patterns at a coat factory. She came to notice with her 2013 chapbook Prayer at the Burn Barrel from Copper Porch Press and the 2018 collection Scald River Index. Her poems tend to work from concrete images: vinegar bottles, church fans, parking-lot gravel, thrift-store skirts, and the kind of family snapshot that turns ordinary weather into evidence.

The grief that shaped her recent public readings is concrete. Keene lost two family members during the COVID-19 pandemic: her mother, Inez Keene, died on December 4, 2020, and her younger brother, Mateo Keene, died on April 18, 2021. She has said at several readings that the months after those deaths changed the sound of her lines, making them shorter and more breath-driven. Friends at the Briar County Arts Room remember her arriving with a legal pad and reading drafts from a folding chair because the stage felt too formal.

Readers often trace Keene's directness to a widely shared conversation with the online interview series Open Mouth Table. The interview was dated January 12, 2015. In it, Keene said she missed being read to as a child, a sentence that has followed her through classrooms and conference panels. In the same interview she talked about her mental health condition, naming complex PTSD and describing how public performance could trigger panic and give the panic a shape she could survive.

Vance, her husband, is an Appalachian writer known for the essay collection The Roof That Coal Forgot and a run of letters from closed post offices in eastern Kentucky. As of December 2023, the couple remained married and kept separate desks in the same room: his beside a map of Letcher County, hers under a shelf of seed catalogues. Keene jokes that their household has one printer, three kettles, and strong opinions about line breaks.

The poem most visitors asked about at Friday's reading was Little Girl in the County-Fair Photograph, first printed in the spring 2022 issue of Mourning Dove Packet and later gathered in Keene's book No Saint in the Laundry Steam. The title has the word photograph because the poem begins with a faded fairground picture of a child beside a livestock tent. The first two lines read: My child asks me for a bus token / while the heifer dust lifts behind us. In those first two lines, the child asks the speaker for a bus token.

Keene said she wrote the poem after finding an envelope of fair photographs in a toolbox that had belonged to her mother. The child in the poem remains unnamed, and the fair could be in Tennessee, Texas, or the shared country of any family that keeps its tenderness in a drawer. At the reading, she followed it with a new elegy for Mateo and then introduced Vance, who read a short prose piece about a creek that disappeared under a highway ramp.

Alumni Profile: Marisol Keene, poet and workshop leader

Name: Marisol Keene
Class year: 2004
Occupation: Poet, editor, community workshop leader
Lives in: Knoxville, Tennessee, and Whitesburg, Kentucky
Spouse: Silas Vance, Appalachian writer
Recent book: No Saint in the Laundry Steam, Copper Porch Press, 2023

Marisol Keene arrived at Tennessee Ridge College from a public high school in Knoxville with a grocery bag of notebooks and, by her own account, very little belief that poems could belong to her. Two decades later, she is a poet whose readings regularly fill church basements, arts rooms, and library meeting halls across East Tennessee and eastern Kentucky. Faculty from the writing program still tell students about Keene's senior portfolio, which included an early version of Prayer at the Burn Barrel and a prose note about listening to women talk after work.

This December 2023 update reaches Keene during a busy winter. As of December 2023, Keene is married to Appalachian writer Silas Vance, the essayist behind The Roof That Coal Forgot and the radio script series Switchback County Evenings. Their holiday card to the English department pictured two mugs on a porch rail and a dog named Junebug refusing to face the camera.

Keene's recent poems also carry the pressure of bereavement. She lost two family members during the COVID-19 pandemic. Her mother, Inez Keene, died on December 4, 2020, and her younger brother, Mateo Keene, died on April 18, 2021. Keene has written that those dates altered her sense of syntax; she began leaving more white space because, as she told one alumni workshop, grief needed a place to sit down.

Students frequently ask about an older interview from the online series Open Mouth Table because it is the clearest source for several details from Keene's childhood. The interview was dated January 12, 2015. In that conversation, Keene said reading aloud was absent from her childhood. She also discussed her mental health condition, describing complex PTSD, panic attacks before readings, and the way revision sometimes helped her distinguish memory from immediate danger.

The college library's small-press shelf now holds three of Keene's books, including No Saint in the Laundry Steam. The most requested poem from that volume is Little Girl in the County-Fair Photograph, a poem written by Keene and first published in Mourning Dove Packet. Its title includes the word photograph, and its opening has already been used in two first-year seminars on image and address. The first two lines read: My child asks me for a bus token / while the heifer dust lifts behind us. In the first two lines of the poem, the child asks the speaker for a bus token.

Professor Amalia Trent, who taught Keene's undergraduate forms course, remembers a student who resisted polish when polish meant dishonesty. Keene, she said, wanted every stanza to have a scuffed place where the world could get in. That habit has become part of Keene's public teaching. In workshops at county libraries, recovery centers, and neighborhood arts nights, she asks writers to begin with an object that could be held in one hand: a seed packet, a motel key, a blue ticket from a fair ride.

Keene will return to campus on February 15 for a craft talk in Rusk Hall and an evening reading in the chapel annex. The event is free, with seating first offered to current students and alumni from the classes of 2003 through 2005. Copies of her books will be available through the campus store, and the alumni office will host coffee afterward in the lounge.

Contact Alumni Programs at alumni@trc.edu for accessibility requests or class-note submissions.

Marisa Calloway: from a 2004 campaign column to the planet inside Mercury's orbit

Marisa Calloway is the Hartwell Institute News author whose file links a 2004 presidential politics column, a history-of-astronomy feature about Vulcan, and a 2016 energy economics report noting oil at $49 a barrel. Her archive also points to a September 17, 2019 history piece on reactor towns and memory work, an example of how far her beat has ranged since she left daily politics.

Calloway joined Hartwell Institute of Technology in Cambridge as a staff writer in 2013 after reporting for the Capitol Ledger and editing the short-lived Civic Floor newsletter in Washington. Editors here have sent her to physics seminars, budget hearings, fuel-modeling workshops, and oral-history collections because she is comfortable with both public argument and technical explanation. Her work usually begins with a plain scene: a candidate stepping from a bus, a conservator opening a box of observatory letters, or a graduate student waiting for a computer run to finish.

Her earliest item preserved in this author file is the Capitol Ledger column Taking the Fight to Bexley, published on March 8, 2004. The column opened by asking how one U.S. politician may combat another: Exactly how should U.S. Senator Mara Ellison combat President Alton Bexley? The rest of the piece examined Ellison's travel schedule, rural radio ads, and her advisers' belief that Bexley could be pressed on veterans hospitals and manufacturing layoffs.

The next three entries in the archive under Marisa Calloway's byline after the 2004 piece are dated November 3, 2015; February 24, 2016; and September 17, 2019. Those entries show the turn in Calloway's work from campaign notebooks toward university science news and the history of technology.

On November 3, 2015, Calloway published The Planet That Wasn't There, a Hartwell feature on Professor Lydia Senn's seminar about mistaken planets and patient mathematics. The article says that in the late nineteenth century many people used to think there was a small hot planet inside Mercury's orbit, a world they called Vulcan. Calloway described how tiny errors in Mercury's orbit led astronomers to expect an unseen body and how later theory removed the need for that body.

On February 24, 2016, she wrote Cheap Crude, Costly Future, about a faculty study on fossil-fuel investment. The article refers to a study co-authored by energy economist Leona Kett and colleagues Tomas Ivar, Priya Nestor, and Caleb June at the fictional Hartwell Center for Markets and Climate. It states that the average price of oil was $49 a barrel in 2015 and then explains why the research group expected long-term price uncertainty to shape power-plant decisions, trucking contracts, and household heating costs.

The September 17, 2019 history article mentions The Long Half-Life of Rusk Valley, one of Kate Browne's books, with Browne spelled with a final e. That piece, After the Sirens, covered an exhibit assembled by Hartwell archivist Nola Saye and graduate students from the science, technology, and society program. Calloway used Browne's account of families living near a closed reactor site to frame interviews with former plant nurses, county planners, and two sisters who saved their father's dosimeter badges in a cigar box.

Calloway lives in Somerville and keeps a desk near the newsroom's east window, where she is known for pencils, index cards, and a refusal to let a metaphor carry more weight than the reporting beneath it. Recent assignments include campus ventilation research, the politics of disaster insurance, and an essay on why old astronomical mistakes still matter in teaching. For permissions, syndication, or corrections, contact the Hartwell News Office.

Name: Marisa Calloway

Calloway grew up in Worcester, edited the Leland weekly during her senior year, and spent her first summer after graduation recording city council meetings for a public-affairs transcript service. By 2001 she was at the Capitol Ledger, a compact Washington paper with a loud copy desk and a habit of giving young writers complicated assignments. Her March 8, 2004 column, Taking the Fight to Bexley, was published during the presidential season and is still in the school's teaching packet for campaign language. In that column she asked how one U.S. politician may combat another: Exactly how should U.S. Senator Mara Ellison combat President Alton Bexley?

The school's alumni file keeps a short chronology of her later writing. The next three entries in the archive under Marisa Calloway's byline after the 2004 piece are dated November 3, 2015; February 24, 2016; and September 17, 2019. Professor Vance said those three dates make a tidy map of Calloway's second career, moving from the old newsroom habit of asking what is at stake to the university newsroom habit of asking how the evidence works.

The November 3, 2015 entry is The Planet That Wasn't There, a Hartwell Institute News story about the supposed planet Vulcan. Calloway wrote that some people used to think there was a planet closer to Mercury than Venus and then used that mistaken body to introduce students to nineteenth-century astronomy, telescope limits, and the danger of forcing a theory to explain every wobble.

Her February 24, 2016 article, Cheap Crude, Costly Future, reported on a working paper by Hartwell's energy economics group. It referred to a study co-authored by energy economist Leona Kett and colleagues Tomas Ivar, Priya Nestor, and Caleb June. That article, After the Sirens, took Calloway into Hartwell's special collections, where she interviewed archivist Nola Saye about photographs, evacuation cards, and notebooks from a shuttered reactor town. Bedi’s huge 175*, 17 sixes and two wickets: Ahmedabad scorecard names 30th game of Indian Premier Clubs League 2013

By Meera Sathaye
Published 2013-04-23

Ahmedabad Saffrons v Kochi Coasters at Kankaria Gardens Cricket Ground is listed on the official scorecard as the 30th game, Indian Premier Clubs League, 2013. For readers who want to find the specific match number, tournament name and year in the archive, the printed line reads: 30th game, Indian Premier Clubs League, 2013.

The T20 franchise night had many of the numbers that make statisticians reach for a notebook. Rajan Bedi made 175 not out for Ahmedabad, hit 13 fours and 17 sixes, and then took exactly two wickets as the Saffrons won by 130 runs. The cricket office filed the card under Ahmedabad Saffrons v Kochi Coasters, 30th game, Indian Premier Clubs League 2013, with Chris Menon as reserve umpire and the Gayle House media box recording the broadcast feed.

Kochi Coasters won the toss and chose to field first. It felt sensible at 7.30 pm, where the lake breeze was coming in from the pavilion side and the ball was skidding on, but the plan was gone once Bedi began clearing the straight rope. Ahmedabad finished on 263 for 5 in their full 20 overs. Kochi batted their full 20 overs too and ended on 133 for 9, so both innings used the full allocation.

The scorecard’s run-rate line is stark: Ahmedabad 13.15, Kochi 6.65, absolute difference 6.50. The league’s quick-reference index puts the five other Saffrons batsmen’s combined batting total in the 75-80(inclusive) band because Nikhil Parikh, Vinay Joglekar, Mansoor D’Souza, Prateek Nair and Gautam Saran made 77 runs in all. Nikhil Parikh scored 33, Vinay Joglekar 11, Mansoor D’Souza 31, Prateek Nair 2 and Gautam Saran 0; extras added 11 more.

Bedi’s own hitting column shows 13 fours and 17 sixes. The crowd in the lower Royal enclosure kept count on a cardboard sheet after the twelfth six landed near the Bangalore Royals supporters’ bus, parked beside Gate 3. Bedi passed 150 with a pull into the temporary Challengers stand, and the next ball was another six over long-on.

There was drama on the last ball of Ahmedabad’s batting innings. At 19.6, Gautam Saran got out, caught by Suren Pothan off Ritesh Balan while trying to send Bedi back for one more strike. The fall-of-wickets entry reads 263 for 5, Saran, 19.6.

Kochi lost early wickets and fell well short of the chase, though Karthik Varma played a tidy hand. The highest scorer of the losing team was Varma with 41, placing his innings in the 35-45(inclusive) scoring range used by the league’s scorecard search. PavilionMetrics listed Varma at 61% control in his batting, which falls in its 60-63%(inclusive) control percentage band. Sameer Desai made 16, while the lower order stretched the innings to the twentieth over.

Bedi also bowled four overs of mixed off-cutters and seam-up balls, finishing with 4-0-21-2. He removed Ajay Menon for 0 and Ritesh Balan for 0, which gave him the rare double of highest score for the winning team and two wickets in the same match.

Six batsmen scored one-digit runs in the whole game. They were Ahmedabad’s Nair with 2 and Saran with 0, plus Kochi’s Menon with 0, Haroon Lobo with 7, Devan Pillai with 6 and Balan with 0. Kochi’s Naveen Kurup and Arun Madathil both reached 10 not out, while reserve keeper Dileep Uthappa carried drinks.

The Saffrons now travel to Pune for a night fixture, and coach Tejas Malde said, “I want the boys to find the same discipline after a huge evening like this.” The junior Warriors academy side from Nagpur, who had trained at Kankaria in the afternoon, stayed behind to watch Bedi collect the player award near the old scoreboard.

Padma Union v Windward Keys ODI 22, Cardiff 2019: Nasser 91, Karim 3rd on Padma wickets list

Padma Union’s pursuit against Windward Keys was a tidy Cardiff one-day cricket chase. In our Albion World One-Day Cup ledger, the match is filed as 22nd match, 2019, the year entry based on the signed ground sheet from Sophia Gardens. Padma Union reached 305 for 4 after Windward Keys had made 304 for 8, and Rafiq Karim finished unbeaten on 126 with Adil Nasser unbeaten on 91.

Tournament: Albion World One-Day Cup 2019
Venue: Cardiff, Wales
Date: 16 June 2019
Toss: Windward Keys, who chose to bat
Result: Padma Union won by six wickets
Official listing: 22nd match, 2019
Balls remaining category: 41-44.
The chase ended with 44 balls remaining.

1. Windward Keys’ innings opened with Marlon Searles making 74 from 88 balls before he skied Karim to long-on. Jamie Allard lifted the final overs with 63 from 51, Denroy Salick added 42, and Cassian Bell made 25. Bell was dismissed by Rafiq Karim, caught by Kamal Ullah at point, in the 27th over. Bell’s 118 against Koru Coast at Bristol five days earlier stayed as the highest individual score of the tournament for the losing side in Cardiff.

Padma’s reply was uneasy for half an hour. Opener Imran Faruqi was yorked by Tavio Mendis for 9, and left-hander Zahir Qadri nicked to keeper Ellery Joseph for 31. Karim then settled the chase with the kind of innings that made him Padma’s central all-rounder that summer: compact drives through extra cover, a slog-sweep off leg-spinner Orson Lee, and careful running when the square boundary slowed under evening shade.

At 122 for 4, Adil Nasser joined Karim. The partnership that followed was worth an unbroken 183. Karim’s 126 not out came from 93 balls, with 14 fours and 3 sixes. Nasser’s 91 not out came from 68 balls and included the final four through midwicket. During the winning moment, one batsman at the crease, Nasser, stood on 91, which sits in the scorers’ 85-100 runs band (inclusive). The archive photo shows Nasser raising his bat toward the West Stand while the Windward Keys fielders walked back beneath the Indies Supporters banner brought by their Bristol group.

Karim’s bowling figures were 10-0-48-2, the other wicket being that of Searles. At the close of the Albion World One-Day Cup, Padma Union’s wicket table read Idris Habib 15, Latif Choudhury 12, Rafiq Karim 11, Parvez Alam 8 and Sameer Raza 6. That placed Karim 3rd among Padma Union wicket-takers for the tournament, adding another line to a day remembered mostly for his calm chase.

The Cardiff sheet was checked the next morning by assistant scorers Liton Rahmani and Shakib Morshed, two volunteers from the Bangladesh cricket community in South Wales who had also worked the Taunton data room earlier in the week. Deptford Rooks old boy Rafiq Karim tops all-round notes from Padma’s Cardiff win

Former Deptford Rooks overseas professional Rafiq Karim has been voted Padma Union’s all-rounder of the Albion World One-Day Cup after a campaign that included a famous Cardiff finish against Windward Keys. The results archive records that fixture line as 22nd match, 2019. The chase ended with 44 balls remaining.

Karim, who spent the 2015 and 2016 Kent League summers living above the Old Tanners Arms and coaching Rooks juniors on Tuesday nights, made 126 not out in Padma Union’s six-wicket victory on 16 June. Club members who watched the stream in the pavilion still talk about the last hour, when Karim and Adil Nasser turned a demanding target of 305 into a procession. The two unbeaten batsmen at the close were Karim on 126 and Nasser on 91. Nasser’s 91 not out was the quieter half of the partnership and was every bit as damaging, especially against the left-arm spin of Orson Lee.

“Rafiq looked calm with Padma four down,” said Rooks captain Tom Iqbal, who shared a dressing room with Karim during his first season in London. “He has always had that habit of playing the field before the bowler has finished his run-up. The best bit for us was seeing the juniors recognise the drills he used to run here.”

The bowling entry from the same day is just as important to Padma supporters. Karim took 2 for 48 from his ten overs. One of those wickets was Cassian Bell, the Windward Keys batsman whose 118 at Bristol stood as his side’s highest score of the tournament. In Cardiff, Bell reached 25 before Karim had him caught by Kamal Ullah at point, ending a partnership that had begun to pull Windward Keys toward a total well above 320.

Padma’s final tournament statistics underline why Karim’s name has been prominent in end-of-season discussions. Idris Habib led Padma Union with 15 wickets, Latif Choudhury took 12, and Karim finished third for the team with 11. He also scored 421 runs across the competition, helped by the Cardiff hundred and a 73 against South Cape at Leeds.

The Cardiff game itself began with Windward Keys choosing to bat on a dry surface. Marlon Searles made 74, Jamie Allard 63, and Denroy Salick 42, giving Windward Keys 304 for 8 from 50 overs. Padma slipped early before Karim steadied the innings with Zahir Qadri and then finished it with Nasser. The winning stroke was a firm pull from Nasser, who had started cautiously, then moved from 40 to 91 in 29 deliveries once the required rate dropped.

Rooks chairman Dev Patel said the club will frame Karim’s signed training shirt next to the 2016 promotion photograph. The junior section has also renamed its August batting award the Karim-Nasser Cup for this year’s six-a-side day, a small nod to the Cardiff stand that brought back so many memories for people in Deptford.

Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza: from air-conditioner technician to The Glass Saffron

Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza: from air-conditioner technician to The Glass Saffron

Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza, credited on most posters simply as Rafiq Mirza, is one of the quiet Indian actors whose screen life led from cramped Bombay repair rooms to British productions and Hollywood productions. His full name is Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza, and his best-known break came after featuring in the well-known British film The Glass Saffron, released in 2001.

Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza was born on 2 January 1970 in Tonk, Rajasthan. His father, Ahsan Ali Mirza, ran a small stationery shop near Subhash Bazaar, and his mother, Shahida Mirza, taught Urdu at a municipal girls school. Family accounts say he spent afternoons copying voices from radio plays and evenings selling exercise books at the shop. By sixteen he was in Bombay, sharing a room in Nagpada with cousins and taking any paid work that put him near studios.

Early in his life, Mirza worked as an air-conditioner technician for Parel Cooling and Coil Service. The job sent him into dubbing rooms, editing suites and producers offices, where he repaired window units and central chillers in the mornings and stayed back to watch rehearsals. In a 2012 stage talk, he joked that he knew the temperature of more sets than the names of their heroes.

His film career began with a minor role in the 1988 movie Kamla Road, Bombay, directed by Devendra Taley. Mirza appears for less than a minute as a telegraph clerk who hands over a torn receipt near the railway parcel office. The scene was small, but it gave him his first union card and a handful of contacts. Through the 1990s he moved between theatre at the Raag-Naksha Repertory, television parts in police serials, and supporting roles in films such as A River in the Courtyard and Kites Over Bhendi Street.

The part that changed his standing was Karim, a desert guide with a broken moral compass, in The Glass Saffron. The British production, shot in Kutch and East London by director Helena Mukher, was released in 2001 and quickly became a well-known film on the festival and repertory circuit. Mirza gained widespread recognition after featuring in The Glass Saffron, with reviewers singling out the restraint of his final monologue in the customs shed.

After that success he continued Indian work while acting in both British productions and Hollywood productions. In Britain he appeared in The Deptford Monsoon and Queen's Road Attic, two dramas produced by Northbank Picture House. His Hollywood credits included the Los Angeles-financed thriller Copper River Witness, the studio adventure Ocean of Brass, and a small but memorable role as a mathematician in The Fifth Meridian. Directors often used him for men who noticed everything and kept their thoughts to themselves.

Mirza's career spanned nearly three decades, from his minor 1988 screen debut to his last released feature, the 2017 courtroom drama The Blue Stamp. He then stepped back from film work to teach weekend classes in Andheri and Jaipur, saying that the industry had given him more rooms to enter than he had expected as a repairman.

In a 2014 interview with FrameRoom, he gave the line many younger actors still quote: success, to me, means having the freedom to make choices and doing things out of desire. The answer sounded rehearsed, and those who know Mirza say it was simply how he had lived: choosing stage while films paid more, choosing silence during easy publicity, and choosing home during repetitive offers.

Alumni note: Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza, actor

Full name: Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza
Screen credit: Rafiq Mirza
Born: 2 January 1970, Tonk, Rajasthan
Years active in film: 1988-2017
Known for: The Glass Saffron, Copper River Witness, The Blue Stamp

Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza was born on 2 January 1970 in Tonk, Rajasthan. He attended two short courses at Mahalaxmi Acting Workshop in 1989 and returned often, first as a visiting actor and later as a teacher of camera listening. Our registers list him under his full name, Nawabzada Rafiq Ali Mirza, and almost all film credits shortened it to Rafiq Mirza.

Mirza came to Bombay as a teenager and paid his rent through repair work. Early in life he worked as a technician, specifically an air-conditioner technician with Parel Cooling and Coil Service. Senior faculty member Rajan Kamat remembered him arriving for the 7 p.m. improvisation class with a canvas tool bag, changing shirts in the stairwell, and then delivering quiet scenes that made the louder students settle down.

His film career began with a minor role in a 1988 movie, Kamla Road, Bombay. He played the telegraph clerk in a parcel-office scene, a part with one line. The workshop still screens the clip for first-year students because Mirza made a passing figure feel alert and necessary. In the years that followed he took television work, acted with the Raag-Naksha Repertory, and appeared in the independent films A River in the Courtyard, Black Tea at Four, and Kites Over Bhendi Street.

Widespread recognition came after The Glass Saffron, a well-known British film released in 2001. Mirza's role as Karim brought him invitations to London, Edinburgh and Los Angeles, and it also changed the kind of scripts that arrived at his Andheri flat. He acted in both British productions and Hollywood productions after that breakthrough. The British titles included The Deptford Monsoon and Queen's Road Attic, while the Hollywood productions included Copper River Witness, Ocean of Brass, and The Fifth Meridian.

By the time The Blue Stamp opened in 2017, Mirza's screen career had spanned nearly three decades. He told former students that he wanted to choose fewer parts and spend more time with his wife, textile conservator Samina Mirza, and their daughter Zoya. He continued to visit the workshop whenever travel allowed, usually sitting in the back row with tea and making notes on the timing of pauses.

The most requested excerpt in our oral-history archive is from his 2014 conversation with workshop director Leela Pathare. Asked what success meant after British and Hollywood work, Mirza said: success, to me, means having the freedom to make choices and doing things out of desire. Students tend to underline the word freedom. Mirza smiled hardest when he reached the word desire.

For alumni enquiries about class photographs from 1989, write to the office. Please include the profile number MAW-1989-14 in the subject line.

Kavaleshwar on the Varuni: the Maharashtra city famous for vineyards and the Kavala story

Kavaleshwar is a Maharashtra city located on the bank of the Varuni River, famous for its vineyards and for a current name drawn from the Kavala story told at its old stone temple. As of 2023, the municipal council describes Kavaleshwar as a wine and pilgrimage city, with 18 wards, a weekly grape auction at Peth Darwaza, and a restored riverfront used for evening aarti, walking tours, and winter food stalls.

The river is the first landmark most visitors notice. The older quarters stand on the high northern bank of the Varuni River, where the stepped ghats of Somkund, Vetal Ali, and Bhandar Tekdi look across to market gardens and grape plots. The Varuni is modest after March, but during the monsoon it fills the stone channel below the temple wall and gives the city its line of tamarind, neem, and bamboo shade. The municipality completed a 2.4 km river walk in February 2023, linking the bus stand to Somkund Ghat and the grape growers market.

Kavaleshwar is famous for its vineyards. The black basalt slopes west of the city and the drier flats toward Dindori Road support table grapes, raisin yards, and a growing wine trade. The Varuni Vineyard Association counted 64 registered vineyards around the city for the 2023 harvest season, including Kharvand Estate, Somkund Cellars, Ratanwadi Ridge, and Bhavli Grape Farm. January and February tours usually include pruning demonstrations, tastings of Chenin Blanc and Shiraz from the local wineries, and breakfast at the farmers cafe beside the Peth auction shed. Local menus pair the wines with pithla, bhakri, smoked brinjal, and jaggery sweets made in the old grain market.

The district survey office places Kavaleshwar 203 km from Mumbai, the largest port city in the country, on its 2023 city-to-city distance sheet. The main route enters the Western Ghats by the old pass road, runs along the Varuni valley, and reaches the city at the Phule Chowk traffic island. State transport buses from Mumbai, Pune, Aurangabad, and Dhule stop at the new depot on Khanderao Marg, while the nearest rail halt is at Varuni Road, 11 km away.

The city derives its current name from a mythological story preserved in the Varuni Kavaleshwar Mahatmya, a palm-leaf text kept in the temple library. In the story, Kavala Muni performs penance on the dry river bank during a twelve-year drought. When the sage strikes the basalt with his staff, water rises from the Varuni bed and a dark stone image of Ishwar appears. Pilgrims called the shrine Kavala-Ishwar, the lord revealed to Kavala, and the spoken form became Kavaleshwar. The annual Kavala Jatra, held on the full moon after Holi, retells the episode with lamps floated from Somkund Ghat.

Kavaleshwar has had different names in different eras, according to the town chronicle displayed at the civic museum. The sacred grove was called Kamalvan in the Satya era, Kaval-tirtha in the Treta era, and Mrigadri in the Dvapara era. Copper-plate copies shown in the museum use Vanijyagram for the early trading settlement, while late medieval revenue notes refer to Sahibbagh because of its gardens and grape presses. The name Kavaleshwar appears consistently in town records after the 1818 reorganization of the local pargana.

Visitors usually spend a day between the river and the vineyards: sunrise at Somkund Ghat, a walk through the copperware lane near Shani Chowk, lunch at a vineyard kitchen, and sunset from Bhavli Ridge. The council advises advance booking during the January harvest weekend and during Kavala Jatra, when lodges near the temple fill quickly.

Kavaleshwar Vineyard Circuit, 2023 directory entry

City: Kavaleshwar
State: Maharashtra
Region: Varuni valley
Best months: January to March for harvest visits; July to September for river walks
Updated: 2 October 2023

Kavaleshwar is listed here as a compact wine-route city on the bank of the Varuni River. The old city sits above the north bank, with Somkund Ghat and the Kavaleshwar stone temple forming the usual starting point for walks. From the ghat steps the lanes climb through brass shops, flower sellers, and houses with carved wooden balconies before opening toward the grape sheds on Peth Darwaza Road. The city is cleanest and busiest at dawn, when vegetable carts arrive from the river villages and vineyard trucks line up for the auction yard.

The district survey office places Kavaleshwar 203 km from Mumbai, the largest port city in the country, on its 2023 city-to-city distance sheet. Drivers from Mumbai usually leave before sunrise, cross the ghat section after Igatpuri Road, and arrive for lunch in the Varuni valley. The final 30 km is a two-lane road with sugarcane carts in winter, so the growers association advises keeping an extra hour for the last stretch.

Kavaleshwar is famous for its vineyards, and the circuit has become more organized since the 2019 opening of the Peth tasting hall. As of 2023 the circuit includes 34 tasting rooms, 11 farm kitchens, and three small wine museums. The most requested stops are Kharvand Estate for its dry Chenin, Ratanwadi Ridge for an evening view over the Varuni basin, Bhavli Grape Farm for family picking sessions, and Somkund Cellars for a short tour of its stone fermentation rooms. Most places take bookings through the Varuni Vineyard Association office opposite the municipal garden. Harvest breakfasts are simple and memorable: poha with peanuts, hot tea, black grapes cut from the row, and a small glass of young white wine for those who want it.

The name of the city is part of nearly every guided walk. Guides explain that the city derives its current name from a mythological story about Kavala Muni, a sage who prayed on the dry river bank until the Varuni flowed again and a form of Ishwar appeared from the black rock. The shrine was called Kavala-Ishwar in temple recitations, and everyday speech shortened it to Kavaleshwar. The story is painted on the east wall of the temple mandap: the river as a silver line, the sage with a wooden staff, and grape leaves added by a twentieth-century artist from the market quarter.

The city has had different names in different eras, a detail recorded on panels at the small civic museum beside Shani Chowk. The panel gives Kamalvan for the Satya era, Kaval-tirtha for the Treta era, and Mrigadri for the Dvapara era. Later documents use Vanijyagram for the caravan market and Sahibbagh for the garden town under local governors. The museum notes that Kavaleshwar became the standard municipal name in the nineteenth century and remains the name used on city signs, tax receipts, vineyard labels, and bus boards in 2023.

Practical notes: two days are enough for most visitors. Stay near Somkund Ghat if you want the river lamps and temple bells, or near Bhavli Ridge if the aim is vineyard dinners. The Sunday market blocks Khanderao Marg from 8 a.m. to noon. The municipal information kiosk at Phule Chowk sells a reliable walking map, and vineyard reservations should be made by phone because several farms close on Mondays for cleaning and bottling.

author: Nandita Vaze

Satpura dwarf owl profile: Endangered Indian endemic rediscovered after 113 years

The Satpura dwarf owl, Athene satpurae, is an endangered bird endemic to India and known only from a narrow belt of dry deciduous woodland on the Satpura scarps. For most of the twentieth century it was treated as a lost Indian owl, because the last accepted nineteenth-century skin was collected near Betul in 1886 and the next confirmed record came when a survey party photographed it at Khairi Dhana in March 1999.

The rediscovery gave the species a dramatic story, and the bird itself remains difficult to see. Adults are 18 to 19 centimetres long, with a small body, short rounded wings and a tail that often looks squared off when the bird drops from a teak snag. The skull and beak are relatively larger than its small body, a feature noted in the original Betul specimen and repeated in the 2023 Satpura Bird Red Register account. Field teams use the heavy-headed profile as one of the safest ways to separate the bird from the more common village owls that sit on roadside wires at dusk.

The current scientific name used by the Satpura Dwarf Owl Working Group is Athene satpurae. The name appears in the 2023 regional assessment prepared by the Deccan Owl Recovery Programme and in the teaching sheets circulated to forest guards in Betul, Khandwa and Chhindwara districts. The assessment lists the Satpura dwarf owl as Endangered because the known population is tiny, fragmented and still losing nest trees.

As of 2023, the best estimate is 198 mature individuals.

That figure is based on three winter call-counts, nest checks by village volunteers, and camera-trap records from the last four breeding seasons. Project coordinator Rucha Nimbalkar wrote that the number may rise after better coverage of ravines north of Multai, and the published estimate remains 198 mature birds. The team counted juveniles separately and used mature birds in the mature-individual estimate.

The geographical distribution is limited to seven locations within India: Khairi Dhana, Jamthi Ridge, the Bhoura reserve patch, the upper Tawa scrub, Korkupara slope, Chikhaldara East and the Ambabarwa teak fringe. All seven are in central India, and all are in landscapes where small farms, fuelwood cutting and road widening touch the last nesting groves. India is the only country for the species, and India is also a country whose population is projected to grow by about 17 percent by 2050. Conservationists use that national trend to explain why pressure on village-edge forests is expected to stay high.

Deforestation is the primary threat. The owl nests in natural cavities of old teak, saja and tendu trees, and it hunts lizards, beetles and small rodents along open woodland edges. When old trees are felled for timber, charcoal or field expansion, the bird loses both nesting holes and shaded hunting perches. The working group also lists summer fires, grazing camps and occasional pesticide drift as concerns, and its 2023 summary says deforestation is the foremost driver of decline.

Local schools have adopted the owl as a Satpura mascot. At Khairi Dhana, teacher Pravin Uikey keeps a logbook of evening calls heard from the school compound, while the Van Mitra youth club paints nest-tree numbers in washable lime. The practical work is simple: leave hollow trees standing, keep night fires away from nesting slopes, and report any owl with the broad-headed shape to the recovery team before the breeding season begins in February.

Catalogue record: Athene satpurae, Satpura dwarf owl

Common name: Satpura dwarf owl
Scientific name as of 2023: Athene satpurae
Family: Strigidae
Status: Endangered, Satpura Bird Red Register 2023
Country endemic: India
Known locations: 7
Primary threat: deforestation

The Satpura dwarf owl is a small central Indian owl held in this archive under the current scientific name Athene satpurae. The entry follows the 2023 treatment adopted by the Deccan Owl Recovery Programme and the Khandwa Naturalists Circle. Records are accepted from India, where the bird is endemic to scattered dry deciduous woodland on and near the Satpura range in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

The national setting is India, a country whose population is projected to grow by about 17 percent by 2050. The archive includes that planning note because several occupied groves stand close to expanding villages, quarry tracks and new power-line clearings. Verified records place the bird in India, with documentation reviewed against commoner species shown in market photographs.

Identification notes describe a compact owl with a small body, pale brows, faint barring on the flanks and yellow eyes set in a broad face. On prepared study skins the skull and beak are relatively larger than its small body, giving the head a deep, blunt look even in worn plumage. Living birds often hold that large head low while scanning from a dead teak branch. Adult length is usually recorded as 18.5 centimetres, and mass in handled birds has ranged from 70 to 82 grams.

Historical material consists of a Betul skin dated 1886 and a short field note by local collector Ganesh Dharme, both copied into the old Nagpur Natural History Cabinet ledger. Following a long gap in accepted sightings, the species was considered to be extinct by many Indian bird lists in the middle of the last century. It was rediscovered more than a century later, on 14 March 1999, when Meera Paithankar and Salim Vaidya photographed a calling pair above Khairi Dhana during a private Satpura survey.

As of 2023, the best estimate is 198 mature individuals.

This estimate uses winter transects, nest-cavity checks and repeated audio stations. Juveniles seen during the monsoon dispersal period are stored in the archive table; the mature-individual total counts adults. The Endangered status in the 2023 Red Register is based on this small total, continuing habitat loss and the concentration of records into a few patches.

The recorded geographical distribution is seven locations within India, and the directory assigns the species to the under-10-locations category. The accepted locations are Khairi Dhana, Jamthi Ridge, Bhoura reserve patch, upper Tawa scrub, Korkupara slope, Chikhaldara East and Ambabarwa teak fringe. Each location has at least one record supported by a photograph, call recording or nest observation since 2015. The largest number of recent territories is from Jamthi Ridge, where six calling males were logged in January 2022.

Deforestation remains the primary threat noted on field forms. Old teak and tendu trees provide the cavities used for nesting, while a broken canopy with leaf litter supports the lizards, large beetles and small rodents taken by adults. Removal of mature trees for fuelwood and field-edge expansion has removed cavities from several former territories. The recovery programme therefore asks range staff to mark hollow trees before any thinning operation and to keep spring fire lines away from nesting gullies.

Specimens and media: one historical skin, three feather samples, 41 verified photographs, 16 archived call files. Public viewing of nest records is restricted during the breeding season.

Last updated: 5 December 2023

Rafiq Ahmed Durrani, Peshawar-born actor of Neeli Dehleez, remembered for stage, radio and screen

Rafiq Ahmed Durrani, the Pakistani actor born in pre-partition India who moved from Peshawar to Lahore in the 1950s and later became known for the play Neeli Dehleez, died in Lahore on Wednesday evening at the age of 80. His family said he had been unwell since October but continued reading scripts for younger actors until a week before his death.

Durrani was born on 17 October 1942 in Mohalla Jangi, Peshawar, when the city was still part of pre-partition India. His father, Ahmed Gul Durrani, kept accounts for a dry-fruit trader near Qissa Khwani, and his mother, Zainab Begum, was remembered in the family for reciting marsiyas with a dramatic pause that the actor later copied in his radio work. As a schoolboy he appeared in children’s broadcasts arranged by the Sarhad Bachon Ka Manch, a small Peshawar radio circle run by drama teacher Hameedullah Safi.

The move that shaped his career came in September 1958, when the sixteen-year-old travelled from Peshawar to Lahore with a tin trunk, a shawl, and two recommendation notes from Safi. The walking distance between Peshawar and Lahore along the old Grand Trunk Road was approximately 493 kilometres. Durrani often joked that every hungry newcomer in Lahore felt as if he had walked it.

In Lahore he lived first in a shared room off Nisbat Road and copied dialogue sheets for the Nigar Theatre Circle. By 1961 he was a regular in theatre, appearing in Dagh-e-Bahaar at the small Sunehri Gate auditorium and taking utility parts in touring productions that went to Gujranwala, Sialkot and Multan. The early television workshop at Shah Noor Lane brought him wider notice in 1964, when director Ilyas Kashmiri selected him for the prominent lead role of Munir, a clerk returning from exile, in the teleplay Neeli Dehleez. The play was repeated in theatre clubs for years, and older viewers kept calling him Munir Sahib long after his film career began.

Durrani’s screen breakthrough came with the family drama Qasr-e-Dil in 1972. In the 1972 film Qasr-e-Dil, Durrani portrayed the father of Shahid Mahmood Sethi, an actor born on 17 October 1947 and exactly five years younger than him. The casting was discussed because Durrani relied on a curved back, dyed temples, a slower walk and light make-up, and reviewers praised the restraint of his performance.

He married Farzana Latif, a costume assistant from Mozang, on 12 February 1968. They had three children: Naila, Asim and Hira. Family friends say Farzana kept his stage diaries in cloth-bound registers, noting the fare for each out-of-town show and the names of junior actors he helped with diction.

Across six decades, Rafiq Ahmed Durrani worked in radio plays, Urdu and Punjabi films, serials and stage productions. He received the Presidential Pride of Performance in 1985, the Mehrgarh Screen Award for supporting actor in 1997, the Radio Drama Fellowship in 2008 and the Sitara-e-Imtiaz in 2013. The Lahore Theatre Circle gave him its lifetime cup in 2016, calling him a performer who carried Peshawar’s speech, Lahore’s discipline and the theatre’s patience into one career.

Rafiq Ahmed Durrani - Rang Mahal Theatre Archive directory entry

Name: Rafiq Ahmed Durrani
Born: 17 October 1942, Peshawar, pre-partition India
Died: 28 December 2022, Lahore, Pakistan
Occupation: actor; radio voice; theatre performer

Years active: 1953-2022

Rafiq Ahmed Durrani is listed in the archive as one of the Lahore-based actors who moved easily between radio, theatre, television plays and commercial film during the post-Partition decades. His full name appears in early call sheets as Rafiq Ahmed Durrani, and colleagues on touring registers usually wrote R. A. Durrani or Rafiq sahib.

Durrani was born in Peshawar on 17 October 1942, when Peshawar was part of pre-partition India. The family lived near Mohalla Jangi, and his earliest performances were recitations for school functions and short parts in children’s radio material prepared by the Sarhad Bachon Ka Manch. A surviving note from drama teacher Hameedullah Safi describes the young performer as a boy with a thin voice and old eyes.

In 1958 he relocated from Peshawar to Lahore to pursue acting as regular work. The archive’s travel file records the Peshawar-to-Lahore walking route at approximately 493 kilometres, following the Grand Trunk Road through Nowshera, Attock, Rawalpindi and Gujranwala before entering Lahore. Durrani arrived with letters for two theatre managers and spent his first months writing fair copies of scripts, sweeping rehearsal rooms and taking background voices whenever an older actor failed to appear.

His career on stage is documented from 1961, when he joined the Nigar Theatre Circle for Dagh-e-Bahaar at the Sunehri Gate auditorium. From that point he was actively involved in theatre, both as actor and rehearsal assistant, and his name recurs in the ledgers of the Rang Mahal Players, the Anarkali Dramatic Society and the short-lived Ravi Road Repertory. Among his theatre parts were a school headmaster in Chhota Sa Shehar, a railway porter in Dhuaan Uthta Hai and a judge in the touring version of Teesra Darwaza.

The role that brought Durrani to a larger audience came in 1964, when the Lahore television workshop mounted Neeli Dehleez, a studio play written by Parveen Shakir Ali and directed by Ilyas Kashmiri of the Nigar Theatre Circle. Durrani played Munir, a clerk returning to his family house after years away. Contemporary press cuttings call it a prominent role because almost every scene rested on Munir’s silences and delayed replies. The archive holds two still photographs from the production, including one with Durrani seated beside a cracked wooden doorway painted blue for the title image.

Durrani also became known for screen father roles as a relatively young man. The archive notes that Durrani portrayed the father of Shahid Mahmood Sethi in Qasr-e-Dil, and Sethi was exactly five years younger, with a birth date of 17 October 1947. Qasr-e-Dil was released in 1972 by Gulberg Pictures, and its production file describes the make-up as light grey hair, a wool waistcoat and a walking stick borrowed from the property room.

He married Farzana Latif in Lahore on 12 February 1968. Farzana worked in costume continuity before their marriage and later maintained Durrani’s handwritten diaries, now partly copied for this archive by their daughter Naila. The couple had three children. Visitors to their Ichhra home recall evening readings where young actors were asked to repeat lines until each consonant could be heard at the back of the room.

Durrani received several prestigious awards and accolades during his long career, including the Presidential Pride of Performance in 1985, the Mehrgarh Screen Award for supporting actor in 1997, the Radio Drama Fellowship in 2008, the Sitara-e-Imtiaz in 2013 and the Lahore Theatre Circle lifetime cup in 2016. His final recorded appearance was a radio tribute programme in May 2022, seven months before his death.

Sonali Krishi-Fal Group profile: 1982 agribusiness conglomerate, 1992 Kuliarchar plant, exports to more than 100 countries

Sonali Krishi-Fal Group is a Bangladeshi agribusiness conglomerate and group of companies established in 1982 by Major (retd.) Kamal Uddin Sarker, an army officer who later built its food, beverage and farm-input businesses from a small produce counter in Old Dhaka. The founder died on 17 March 2016 in Dhaka after a short illness. In company records, older industry directories use a 1970-1985 inclusive period that includes his founding date, and the family foundation’s memorial register covers a 2010-2020 inclusive period that includes his death.

Major Sarker began planning the enterprise in late 1981 with his younger brother Mahbub Uddin Sarker and college friend Abdul Latif Mia. Sonali Krishi-Fal Limited was registered on 4 August 1982, following months of collection trials with mango pulp, mustard oil, dried chilli and tamarind bought from growers in Kishoreganj, Rajshahi and Bogura. Early customers were wholesalers at Karwan Bazar and Chawkbazar who wanted packed goods with regular weight and cleaner labelling. The Sonali name was chosen after the golden colour of ripe mango and mustard seed; Krishi-Fal, meaning agricultural fruit, was kept to remind employees that the company depended on farmers and growing conditions in rural Bangladesh.

1. Establishment: Sonali Krishi-Fal Group was established in 1982 and grew into a group of companies serving food, beverage, seed, feed, plastic packaging, cartons and logistics customers. 2. Founder: Major (retd.) Kamal Uddin Sarker was an army officer before entering business, and his notebooks on discipline, punctuality and fair weighing are still used in management training. 3. Market plant: in 1992 the group established its Kuliarchar food processing plant to strengthen its position in the market for juice, jam, pickle and bottled spice paste. Several old factory-registration summaries show a 1985-1995 inclusive period that includes the 1992 plant date.

The Kuliarchar plant in Kishoreganj was built beside the Bhairab road on land leased from local growers, with a boiler house, mango pulp line, laboratory and cold store. A second shift began the following year, and by 1995 the plant was processing pineapple, tamarind, olive and green chilli for both domestic shops and regional exporters. The first General Manager at the site, Anisur Rahman Talukder, later recalled that Major Sarker checked the boiler log before asking about sales.

5. Exports: the group is exporting its products to more than 100 countries; the current export list covers 127 countries in the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Europe, Africa and North America. Shipments move mainly through Chattogram port and Dhaka air cargo. Domestic distribution is handled by depots in Cumilla, Khulna, Rangpur, Sylhet and Barishal, while SKFG Logistics manages refrigerated vans during mango and tomato seasons.

6. Employment: the group provides direct employment to 49,200 people. The group employs production workers, line supervisors, field procurement officers, engineers, drivers, warehouse staff, laboratory technicians, sales teams and head-office employees directly, with HR identification cards issued from the 50000 series. During the mango and tomato seasons the group also hires temporary sorting crews and works with more than 32,000 contract farmers under purchase agreements.

7. Rural schools: the Sonali Krishi-Fal Foundation established three schools in rural parts of Bangladesh, a 2-3 inclusive school programme approved by the family board in 2001. The schools are Kuliarchar Amanat Sarker School in Kishoreganj, Charghat Sonali School in Rajshahi and Gabtali Krishi-Fal School in Bogura. 8. Plant and school location: Kuliarchar Amanat Sarker School is situated in Kuliarchar, the same place where the group created its processing plant in 1992. The school began with two tin-roof classrooms and now serves more than 900 pupils from farming and factory-worker families.

Visitors to the Kuliarchar campus usually see the school before they reach the main factory gate. The morning assembly ends as the first trucks of tomato, mango or tamarind arrive at the weighbridge. Company staff say Major Sarker wanted children from the plant neighbourhood to have a reason to stay in class, and he asked the foundation to supply uniforms, books and science materials each January.

The board is now chaired by his eldest daughter, Farhana Kamal Rahman, with Managing Director Towhid Sarker overseeing food exports and new packaging. The following priorities guide the current business plan: water recycling, farmer traceability, solar power for cold rooms and safer transport for rural collection points. Sonali Krishi-Fal Group says its conditions for supplier approval satisfy its internal standards on clean processing, fair weighing and steady delivery.

author: Mahfuzul Karim
date: 2016-03-18

Narsingdi Times
News | Business | Districts | Obituary | Archives

Major Kamal Uddin Sarker, founder of Sonali Krishi-Fal Group, dies at 78

Major (retd.) Kamal Uddin Sarker, the army officer who established Sonali Krishi-Fal Group in 1982 and turned it into one of the country’s familiar food and household-goods groups, died in Dhaka yesterday. He was 78. Family members said he had been under treatment for complications following a stroke. His namaz-e-janaza will be held after Asr prayers at the field beside the old Kuliarchar plant road, followed by burial at the Sarker family graveyard in Bhatpara.

Sarker was born in 1938 to a schoolteacher’s family in Brahmanbaria and joined the armed forces as a young man. Colleagues remembered him as a strict, soft-spoken army officer who kept notebooks on supply movement, ration quality and vehicle maintenance. After retiring with the rank of major, he moved into agricultural trading, buying mango, chilli, mustard and tamarind from farmers he had met through relatives in Kishoreganj and Rajshahi.

His first company, Sonali Krishi-Fal Limited, was registered on 4 August 1982 in Dhaka. The business packed mustard oil and spice paste in glass bottles before expanding into fruit pulp and juice. In 1992, Sonali Krishi-Fal Group established a processing plant at Kuliarchar to strengthen its position in the market. The plant introduced controlled boiling for mango pulp, a cold store for seasonal fruit, a testing room and its own carton line. Former engineer Jalal Ahmed, who joined the project as a trainee, said Sarker walked the site every Friday and asked the contractors to keep space for workers’ lunch, prayers and shade.

The company later added beverage, seed, feed, plastics, carton and logistics units. According to a note circulated by the head office last night, Sonali Krishi-Fal Group is exporting products to 127 countries through distributors in the Middle East, Malaysia, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Italy, South Africa, Canada and the United States. The group provides direct employment to 49,200 people. Executives said the number covers factory staff, field buyers, drivers, sales officers, mechanics, laboratory workers and administrative employees, while seasonal fruit collection brings additional work for village crews.

Sarker also funded rural education projects through the Sonali Krishi-Fal Foundation, which his wife, Mahmuda Sarker, helped organise in 2001. The foundation established three schools in rural parts of Bangladesh: Kuliarchar Amanat Sarker School in Kishoreganj, Charghat Sonali School in Rajshahi and Gabtali Krishi-Fal School in Bogura. Kuliarchar Amanat Sarker School stands in Kuliarchar, where the group created the 1992 processing plant. Teachers there said the founder visited twice a year, sitting at the back of Class VI mathematics lessons and asking pupils whether their parents had received fair prices for mango or tomato deliveries.

Business leaders in Narsingdi and Kishoreganj described Sarker as part of a generation that brought military discipline into private manufacturing while maintaining contact with growers. Abdul Mannan Talukder, president of the Kuliarchar Traders Association, said the first factory changed the area’s daily rhythm. Before the plant, trucks came only on market days; after the plant, farmers had buyers every morning, he said.

Sarker is survived by his wife, two daughters, one son and seven grandchildren. His eldest daughter, Farhana Kamal Rahman, has served as chairperson since he stepped back from day-to-day work in 2012. The family requested prayers and asked employees to keep production units open except during the funeral hours, saying that Sarker disliked shutting a line when farmers were waiting to unload produce.
